skill.title: Producer vs consumer decision for missing metadata key
skill.trigger: When multiple functions interact over metadata dicts (consumer merges/reads keys; producers construct info dicts) and a KeyError occurs for a missing key (e.g., 'type'), decide which side to fix.
knowledge: If producers (index.info / ls providers) emit entries that omit the key for some valid objects, prioritize fixing the producer so outputs meet the adapter's contract.
If producers consistently include the key but the consumer reads it without guarding for path-dependent absences, prioritize hardening the consumer (add safe lookups or defaults) to avoid exceptions.
Distinguish by sampling actual info dicts from producers (call index.info or ls(detail=True) on failing paths); presence → consumer fix, absence → producer fix; adjust ranking accordingly.

skill.title: Producer vs consumer decision for not_found sentinel caused by early return
skill.trigger: When a producer dispatches inputs to type-specific calculators and returns a not_found sentinel, while consumers call the producer and fall back on that sentinel, and the producer has an unconditional early return of not_found before its dispatch loop, prioritize the producer fix.
knowledge: If the producer contains an unconditional early return of not_found before its dispatch loop, the sentinel is produced for all inputs; prioritize fixing the producer over consumer-side fallback or calculation fixes.

Distinguish by inspecting the producer's control flow: an early return before the type-dispatch loop proves numeric inputs never reach the calculators, while consumers only receive the sentinel or correct distances and are not the root cause.
Rank the producer first as the root cause; downstream consumers cannot recover valid numeric distance until the producer returns actual computed values, so their defects are secondary.

skill.title: Node-local proxy definition vs shared proxy binding path
skill.trigger: When candidates include a node class's own _proxied cached_property returning a builtin type name and shared proxy-binding/brain functions (e.g., _set_proxied, Proxy), and the unresolved question is whether a wrong type comes from a local builtin-name literal or a shared binding path.
knowledge: Compare node-local _proxied cached_property (builtin getattr literal) with shared proxy-binding functions; a wrong literal inside the node's own property is the first incorrect state and should outrank generic setters/brain paths.

Distinguishing observation: the node's _proxied returns builtins.getattr('str')[0] while neighboring classes return their own type literal; shared proxy binding re-uses that property and is downstream.

Ranking implication: inspect the builtin-name argument in the node's cached_property; if flipping only it fixes inferred type and error text, rank the node-local property first and proxy-binding candidates after.

skill.title: Constructor initialization-order vs helper invoked during construction for premature attribute read
skill.trigger: When candidates are an object's __init__ (or constructor body) and a helper method called from that construction path, and an AttributeError reports an attribute read before assignment, decide whether the first incorrect read is inline in the constructor's pre-assignment span or in the helper.
knowledge: Compare construction call sequence with assignment positions: if the attribute assignment occurs after an inline validation/preparation span and before any helper call that could read it, the constructor's own ordering is the root cause; a helper can only be primary if a call to it appears before the assignment.

Distinguishing observation: repository evidence showing the parameter declaration, a validation/error-message span naming the same config attributes, and the attribute assignment only after that span—with later reads in downstream methods—places the first incorrect read in the constructor's inline span.

Ranking implication: rank the constructor (or the specific __init__) first as the responsible function; rank hypothesized helper methods below unless a call site for them exists before the assignment, and treat downstream methods that read the attribute after assignment as secondary.

skill.title: Shared element-rendering pipeline vs specific delimiter/separator branch for malformed serialization
skill.trigger: When candidates are a shared element-rendering pipeline and a type-specific delimiter/separator branch that assembles the final string, and the malformed output concerns separator spacing, decide whether the fault is in generic child rendering or in that branch's delimiter composition.
knowledge: Compare where delimiter/separator text is assembled: if the generic pipeline only renders element strings and the type-specific branch is the sole place composing separators, the fault lies in that branch, not in shared child rendering.

The element-rendering call returns the raw element string with no punctuation; the explicit single-element branch directly emits the comma and space, so changing that branch fixes the output without affecting other renderers.
Rank the type-specific delimiter branch first over generic rendering helpers or container classes; rank shared pipeline methods below only if they also add separators or formatting.

skill.title: Cache-reset owner vs invalidation helper for stale cache state
skill.trigger: When candidates include an object/manager reset method that clears direct caches and a separate invalidation helper that clears derived state, and the issue reports stale cached values after reset, decide whether the reset method or the helper is responsible.
knowledge: Compare the reset method's body with the helper-call graph: if the method directly clears its primary caches but omits a separate helper call that invalidates derived state, the omission is the first incorrect state—the helper never runs and cannot be the root cause.

Distinguishing observation: the reset method clears owner-level caches inline while derived-state cleanup is a one-line helper invocation; repository evidence of a removed import or missing call to that helper places the defect in the reset method.

Ranking implication: rank the reset/owner method first; rank the invalidation helper after it as a dependency, not the root cause, unless evidence shows the helper is invoked but incomplete; treat state-aliasing constructors as secondary.

skill.title: Helper conditional assignment branch vs caller routing for unbound local
skill.trigger: When candidate roles are an internal AST-walking/transformation helper and the caller-level API that routes nodes into it, and a NameError/UnboundLocalError arises from a helper-local variable assigned only in a conditional branch but consumed unconditionally later.
knowledge: Compare binding scope: if the variable is assigned only inside a specialized conditional branch (e.g., starred-argument handling) and referenced unconditionally later in the same helper, the helper's branch structure is the first incorrect state; caller routing is downstream.

Distinguishing observation: grep shows the assignment line inside the branch and later unconditional uses or yields in the same function, while the caller merely extends or recurses over helper results without touching that variable.
Ranking implication: rank the internal helper first; rank caller/API candidates after it unless evidence shows the offending input never entered the helper.

skill.title: Enclosing container vs responsible nested helper for wrong transformed values
skill.trigger: When candidates include an enclosing cached/collection property whose body defines nested parse/transform closures, and the unresolved question is whether a value/output defect belongs to the outer property or to one of those nested helpers.
knowledge: Separate orchestration from transformation: if the outer property merely iterates and assembles results while nested closures perform coordinate/field conversion, compare those nested helpers against the outer property rather than treating the property as the leaf fault location.

Distinguishing observation: the faulty assignment or corrected formula appears inside a nested closure body (e.g., point rotation update or raw coordinate to page-space field mapping), while the outer property only invokes that closure over each item.

Ranking implication: when a container candidate ranks first but evidence shows nested transform/parse helpers contain the arithmetic/assignment that changed, rank the direct nested helper(s) above the container and above sibling derived collections, because this is a helper-granularity rather than top-level property defect.

skill.title: Registry registration swaps predicate/guard and handler/transform callables causing intended handler never to run
skill.trigger: A registry or plugin registration call binds two callable roles (a predicate/guard and a handler/transform) but passes them in the wrong order, producing the observable symptom that nodes/objects that should be handled/transformed remain unchanged (the intended handler is never invoked). Apply when a project has a registration API that accepts a predicate/guard and a handler/transform and registered targets are silently unmodified or missing expected side effects.
knowledge: Locate the registry API signature (definition) and confirm the formal argument order and expected types/returns for the predicate and the handler (e.g., predicate should return a boolean/match object; transform/handler usually returns None and mutates or returns a replacement).

Search the codebase for other call sites of the same register function to establish the common argument order and canonical usage patterns (positional vs keyword). Prefer examples that use keyword arguments as a correct precedent.

At a suspicious call site, compare the names and shapes of the two callables passed: predicates are typically small boolean checks (is_* / matches_*) and return truthy values; handlers/transformers often perform side effects or return None. A mismatch in return shape is a strong indicator of swapped roles.

Inspect the registry dispatch implementation (the code that later invokes predicate and handler) to see which callable is called as predicate (expected to return truthiness) and which as handler (expected to perform mutation/return replacement). Tracing one registered entry through dispatch helps confirm the swap.

Create a minimal runtime reproduction (unit test or small script) that registers the two callables and triggers dispatch; verify whether the predicate or handler was invoked. Swapping arguments at the call site to the registry should toggle the reproduction's behavior and quickly confirm the error.

When fixing, prefer using explicit keyword arguments at registration sites (e.g., predicate=..., handler=... or transform=...), or modify the register API to accept a single small named tuple/struct to avoid positional ambiguity.

Add or update tests that assert the observable side-effects of registration (e.g., that decorated nodes are transformed or that registered handlers run for matching inputs) so future swaps are detected.

If the handler returns None when called as a predicate, look for silent failure modes: the registry may treat None as falsy, causing the entry to never match. Conversely, if the predicate is used as a handler, verify it doesn't abruptly return non-handler values or raise when invoked as a handler.

skill.title: Constructor/factory unconditionally invokes or registers an implementation-specific helper when an optional parameter is supplied
skill.trigger: A producer/constructor or factory (or a context-manager's __init__/__aenter__) raises AttributeError during construction or enter because it unconditionally calls an instance helper or schedules a callback (e.g. self.update(...), loop.call_later(..., self.method, ...)) for a supplied optional/non-None parameter, while the chosen implementation branch (version-gated subclass or alternate implementation) does not define that helper.
knowledge: Search the constructor/factory and nearby version- or branch-gating code (sys.version_info, feature flags, conditional class definitions). Look for unconditional calls like self.update(...), self._reschedule(...), or scheduling callbacks referencing self.<method> when an optional argument is provided.

For each implementation branch, verify the presence of the invoked helper method on that implementation (method defined on the same class, inherited from a base, or added by a shim). If one branch lacks the method, the constructor call is unsafe.

Reproduce the AttributeError and inspect the stack to see the missing attribute name; trace which class was instantiated to confirm the branch mismatch (e.g. subclassing asyncio.Timeout vs local Timeout).

Check factory functions (timeout()/timeout_at()) and constructors for inconsistent initialization of state (e.g. default None vs sentinel values) that change which code path runs and whether scheduling or immediate invocation occurs.

Fix patterns: (a) implement the helper as a no-op/shim on the implementations that lack it; (b) guard the call with hasattr()/getattr(..., None) or use a safe scheduling wrapper that captures missing attribute; (c) move scheduling to enter-time where the implementation guarantees the helper exists; (d) ensure the factory selects the implementation that supports the requested optional behavior.

Look for closely related diffs in changelogs or version-dependent code paths (CHANGES, conditional imports). Tests often reveal the mismatch: add a minimal unit test that constructs the object with the optional param under each gated configuration to prevent regressions.

skill.title: Local representation object read before assignment in serialization/write path
skill.trigger: A writer or serializer function raises UnboundLocalError (or behaves as if a local representation is missing) because a locally-constructed representation object (e.g., HDU, HDUList, writer, buffer) is assigned only on some control-flow paths or after a call site but is consumed unconditionally (or earlier) later in the function.
knowledge: Start from the traceback and identify the first function in project code that appears in the stack (e.g., write(), to_fits(), serialize()). Note the local variable name reported (e.g., 'hdu', 'hdul', 'writer', 'buffer').

Search the function for places where that local representation is assigned. Check whether assignment occurs inside a conditional branch (if/else), after an early return, or only in some exception-handling paths.

Inspect the control-flow ordering: ensure that any calls which use the representation (e.g., hdul.writeto(...), writer.write(...), buffer.getvalue()) occur only after a guaranteed assignment. Look for uses that occur before the assignment or outside the branch that assigns it.

Check for related ordering bugs where preparatory conversions are performed after a write call (e.g., header_to_fits or building fitskwargs happens after hdul.writeto). Reordering such preparatory steps earlier often fixes the use-before-assignment.

Use AST or simple static checks to flag functions named like write/writeto/serialize that reference a variable X but have assignment statements for X only under If/Except nodes: candidate formation heuristics include function names (write, writeto, to_fits, serialize), modules under io/, and local names matching patterns (hdu, hdul, fh, writer, buffer).

When proposing fixes prefer making the assignment unconditional (initialize with a safe default) or restructure branching so every path assigns the representation before use. Avoid duplicating side-effecting construction—extract a small helper that returns the representation, called before any use.

Add small reproducible tests that call the write/serialize path with minimal inputs to exercise both branches. Confirm that the variable is defined and used only after successful construction in all branches.

If the variable is created by calling external constructors (e.g., fits.PrimaryHDU, writer factory), ensure those constructors are invoked before any write calls; for APIs that accept either a pre-built object or raw data, handle both entry forms explicitly so the local representation is always defined.

skill.title: Dynamic-programming cost-matrix arithmetic or backtrack neighbor-index misuse causes incorrect path reconstruction
skill.trigger: A consumer (backtracker) that reconstructs an optimal DP warping/path returns a path that does not reach or map to the expected terminal indices for small deterministic inputs, and the same codebase contains a producer that fills an explicit cost/distance matrix using neighbor lookups and arithmetic (explicit i±k, j±k indices, min/max choice, or sign operations). This structural pairing (cost_matrix producer + backtracker consumer) makes off-by-one neighbor-index mistakes or incorrect matrix-update signs/operands likely.
knowledge: Reproduce with tiny, deterministic inputs and assert the expected terminal mapping; failing on small inputs makes DP-indexing or arithmetic errors likely.

Dump/print the full filled cost/distance matrix for the failing input. Confirm whether the matrix values at and near the terminal cell reflect cumulative costs consistent with the chosen distance function.

Verify the distance computation implementation for each distance mode (e.g., 'absolute_difference' vs 'square_difference') — ensure the correct elements are used (sequence1[i-1] vs sequence1[i+1]) and that the expression uses the intended arithmetic and sign.
Check matrix boundary initialization (first row/column, sentinel values). Incorrect initialization can divert backtracking away from the expected corner.

Inspect the matrix update line(s): confirm the correct use of min (or max when appropriate), and that operands reference the intended neighbors (i-1,j), (i,j-1), (i-1,j-1) rather than (i+1, j-1) or other incorrect offsets.

Step through the backtrack consumer for the failing example, logging the chosen neighbor at each step. Compare the neighbor-selection comparisons against the matrix contents to detect mistaken index arithmetic or reversed comparison logic.
Look for off-by-one mistakes: places where code uses i+1 or j+1 when it should use i-1 or j-1 (or vice versa). Search the function for explicit ±1 index arithmetic and audit each occurrence.

Check whether comparisons in backtracking accidentally compare wrong cells (e.g., comparing distance_matrix[i, j+1] instead of distance_matrix[i, j-1]) or use subtraction/inversion where accumulation is required.

Add a focused unit test that computes the cost matrix and expected path for a minimal pair (e.g., lengths 3 and 4). Use assertions on both the final cell value and the reconstructed path to prevent regressions.

If index arithmetic is complex, introduce small helper functions or named offsets (DIAGONAL, UP, LEFT) and add assertions that neighbor coordinates are within bounds before use to avoid silent misuse.

skill.title: Iterable values short-circuited to whole-string during command-line rendering
skill.trigger: A producer/renderer function that builds command-line strings from a mapping returns a cmd string containing Python-style container representations (e.g. "[1, 2, 'foo']") for dict values that are lists/tuples. Applicable when the renderer contains an isinstance(..., Iterable) or similar branch (or a single-line short-circuit) that runs before explicit scalar/string handling or before element-wise iteration, causing containers to be treated as atomic and stringified rather than flattened into CLI tokens.
knowledge: Locate the small formatting/renderer functions that convert dict entries into CLI fragments (common names: interpolate, to_str, _; search for patterns like "--{k}" or building a result string while iterating dict.items()).

Search repository for suspicious type-checks and short-circuits: "isinstance(..., Iterable)", "for n, i in enumerate(v)", and one-line branches that append f"{v}" or f"--{k} {v} ". These lines often indicate a container was treated atomically.
Reproduce quickly by calling the renderer with a mapping containing a list/tuple value and inspecting the returned cmd string to see whether the list appears as a repr or as expanded tokens.

Check ordering of type checks: ensure strings (str, bytes) are handled before Iterable, or use Sequence with explicit exclusion of str/bytes. Prefer explicit element-iteration for Sequence-like containers instead of relying on broad Iterable checks.

If a one-line short-circuit (e.g. result += f"--{k} {v} ") exists in an Iterable branch, remove it and replace with element-wise logic that escapes items and/or repeats the flag per element, matching the intended CLI format.

Verify escaping, spacing, and flag-repetition semantics (e.g., "--k a --k b" vs "--k a b") and add a unit test that passes heterogeneous list items (ints, strings) to ensure correct flattening and escaping.

Also inspect nearby small helpers and call sites (Context.resolve_str, DataResolver.resolve) to confirm the renderer's contract: whether callers expect a flattened token string or a single scalar; correct the renderer rather than callers when the renderer violates that contract.

skill.title: Recursive descendant search with inverted match predicate or unintended result reversal
skill.trigger: A consumer (iterator/helper) returns descendant elements that do not match the requested type(s) and/or returns them in reverse of source order. The helper implements a recursive scan over a node's children with an explicit type test and either yields results or builds a collection before returning.
knowledge: Reproduce quickly with a minimal tree: build a small node/children structure and call the helper to observe which node types are returned and in what order.

Inspect the matching predicate: confirm whether the code uses inclusion (if element.type in requested_names: yield/collect) versus exclusion (if element.type not in requested_names: ...). An inverted condition will return the opposite set of nodes.

Check the recursion guard separately: verify which node types are considered containers and whether recursion should descend into matched nodes. Ensure recursion condition (e.g., element.type in CONTAINERS) is using the intended membership test and not inverted in the same way as the match test.

Look for accidental final-order inversions: search for list(...)[::-1], reversed(list(...)), .reverse(), or post-order traversal that is later reversed. Such code may have been added to address a different traversal expectation but can invert the desired source order.

Distinguish pre-order vs post-order semantics: decide whether the API expects matches yielded before recursing into children (pre-order) or after (post-order). Align the implementation and callers to the chosen convention rather than patching order via a final reversal.

Generator vs list semantics: if the helper yields (generator) but callers convert to a list or rely on order, be careful when switching to list-building to avoid introducing an unintended reversal step.

Examine all thin callers: find small delegating iterator functions that pass different requested type-names to the helper. Confirm they rely on preserved source order and only expect matching node kinds.

Write a small unit test that asserts both the set and the order of returned nodes for a few representative trees (including nested container nodes and matched nodes). Use that test to verify fixes and prevent regressions.

If fixing, prefer correcting the matching predicate and recursion condition (e.g., switch 'not in' to 'in' or vice versa as intended) and remove any ad-hoc reversal at the end. If reversed order is intentionally required by other callers, document the helper's order contract and centralize any required ordering transformation at call sites.

When the traversal interacts with structural containers (e.g., function/class suites), validate whether container nodes themselves should be considered matches or only their child nodes; mismatching this expectation is a common source of inverted inclusion logic.

skill.title: Serialized representation prints constructor fields in wrong order (constructor ↔ serializer ordering mismatch)
skill.trigger: A consumer prints or otherwise serializes an object (for example, an Exception's __str__/__repr__ or a custom to-string routine) and the textual output shows fields in a different order than callers supplied to the constructor. Applicable when the type stores input parameters as attributes or via Exception.args and implements an explicit serializer/formatter that composes those attributes or uses the args tuple.
knowledge: Open the class's __init__ and verify parameter names and assignment sites: confirm each constructor parameter is stored into the intended attribute (e.g., self.code = code, self.text = text) and watch for copy-paste or reversed assignments.

Inspect any use of Exception base-class behavior: if the class sets self.args or calls super().__init__(...), check that the args tuple ordering matches the constructor parameter order and how the serializer consumes args (by position).

Examine the serializer (__str__, __repr__, to_string, or format call): find the format string or f-string and confirm the order of arguments passed to .format()/% or the order of attributes referenced in the f-string; ensure they correspond to the constructor's semantic order.

If formatting uses an attribute tuple or list (e.g., tuple(self.args) or self.<fields>), print or log the tuple contents to confirm their order at runtime — a quick repro (construct and print) demonstrates whether the storage or formatting is faulty.
Search the repository for other classes/exceptions with similar patterns (copy-paste of format strings or assignments) to detect recurring mistakes and to find canonical implementations to copy.

Add a small unit test that constructs the object with known distinct values and asserts the exact serialized string; when fixing, update or add tests to lock the intended ordering and prevent regressions.

When ambiguity exists about the public API ordering (constructor docs, call sites, or tests disagree), prioritize the documented/canonical order and update either the constructor, the serializer, or the API documentation consistently.

skill.title: Mutator method iterates targets but never updates state (missing or misplaced assignment)
skill.trigger: A public mutator/producer method (state owner role) is invoked and callers observe no persistent change to the object's state (attribute still absent or unchanged). The method contains iteration or computation that suggests a mutation should occur, but there is no observable assignment or the assignment lies outside the function's executed body (e.g., misplaced after a return, outside indentation, or implementation/docstring ordering error).
knowledge: Confirm the observable: reproduce minimal case that calls the mutator and inspects the owning object's persistent attribute/state (not just a wrapper view).
Search the target function for assignment patterns that change the state (e.g., .set(...), dict/attribute assignments, list appends). If none exist, the mutator is likely missing the assignment.

Check for misplaced/unused code: look for implementation text placed outside the function body (indentation errors), code after an early return, or the implementation accidentally moved relative to the function's docstring so the executable body contains only a literal/return.

Compare with a working sibling or reference implementation (e.g., remove_class versus add_class) to see the expected mutation pattern and the exact call/assignment used to update state; this often reveals what assignment was omitted or moved.
Inspect decorators and aliasing/mirroring utilities: these can copy or rebind a broken implementation to other API names (so both snake_case and camelCase may mirror the same defect).

Use grep/AST searches for common assignment sites (e.g., "set('class'", "attr( 'class' )", "= ", ".set(") and for suspicious patterns like a string literal immediately following def that might indicate docstring/implementation ordering problems.

When code appears present but not executed, run quick instrumentation (print/log or a debugger) inside the function to see whether the loop runs and whether the assignment statement executes; unreachable assignment indicates ordering/return/indentation issues.
If implementation is moved or missing, prefer a minimal fix that restores the assignment into the executed body and add a unit test reproducing the no-op to prevent regression.

skill.title: Validation exception swallowed at parser/argument-action boundary and replaced with sentinel
skill.trigger: A user-provided input is validated/compiled by a producer (e.g., an argparse Action, constructor, or validator) and the validation raises a domain-specific exception (e.g., re.error). The producer's try/except handler catches that exception and assigns a sentinel/default value (e.g., None, '') to a local value or namespace field, or returns early, so the downstream consumer proceeds without signaling an error to the user.
knowledge: Search for try/except blocks around validation/compilation calls (e.g., re.compile, json.loads, int(), parsing helpers) inside argparse Action subclasses, custom validators, or option-parsing helpers.

Look specifically for patterns that set a namespace attribute or field inside an except block (e.g., setattr(namespace, dest, None) or namespace.dest = None) or that return from an Action/constructor inside an except instead of raising or re-raising.

Check whether the correct exception type (e.g., re.error) is being caught narrowly or whether a broad Exception is used; broad catches often hide the original cause and are likely sites of silent failure.

Trace the producer→consumer chain: find where the parsed option is wired (make_parser / add_argument wiring) and where the consumer reads it (main, generate, or downstream processing). Confirm how consumers treat sentinel values (None/''), and whether they ignore, default, or silently skip behavior when sentinel is present.

Inspect whether argparse.ArgumentError or SystemExit would be appropriate at parse time; if an argparse Action should reject the value, prefer raising argparse.ArgumentError to let the parser produce a user-visible error, or re-raise the validation exception to be handled at a top-level CLI driver.

When repository tests exist, search for unit tests that assert invalid input causes an error (pytest.raises or CLI exit codes). Lack of such tests around invalid inputs is an indicator that swallowed validation may be untested.

For triage, look for logging/warning calls in except blocks; sometimes maintainers log and return instead of raising—decide whether the intended behavior is silent degradation or visible failure by checking CLI contracts and README/usage docs.

If fixing, prefer explicit error propagation or controlled user-visible failures at the boundary (raise argparse.ArgumentError, call parser.error, or re-raise) and add tests asserting that invalid inputs produce the expected error behavior.

skill.title: Per-item local value consumed (appended/returned) without a producer binding in data-preparation loop
skill.trigger: A function raises NameError or UnboundLocalError during data-preparation because inside a per-item loop a local value (producer) that should be constructed/assigned (e.g., via a helper call or assignment) is missing or not executed, yet a consumer (e.g., list.append(local), yield/return, or downstream use) unconditionally reads it.
knowledge: Start at the consumer site (append/return/use) and scan the surrounding loop to find where the local value should be produced; confirm there is no prior assignment on all control-flow paths leading to the consumer.

Look for an immediately-previously-removed or dedented block: accidental deletion or indentation errors commonly remove a producer call (e.g., a build_x_from_trace invocation) while leaving the consumer line.

Check for gating logic: the production may be inside a conditional (if/try/for) whose condition is never true or accidentally uses the wrong variable name/loop index, leaving some iterations without assignment.

Search for a helper/factory function (producer) that previously returned the value (e.g., build_call_data_from_trace). Confirm the caller still invokes that helper in the loop and that the helper's signature/return hasn't changed.

If the consumer is unconditional, consider adding a guard or default binding before use (temporary fix) to reproduce and narrow the missing-path; e.g., assert producer was run or skip append when value is None/missing.
Inspect recent diffs or commits around the loop to detect an accidental removal of the producer call; correlate with tests or examples that exercised the code path.
For reproducing, construct a minimal per-item input (one trace element) to trigger the failing iteration and print/trace control flow to see whether the producer branch ran.

If the producer should come from another module, confirm that the module-level API still returns the expected value and that any refactor didn't rename the variable or change responsibilities between producer/consumer.

skill.title: Handler class missing required class-level dispatch/registration entry points after base-class or registration removal
skill.trigger: A router/dispatcher raises AttributeError naming a class attribute (e.g., setup_class, dispatch) when invoking a service/handler class; the project uses a pattern where the dispatcher expects class-level entry points on the handler class (rather than on an instance). The handler class definition either no longer subclasses the framework base that supplies those classmethods or its class-level registration/adapter was removed or renamed.
knowledge: Start from the exact AttributeError text — it names the missing attribute and the class; grep for that attribute name and the handler class to find where the dispatcher calls it.

Inspect the handler class definition for its base classes. If the base that previously provided the classmethod is absent, restoring inheritance or providing an adapter classmethod often fixes the contract.

Search the framework core for the provider of the class-level methods (e.g., BaseResponse.setup_class / dispatch). Confirm whether those methods are classmethods/staticmethods or expected as class attributes.

Trace the callsite in the router/registration layer that invokes the class-level method. Confirm the router is intentionally calling on the class (not on an instance) and look for registration/initialization sequences that expect class-level hooks.

If base-class inheritance was intentionally removed, implement the required class-level methods on the new class to forward to the framework contract, or add a small adapter that preserves the same class-level API expected by the dispatcher.
Check for renames: sometimes the method was renamed in the base class but callers still use the old name; align names or add compatibility shims with deprecation comments/tests.
Confirm there are no metaclass or decorator changes that would hide or replace class attributes (e.g., replacing class with function that returns instance).

After code changes, run a minimal repro that triggers the dispatcher (not only unit tests of action handlers) to ensure the class-level registration/dispatch path is exercised and the AttributeError is resolved.
When multiple services share the same dispatch mechanism, search for the same pattern in other service handler classes to ensure the fix preserves the framework contract across the codebase.

skill.title: Local accumulator used before initialization (setdefault / assignment order bug)
skill.trigger: A function/method raises UnboundLocalError for a local accumulator (list/set/dict) because code on the failing path performs mutation or membership checks (e.g. .append(), value not in X, X.add(), X.update()) against a local name that is only assigned later or only on other control-flow paths; often the intended initialization uses context.setdefault(...) or an assignment that is placed after the consumer.
knowledge: Search for nearby .append(), .add(), .extend(), membership checks ("in"/"not in"), or reads of a collection variable (common consumer patterns) and then look upward/earlier in the same scope for an assignment or setdefault that should have initialized it.

Pay attention to context retrieval helpers (get_context(), context variable, entry/context dict) combined with context.setdefault("key", []) patterns. If setdefault is later in the function (or guarded), the variable may be referenced before assignment.

Inspect control-flow: early returns, guards, or conditional branches that can skip the initialization statement but still execute the consumer. Trace through the simple execution order in the function rather than only scanning for variable names.

In shared mixins/handlers, prefer locating the shared consumer (e.g. _add_tag) rather than per-namespace end/start handlers—consumers in mixins often manipulate per-entry context and are common causes of this bug.

When an UnboundLocalError names a specific local name, grep for that name and then look for patterns where the name is later assigned from context.setdefault or assigned inside a different branch; reorder initialization before any possible use or use context.get/setdefault at the point of consumption.
Consider tests (small feed snippets) that exercise the element being processed so you can trigger the exact control-flow and confirm whether initialization is skipped on some paths.

skill.title: Lookup/normalization helper returns values outside its documented sentinel-or-tuple contract
skill.trigger: A consumer (e.g., a save/reducer or dispatcher) immediately unpacks or branches on a producer's helper return value assuming it is either a sentinel (None) or a specific tuple (e.g., (module, name)), but the producer sometimes returns other types (raw module object, bare string, or the original object) because it delegates to upstream resolution or has multiple unsynchronized return paths. The mismatch causes TypeError or incorrect control flow when callers treat the value as the expected tuple/sentinel.
knowledge: Reproduce with dynamic/interactive objects (objects defined in __main__, enums, slotted classes, lambdas) which exercise module/qualname resolution and expose nonstandard return paths.

Audit the helper implementation: list every return site and ensure each return value matches the documented contract (explicit sentinel or tuple). Grep for returns of the input object, module_name strings, raw module objects, or pass-through returns.

Inspect upstream resolvers and compatibility shims (e.g., functions that compute module_name or attribute access fallbacks). They may return strings or objects that the helper must normalize; track where values originate (_whichmodule, fallback __getattr__ implementations).

Audit all callers: find code that unpacks the helper's return or tests only for truthiness rather than type (e.g., `module, name = helper(obj)` or `if helper(obj):`). Replace unsafe unpacking with guarded patterns or explicit type checks (e.g., check isinstance(ret, tuple) before unpacking).

Prefer normalizing at the producer: make the helper always return the documented types (None or (module, name)). If the helper must expose additional diagnostics, return a structured wrapper object or split the API so callers opt-in to extended info.

If changing the helper's return type is breaking or risky, add defensive guards at callers (isinstance checks, explicit handling of strings/module objects) as a compatibility mitigation while refactoring the producer.

Add unit tests that assert the helper's contract across edge cases (module not in sys.modules, dynamically created modules, attribute-not-found, enum members and slotted classes). Include tests that exercise both producer and consumer behavior to prevent regressions.
Document the helper's contract in docstrings and consider runtime assertions (or type hints + optional checks) to make contract violations fail fast and produce clearer diagnostics.

When normalizing values that are module names (strings), decide whether callers expect module objects or module names; prefer returning the same concrete type the callers expect (or change callers together) and ensure lookups use sys.modules safely.

After fixes, run end-to-end scenarios (pickling of interactive functions, enums, dynamic classes, classes with __slots__) and update compatibility-shim tests to confirm no unintended semantic changes.

skill.title: Sequence-type contract mismatch between fragment producers and cell-combiner
skill.trigger: A rendering/printing function (consumer) raises a TypeError like "can only concatenate list (not \"tuple\") to list" (or the converse) because it concatenates or extends concatenated fragments assuming a concrete sequence type (e.g., list) while one or more fragment producers (ETA/text widget, monitor producer, spinner/player) return a different sequence type (e.g., tuple) or otherwise heterogeneous iterables. Applicable when the visual composition pipeline builds fragments from multiple producers and uses concrete concatenation (sum with a start value, list + other) or in-place extension without normalizing producer outputs.
knowledge: Reproduce with minimal rendering path that triggers the specific widget (ETA/elapsed/stat) so producers produce the problematic fragment shape (e.g., exercise ETA code paths that return an empty/placeholder tuple or yield tuple literals).

Search for combiners that rely on concrete sequence starts or use sum(..., start) for concatenation; grep for patterns: "sum(.*, )", "list +", "+= []", or usage of list concatenation in print/join helpers. These are sensitive to start-type mismatch.

Audit every fragment producer feeding the combiner: list all return sites and generator yields and verify each returns the same concrete sequence type or at least an iterable the combiner can accept. Pay attention to small/edge-case returns (empty variants, sentinel values) that may use different literal constructors ((), []).

Prefer normalization at the consumer: convert incoming fragments via list(fragment) or use itertools.chain.from_iterable(fragments) to avoid depending on the fragment's concrete sequence type. Replace sum(fragments, ()) or sum(fragments, []) with list(chain.from_iterable(fragments)) or an explicit loop to accumulate consistently typed elements.

If normalizing at the producer, ensure helper/docstring states the concrete contract (returns list of cells or iterable of strings) and make all returns follow it (including empty cases). Avoid returning heterogeneously typed empty values (use [] consistently instead of () for empty cell lists if callers expect list).

Add defensive runtime assertions near the consumer (e.g., assert isinstance(fragment, (list, tuple, collections.abc.Iterable))) and clear error messages that include producer identity when types differ to make future regressions easier to diagnose.

Write unit tests that exercise both normal and edge-case branches of fragment producers (empty ETA/unavailable ETA, zero/negative timings) and verify the combiner accepts their outputs without raising TypeError. Include tests that intentionally return tuples to ensure the consumer still handles them after normalization.

When fixing, check nearby related helpers (timing/eta, spinner/player, monitor text) for literal tuple usage (e.g., p = (0.,), returns of singletons) and harmonize their empty/placeholder shapes to the chosen contract.

Consider changing combiner implementations to accept any iterable-of-iterables and to avoid using addition for concatenation (addition is sensitive to concrete type). Use chain.from_iterable or explicit extend semantics on a fresh list accumulator.

After changes, run end-to-end rendering scenarios with different backends (tty, jupyter, non_tty) and configuration permutations that toggle widgets to ensure no other producer emits an incompatible shape.

skill.title: Conversion helper unconditionally casts non-null fields to string
skill.trigger: Callers or tests observe that primitives (numbers, booleans) produced by a producer become strings when consumed: type assertions fail or numeric operations break. The code path contains a conversion/serialization helper that iterates fields of a structured input (namedtuple, object, or mapping) and assigns result[field] = str(value) or otherwise formats every non-null value without preserving native types.
knowledge: Focus search on conversion/serialization helpers that map structured inputs to dicts/JSON: functions named *to_dict, to_json, serialize, dump, asdict, or similar wrappers around a structured object (namedtuple, dataclass, record).

Look for blanket stringification patterns in the helper body: explicit str(value), map(str, ...), f-strings or format() applied to every field, or unconditional calls to repr/__str__ for field values.
Confirm expectations by locating callers and tests: unit tests that assert numeric types or consumers that perform numeric operations reveal whether native types should be preserved.

Distinguish presentation-layer formatting from data representation: if helper is used both for CLI formatting and for machine-readable outputs (JSON, programmatic callers), prefer preserving native types in the representation helper and applying string formatting only at the presentation boundary.

Check None-handling rationale: authors sometimes call str(v) to avoid None -> TypeError in formatting; prefer explicit None checks (e.g., if v is None: keep None) or use conditional formatting only when producing textual output.

Repair patterns: remove the unconditional str() and assign the raw value; apply type-preserving serialization (json.dumps) at the outermost output; or, when needed, selectively format only fields intended for display while leaving data fields unchanged.

When uncertain, reproduce with a minimal snippet (construct the structured input with numeric fields and call the helper) and run relevant unit tests to validate that fixes preserve types and do not break presentation consumers.

skill.title: Data-sniffing termination predicate misclassifies completeness for finite known domains
skill.trigger: A function computes a boolean 'confidence' or 'complete' flag about whether it has observed all possible values and returns False for inputs whose full value universe is knowable up front (for example, numpy boolean arrays or objects with an explicit enumeration like pandas.Categorical.categories). The code has per-type fastpath branches or an iterative aggregation (e.g., a level_set compared to an expected set) that determine the return value.
knowledge: Check per-type fastpaths first: for types that explicitly enumerate their domain (e.g., pandas.Categorical.categories) or have a bounded dtype (e.g., boolean dtype), the branch should both record the canonical levels and return the completion flag consistently (declare completeness) rather than deferring to iterative aggregation.

Verify return-value consistency across branches: ensure branches that set an explicit levels list or canonical level_set return True (complete) unless NA handling or other contract reasons require otherwise; look for accidental inversions (return False where True was intended).

Inspect iterative aggregation logic for side effects: clearing, resetting, or overwriting the accumulated level_set on encountering certain values (e.g., booleans) can lose previously-seen information and change the final equality test. Prefer idempotent updates or explicit canonicalization rather than destructive clears triggered by value checks.

Use canonical representations for expected full domains when comparing: e.g., compare against a well-defined frozenset or a module-level constant (frozenset({True, False})) to avoid ordering or identity pitfalls and make equality checks explicit and easy to test.

Be explicit about NA handling and provenance: if a per-type detector (like pandas.Categorical) already handles NAs, document and preserve that contract. If NA_action filters values before aggregation, ensure branches that short-circuit completeness incorporate the same NA semantics.

Add unit tests that exercise finite-domain inputs and their edge cases: numpy arrays dtyped as bool with both values present, pandas.Categorical with & without NA, and mixed-type iterables. Tests should assert that sniff/complete returns True when the domain is fully known and false only when truly ambiguous or incomplete.

When changing fastpaths or aggregator logic, add regression tests that cover previously short-circuited branches as well as the iterative path so a refactor cannot invert or remove a completeness declaration silently.
When jettisoning a fastpath's early-return in favor of a unified aggregation, document why and maintain explicit checks to preserve the semantics that known-finite domains are complete.

skill.title: Document/DOM consumed without parsing/initialization in content-processing pipeline
skill.trigger: A NameError or UnboundLocalError occurs because a consumer (e.g., link-rewriting, DOM traversal, or make-links-absolute) dereferences a local document/DOM value that should have been created by a parsing/initialization call (producer). The parsing/initialization call is absent, removed, or executed only on some control-flow paths (for example due to early returns for particular file extensions, conditional branches, or exception handlers), and the consumer is unguarded.
knowledge: Start at the consumer site that raises NameError/UnboundLocalError (calls on document/DOM). Confirm the exact identifier and whether it is a local value expected to be produced by a parser call.

Search nearby code for parsing/initialization calls (e.g., lxml.html.fragment_fromstring, lxml.html.fromstring, parser.parse, html5lib.parse) and verify they are executed on all control-flow paths that reach the consumer.

Inspect conditional guards and early returns (e.g., fast-return for certain file extensions like '.php'); these often skip parsing and leave the consumer uninitialized. Ensure parsing is performed before or not bypassed by such returns.

Check exception handling around parsing: removed try/except blocks, swallowed ParserError returns, or recently deleted branches can remove both the producer and its fallback behavior. If parsing used to return an empty document on 'Document is empty', confirm similar fallback remains.

Look for accidental deletion/dedentation: producer calls are commonly removed in refactors while leaving the consumer. Compare with older commits or file history to identify the missing producer call.

If parsing may legitimately fail, ensure the consumer is guarded (e.g., only call document.* when document is truthy) or the parser returns a safe empty document object; prefer moving parsing earlier and handling ParserError explicitly.

When the producer is in a different helper/module, verify the call site still invokes that helper and the helper's signature/return contract hasn't changed (renames or moved responsibilities can break initialization).

Reproduce with a minimal content sample that exercises the non-parsed path (simple HTML, or file type that triggers early return). Add temporary logging or assertions before the consumer to observe whether the parser ran and what value was bound.

For fixes, either restore or add the parsing/initialization call before the consumer, reintroduce robust exception handling and fallbacks, or add a guard around the consumer so it only runs when a valid document is present.

When applicable, add unit/integration tests that exercise both normal parsing and the edge cases (empty document, parser error, file-type fast returns) to prevent regressions that remove the producer again.

skill.title: Public facade forwards/binds arguments to wrong semantic roles (foreground/background/flags)
skill.trigger: A public-facing function (consumer of caller-supplied parameters) emits KeyError, applies the wrong semantic mapping (foreground vs background/ highlight), inverts capability/flag behavior, or produces incorrect/missing cleanup (reset) because one or more parameters were forwarded or bound to the wrong parameter names/positions before first use (e.g., passed positionally into a helper or lookup where roles differ). Applicable when the module contains simple role-to-code lookup tables (state owners) and the facade forwards inputs directly into those tables or a capability gate.
knowledge: Reproduce minimal failing calls: exercise the facade with foreground, background (on_color), attrs, and capability flags (no_color/force_color) both by position and by explicit keyword to observe differences and KeyError traces.

Inspect the facade signature and each occurrence where it forwards arguments to helpers or lookup tables; prefer named-argument forwarding (param=param) to preserve semantic binding instead of positional forwarding.
Locate first-use sites of caller values: check which lookup table (e.g., COLORS vs HIGHLIGHTS) is indexed for each parameter and confirm the table identity aligns with the parameter's semantic role.

Verify capability gating flags are passed with correct parameter names to the capability checker (no_color vs force_color) — swapped names invert behavior and can silence or force formatting incorrectly.

Check attribute application ordering and cleanup: confirm attribute codes are applied in the intended SGR stacking order (reverse-order bugs can change effective styling) and ensure RESET (or equivalent cleanup) is appended to the assembled string.

Greps and quick checks: search for positional forwarding patterns (calls that pass variables without names), fmt_str % (HIGHLIGHTS[<var>] vs COLORS[<var>]), and capability gate calls where boolean args appear in the wrong order; add unit tests asserting colored('text', color='cyan') yields expected escape sequences to prevent regressions.

When modifying forwarding sites, prefer explicit keyword passes or a small adapter that maps facade parameter names to internal roles; add targeted tests for combinations (foreground/background/attrs/flags) to catch swaps.

skill.title: Token boundary computed with exclusive vs. inclusive index convention (scanner off-by-one)
skill.trigger: A tokenizer/lexer (producer) emits tokens with numeric start/end positions and tests or examples show token.end is consistently one position off (commonly token.end == index after the last character or token.end == token.start + length + 1). Structurally, the scanner records start and advances a shared scan cursor/current while consuming token body and terminator, then constructs the token using arithmetic like end = current ± N or slices using start:current without confirming whether end should be inclusive or exclusive, or whether subsequent trimming changed the token length.
knowledge: Reproduce with the smallest representative inputs (single-quoted, multi-quoted, escaped-terminator) and assert expected start and end indexes for each token to make the off-by-one deterministic.

Instrument the scanner: log start, current (cursor) before consuming the terminator, after consuming the terminator, and immediately before token emission. Confirm whether token emission uses the pre- or post-terminator cursor.

Search the code for index arithmetic at emission sites: patterns like end = current, end = current - 1, end = current + 1, end = start + len(text) ± N, and examine nearby comments to determine whether end is intended to be inclusive or exclusive.

Check slicing and trimming interactions: if token text is computed with sql[start:current] and then text.strip() is used, verify whether the stripped length still corresponds to the original start/current indexes used to compute end.

Inspect token construction helpers (e.g., _add, Token constructor): confirm whether they expect end to be inclusive or exclusive and whether any caller applies additional adjustments. Audit all call sites for consistent conventions.

Pay attention to multi-character terminators or quote sequences (e.g., triple quotes) and escaped characters: the scanner might advance multiple positions for the terminator, so verify whether the emission arithmetic accounts for multi-char terminators versus single-char.

Add focused unit tests that assert both token.text and (start,end) semantics for minimal cases (e.g., "'a'", "'''a'", strings with escapes). Use assertions that fail when end is off by ±1 to prevent regressions.

When reading existing tests or code, prefer reasoning in terms of inclusive vs exclusive boundaries: convert all emission points to a single convention (document it) and add a short comment in the emission site clarifying the convention.

If multiple functions compute token text and boundaries (producer + helper + constructor), trace the exact values through each layer. A mismatch often happens when one layer expects exclusive end but another provides inclusive end.

When possible, centralize boundary computation in one helper so that callers provide only start and current cursor and the helper returns consistent (start, end, text) respecting the documented convention.

skill.title: User-facing string contains literal template placeholder due to provider/assembly formatting mismatch
skill.trigger: A consumer (error/message constructor, CLI output, logger, or doc-link builder) emits a user-visible string that includes an unsubstituted templating token (e.g. '{VERSION}', '{0}', '{name}') AND the code path constructs the string by combining a value provider (version helper, constant, i18n/template loader) with a formatting step (f-string, .format, %-format) so that the bug can stem from either the producer returning a template or the consumer using the wrong formatting/literal.
knowledge: First disambiguation: check the provider's return value separately. Locate the value provider (version constant, helper like version_short(), template loader) and inspect or call it in isolation; if it returns a string containing the placeholder, the producer is faulty.

If the provider returns a concrete value, inspect the consumer / message assembly: look for missing interpolation (e.g. using a plain string with '{VERSION}' instead of an f-string), misuse of .format (mismatched placeholders, double-braced escapes), or building the message by concatenation of a literal token and not substituting.

Search heuristics: grep the repository for common placeholder patterns (literally '{VERSION}', '{0}', '{name}', or single-brace patterns) and for nearby formatting APIs (f'...', .format(…), % formatting, Template.substitute()). Also search for provider names (VERSION, version_short, get_version, version.py).

Consider import-time vs runtime resolution: constants imported from version modules may be strings; helpers may return templates in packaging/dev contexts. Verify whether the provider is intended to return an already-resolved string or a template to be formatted later.

Watch for subtle causes: missing leading f on f-strings (e.g. "See https://.../{VERSION}/..." vs f"See https://.../{VERSION}/..."), using str.format on a string that already contains literal braces that were never passed arguments, or returning a string that intentionally includes braces for later formatting but is mistakenly used directly.

Minimal reproducible check: call the provider or the message-builder in a REPL or small unit test to observe the emitted string. If provider is the culprit, fix provider to return resolved value; if consumer is the culprit, change assembly to use the correct formatting API or pass the provider value into .format/f-string.

When assembling candidates, prefer functions that directly own the message text (message constructors, wrapper functions that raise user-facing exceptions) and also include the provider function/constant as a second candidate to resolve whether substitution happens upstream or downstream.

skill.title: Comparator arithmetic error when combining X/Y coordinates with a flow-weight parameter
skill.trigger: A consumer (an element-sorting routine) emits a non-monotonic or unexpectedly ordered sequence when a local value (a flow-weight parameter passed from a constructor or config like LAParams) is applied to a sort/comparator that combines X and Y coordinates. The comparator/key expression mixes scaled coordinate components (e.g., x0/x1/y0/y1) with the flow-weight; varying the parameter (extreme values like 0 and 1) produces swapped, inverted, or non-monotonic ordering.
knowledge: Reproduce with extreme parameter values (e.g., 0.0, 0.5, 1.0). If ordering flips or becomes non-monotonic, suspect sign/term or axis-component errors in the comparator.
Instrument the sorter: compute and log the comparator/key for each object before and after sorting; compare numeric keys to expected monotonic pattern (top-left → bottom-right).

Inspect the comparator expression for swapped axis terms (x vs y), wrong coordinate components (x0 + y1 vs x0 + x1), or inverted signs (minus vs plus) and for incorrect grouping/parentheses that change precedence.
Check coordinate system conventions (origin at top-left vs bottom-left) and whether the algorithm assumes y increases upwards or downwards; mismatched conventions can appear as sign inversions.
Construct small synthetic test cases with a handful of boxes placed at known coordinates to assert expected ordering; add unit tests that vary the flow-weight to capture regressions.
Search for similar comparator patterns in sibling analyzers or group classes (other flow directions) to find duplicated logic; fixes often need to be applied consistently across variants.

Verify that the parameter is the consumer's local value (not mutated elsewhere) and that assertion/guards (e.g., assert boxes_flow is not None) exist so the comparator always uses a defined numeric value.
When possible, express the sort key as a named helper function and add comments documenting intended sign and axis roles to reduce risk of future term swaps.

skill.title: Optional registry-backed validation/merge stage removed from composition pipeline
skill.trigger: A composition/loader function (consumer) returns an assembled result unchanged or without expected defaults or warnings when a matching schema/provider exists in a registry (producer, e.g., ConfigStore). The code-path that previously performed a schema lookup + merge/validation and emitted a deprecation/migration warning has been deleted, gated by a condition, or bypassed by a refactor.
knowledge: Start at the composition/loader function that returns the assembled result (e.g., ConfigLoaderImpl.load_configuration). Look for places that previously inspected a registry (ConfigStore, registry.get, schema lookup) and performed a merge or validation step before assigning the returned config.

Search the repo for identifiers and calls commonly used for this stage: registry names like 'ConfigStore', 'schema', helpers calling 'get_schema', 'schema_source', 'OmegaConf.merge', 'deprecation_warning', or the project's migration URLs/strings. Deleted blocks often include both the merge and a nearby warning string.

Confirm observable behavior by registering a matching schema in the registry and loading the same config name/group: if no merge occurs and no deprecation warning is emitted, the schema-lookup/merge path is likely absent or short-circuited.

Inspect surrounding variable flow: check the local config object (e.g., ret.config) and whether any 'merged' variable used to be assigned and then stored back into the result. Refactors sometimes remove the assignment to the result or move the return before the merge.

Examine special-case handling that manipulates embedded nodes (e.g., a 'hydra' node): earlier code may temporarily remove an embedded node before merging and restore it after. Missing that logic can be a clue that the merge block was removed.

Look for exception handling around the merge (OmegaConfBaseException or similar) and for code that raises a ConfigCompositionException on merge failures; the absence of such try/except and the related error messages suggests deleted merge logic.

Check for conditional guards that would skip the stage (e.g., 'if schema is not None:' or feature-flag checks). A gating condition accidentally changed to always false or removed entirely will cause the stage to be omitted without a broad refactor.

Compare with prior commits or file history to find an exact deleted block: the removed code often includes deprecation_warning text, URL references, logic around 'defaults' in the schema, the merge call, and reassignment to the result. Use the diff to identify what to restore.

For reproducer and tests: write a small test registering a schema via the registry, call the loader with the matching config name/group, assert that defaults from the schema are present in the result and that a deprecation warning or specific migration message is emitted. Also test the case where the schema contains a 'defaults' list to ensure the special-case error is raised.

Fix guidance: restore or reintroduce the registry lookup + merge/validation block (with correct variable names), including hydra-node extraction/restoration if present, proper exception handling that raises a composition exception on merge failure, and emission of the deprecation/migration warning. Ensure the merged DictConfig is assigned back to the returned result before embedding/returning.

After fixing, add unit/integration tests that exercise schema-matched loads (normal merge, schema-with-defaults error path, and deprecation-warning emission) to prevent regressions where the optional stage is accidentally removed again.

skill.title: Capability/guard predicate inverts membership test or consults wrong set
skill.trigger: A consumer-facing capability/compatibility predicate (guard) returns the opposite boolean of the intended membership test for an item (e.g., reports 'not supported' for a known-supported value). The predicate's implementation uses a membership test (set/list/constant or delegated helper) or an early return, and the structural mismatch (negation, wrong collection, type/equality mismatch, or short-circuit return) can flip the result.
knowledge: Reproduce quickly with one known-supported item and one known-unsupported item to confirm inversion behavior.
Inspect the predicate body for explicit negation patterns ('not in', 'not (x in S)', '!=', double negatives) and for early/constant returns that bypass the membership check.

Trace delegation: if the predicate calls another helper or module constant, follow the delegation chain and inspect the referenced collection/constant for omissions or inverted semantics (include vs exclude lists).
Check imports and symbol names: ensure the predicate tests against the intended set/constant and not a similarly-named but different collection.
Verify types and equality semantics used in membership tests (e.g., string vs UID/object, or identity vs equality) that can cause 'in' to fail even when the logical entry exists.
Look for inverted documentation or naming mismatches (function name implies 'supports' but code tests an 'unsupported' list); confirm docstring/tests align with implementation.
Add a minimal unit test asserting predicate(True) for canonical supported values to capture regressions; reproduce failing and passing cases.
If a negation was intended to flip include/exclude semantics, prefer explicit naming (is_excluded/is_supported) and centralize the include/exclude decision to avoid double-negation bugs.

When fixing, prefer returning the direct membership expression (return item in SUPPORTED) rather than return not (item in SUPPORTED) after transformations; ensure Boolean logic is as simple as possible.

skill.title: Successor-acceptance guard rejects valid operand forms (parenthesized expressions / grouped queries)
skill.trigger: A grouping-stage consumer (e.g., an alias/AS merge routine) leaves an alias/keyword token unmerged because its successor-acceptance guard/helper predicate returns false for a following token that is actually a valid operand (for example, a parenthesized expression, a grouped subquery or a CTE body emitted by the lexer). The predicate uses token-type/keyword checks that are too narrow or treat grouped tokens as invalid.
knowledge: Reproduce with minimal SQL examples that use AS followed by parenthesized operands (CREATE TABLE ... AS (SELECT ...), WITH cte AS (SELECT ...), SELECT x AS (SELECT 1)) to confirm the grouping is skipped.
Inspect the successor predicate (helper) implementation: confirm it checks for token is None early and does not treat grouped/Parenthesis tokens or Identifier-like groups as acceptable operands.

Examine token representations from the lexer: parenthesized subqueries/CTEs may be represented as grouped tokens (Parenthesis, TokenList) or as sql.Identifier/IdentifierList wrappers; predicates should test for grouping (token.is_group or isinstance(token, Parenthesis/TokenList/Identifier)) in addition to ttype values.

Avoid equating 'is_keyword' with invalid identifier use: some keywords are usable as identifiers except explicit sentinel keywords (e.g., NULL). Prefer explicit exclusion lists for reserved cases rather than whitelisting only non-keyword tokens.

Check token type checks: prefer accepting tokens with T.Name, string tokens, grouped token lists, or explicit Identifier classes rather than only non-keyword ttypes. Be careful with library-specific ttype enums vs structural classes.

Add focused unit tests that assert AS merges with (a) Parenthesis-wrapped SELECT subqueries, (b) CTE-style expressions, and (c) simple parenthesized expressions; include negative tests for truly invalid successors (e.g., end-of-stream or explicit reserved tokens like NULL if intended).

When fixing, handle None and end-of-stream explicitly (return False), then allow grouped tokens and identifier-like objects; centralize the acceptance logic so outer grouping loops rely on a single clearly-documented predicate.
If the predicate delegates to further helpers, trace delegation to ensure grouped-token checks are not accidentally bypassed by earlier token-type-only checks or inverted logic.

skill.title: Separator-token misparsing in componentized semantic strings (component index shift)
skill.trigger: A consumer or accessor (e.g., a property like patch or a comparison method) returns or compares components of a parsed semantic string incorrectly because the tokenizer/normalizer splits or indexes components wrongly when optional separator-delimited segments (such as prerelease or build metadata) are present.
knowledge: Locate the tokenizer/normalizer that converts the raw string into a canonical component sequence/structure. Print or log the canonicalized output for representative complex inputs (including combinations of separators) to confirm the intended component array/tuple/fields are produced.

Verify property accessors and convenience fields map to the intended component positions of the canonical representation (e.g., main[2] == patch). Watch for off-by-one or removed/renamed intermediate fields that shift indexing when optional segments exist.

Check how separators are handled: ensure prerelease and build delimiters are parsed into separate fields (or explicitly ignored for ordering per spec) rather than truncating or merging adjacent components. Add unit repro cases with combinations like: main.pre-release.build, missing components, and numeric+alphanumeric mixes.

Examine comparison and range-membership logic to confirm it uses the normalized canonical representation (not a stale raw string or partially-parsed fields). If comparisons compose tuples, ensure the tuple structure consistently includes the same component positions and that prerelease/build treatment follows the intended ordering rules.

Run small, focused boundary tests: compare versions at operator boundaries (>, >=, ==) and evaluate range expressions that hinge on equality vs strict inequality (e.g., >1.0 vs >=1.0) to confirm operator semantics align with component parsing.

Search for recent edits that removed or changed intermediate accessors, fields, or normalization steps (for example, deleted a patch property or changed how main/pre-release/build are stored). Such refactors commonly leave accessor indices stale.

If build/prerelease tokens are intended to be ignored for ordering, ensure that logic explicitly strips or separates build metadata before tuple comparison; conversely, if they affect representation, ensure consistent inclusion across accessors and comparisons.

Add unit tests that construct versions containing boundary separators and assert both the canonical component structure and the expected comparison/range outcomes. Lock these tests to prevent future regressions from refactors that change indexing or token boundaries.

skill.title: Instance attributes consumed before constructor/initializer assigns them
skill.trigger: An AttributeError is raised when code (an instance method or an external caller) attempts to read an instance attribute (state owner) because the class lacks a constructor/initializer that assigns that attribute (or the initializer was removed/renamed/relocated), and callers construct the object and use it immediately (i.e., no alternate initialization has been performed or awaited).
knowledge: Start at the AttributeError site: record the missing attribute name and confirm it is referenced as an instance attribute (self.<name>) rather than a local or global.

Inspect the class for an __init__ method. If absent, look for alternate initializers (async initialize, class factory, classmethod constructors) or class-level defaults; note whether any alternate initializer must be called/awaited by callers.

Search call sites that construct the object. If callers call methods or access attributes immediately after construction (e.g., mgr = X(); mgr.do_something()), the constructor must have assigned the attributes or callers must be using a factory that returns an initialized instance.
Check for a recently-removed or dedented __init__ or assignments in VCS/file history; refactors sometimes delete initializer lines while leaving consumers.
Distinguish class attribute vs instance attribute bugs: ensure the code uses self.attr in __init__ rather than assigning to the class object (Class.attr) by accident.

When an async initializer exists, verify the initialization lifecycle: confirm callers await or otherwise guarantee initialization has completed before using the instance; look for race conditions where methods are invoked before initialize() runs.

Inspect framework-specific initialization needs (e.g., Config.get_conf, registration calls) and ensure they run during construction or before any consumer use; missing registration can cause later AttributeError or wrong behavior.

Reproduce with a minimal test that instantiates the class and calls the failing method immediately. Add temporary logging/print statements in __init__/initialize to see whether initialization is executed.

Fix options: add or restore a constructor that assigns required instance attributes, make a factory that returns an initialized object, ensure callers perform and await required initialization before use, or make methods defensively guard and lazily initialize attributes when safe.

Add unit/integration tests that instantiate the object and exercise its public API without requiring external initialization steps; include tests that verify the initialization sequence (synchronous or async) to prevent regressions.

skill.title: State-machine transition error in tokenizer around comment terminators
skill.trigger: Downstream output shows missing, truncated, malformed, or duplicated comment tokens (or the parser appears to stall) while the codebase includes a producer component that implements an explicit tokenizer/state-machine for comments and a consumer/serializer expected to preserve comment tokens (e.g., sanitizer/serializer preserves comments when strip_comments=False).
knowledge: Reproduce with minimal inputs that exercise comment edge cases (e.g. <!--comment-->, <!-- comment -->, comments adjacent to text, comments at start/end) and capture the tokenizer's raw token stream before any filters or serializers to determine whether the producer emitted correct comment tokens.

Inspect tokenizer state-machine routines that handle comment states (common names: commentState, commentEndState, commentEndBangState, commentStart/state transitions). Look for incorrect state assignments (setting a state to itself), mismatched return values that control the calling loop, and branches that drop or fail to append the consumed character into currentToken['data'].

Compare implementation to a known-good reference (upstream html5lib) for the exact transitions on characters '-', '!', '\u0000', EOF, and default branches; ensure ParseError entries are created correctly and currentToken is enqueued when appropriate.

Differentiate producer vs consumer faults: if tokenizer emits correctly formed comment tokens, instrument or log the sanitizer/filter and serializer path to find where tokens are dropped or mutated; if tokenizer emits malformed/missing tokens, focus fix on state transitions and token-data assembly in the tokenizer.

Check return semantics of tokenizer state handlers (True/False or other controls) — an incorrect return value can cause the outer processing loop to stop consuming input or to re-enter the same state repeatedly, producing apparent stalls or infinite loops.

Search for recent vendored changes or one-off edits to tokenizer code (e.g., removal of '+ data' in default branches, stray changes that replace replacement characters, or incorrect state assignment on EOF) as likely culprits in vendored copies.

When preparing a fix, add unit tests that assert the tokenizer emits a single correct comment token for each minimal input and that end-to-end sanitizer.clean(..., strip_comments=False) re-emits identical comment markup; include tests for boundary characters (U+0000, EOF, unexpected '!' and '-' after double-dash).

skill.title: Decorator wrapper reads or returns its local cache-payload before it is computed/assigned
skill.trigger: A decorator-installed wrapper that memoizes results per resource/context (e.g., per-ParseContext) raises NameError/UnboundLocalError or returns an undefined local because a local variable intended to hold the cached payload (e.g., 'result' or 'cached_value') is referenced or returned on a control-flow path before the wrapped function has been invoked and that variable assigned. Applies when the wrapper implements explicit cache-hit vs cache-miss branches, try/except cache lookups, or early returns and maintains the cache value as a local variable in the wrapper scope.
knowledge: Confirm the failure: reproduce the NameError/UnboundLocalError and capture the stack trace to identify the wrapper function and the exact local variable name referenced.

Locate the decorator wrapper that implements per-context memoization. Search for wrappers that compute a cache_key, use an object-level cache (e.g., self.__dict__[cache_key] or similar), and call the wrapped function on cache-miss.
