Inspect wrapper control flow closely: distinguish the cache-hit branch (often an early return) and cache-miss branch. Look for return statements that reference the local payload variable before any assignment on the miss path.

Remember Python scoping: an assignment anywhere in the function makes the name local. If the wrapper assigns to the same name later, earlier references cause UnboundLocalError even if they appear syntactically before the assignment. Consider renaming variables or rearranging assignments to avoid shadowing.

Verify ordering on the miss path: compute the value by calling the wrapped function first, then store it into the cache, then return it (compute -> store -> return). Avoid returning a local that will only be assigned after the return or relying on falling-through variables set in other branches.

If a try/except is used around cache lookup, ensure the except branch does not fall through to a return that references an uninitialized local; explicitly compute and assign before any return in that branch.

Fix options: move the call to the wrapped function earlier (before any return that references the value), assign to the local then to the cache before returning, or use a clearly separate temporary local name to avoid scoping confusion. Add unit tests that exercise both cache-hit and cache-miss paths to prevent regressions.

To find other instances, search for patterns like: decorator wrappers named 'wrapped'/'wrapper', usages of __dict__[cache_key], per-context keys (e.g., parse_context.uuid), or functions annotated with cached/memoize and then inspect their wrapper control flow for early returns that reference a local payload.

skill.title: Parser swap produces incompatible return/exception semantics for text→date/datetime conversions
skill.trigger: A consumer (e.g., scalar parse_value/parse_literal) begins rejecting or erroring on inputs that were previously accepted after the text→date/datetime parsing code was changed to call a different parser implementation (producer). The guidance applies when the wrapper code assumes the old parser's return types, timezone-awareness, accepted formats, or raised exception classes and only handles those shapes (e.g., catches ValueError, expects datetime.date vs datetime.datetime, or assumes naive vs aware datetimes).
knowledge: Reproduce: pick representative inputs (plain date, datetime with Z, offset datetimes, times, fractional seconds) and call both the old parser (fromisoformat / isoparse / previous dependency) and the new parser (aniso8601.parse_date / parse_datetime / parse_time) on the same strings to see differences in return value types, timezone awareness, and accepted formats.

Inspect exception semantics: run inputs that previously failed and capture the exact exception classes/messages from both parsers. The wrapper may be catching ValueError only; new parser libraries often raise library-specific exceptions (e.g., aniso8601 exceptions) that are not subclasses of ValueError — adjust except clauses or normalize exceptions.

Check return types and coercion: verify whether the new parser returns datetime.date vs datetime.datetime (or returns timezone-aware vs naive datetimes). If the consumer expects a specific type, add a small adapter that coerces/normalizes (e.g., convert datetime→date, drop/normalize tzinfo) before returning to callers.

Compare accepted formats and timezone handling: some parsers accept additional ISO variants or reject ones previously tolerated. Identify the exact format(s) that started failing and decide whether to accept them (wrap with fallback parser) or tighten expectations and update docs/tests.

Search for other call sites: grep for the original parser usage and for other places that call the wrapper; a parser swap often impacts multiple scalars/serializers. Add regression tests that assert behavior for representative inputs to prevent future regressions.

Guard dependency and version drift: confirm whether the code intended to switch to a new library/version; if not, pin or revert. If switching, update the wrapper to translate new parser errors into the project's expected error type (e.g., GraphQLError) and to preserve prior API contracts.

Adapter pattern: implement a small adapter layer around the new parser that (a) normalizes exceptions to the existing exception type(s), (b) coerces return value types, and (c) documents any format differences so callers do not need to know parser internals.
When changing parsers, add unit tests that exercise both success and failure shapes (return types, tzinfo presence, and exact exception text) so future swaps surface clear, localized failures.

skill.title: Public facade forwards/binds arguments to wrong semantic roles (foreground/background/flags)
skill.trigger: A public-facing function (consumer of caller-supplied parameters) emits KeyError, applies the wrong semantic mapping (foreground vs background/ highlight), inverts capability/flag behavior, or produces incorrect/missing cleanup (reset) because one or more parameters were forwarded or bound to the wrong parameter names/positions before first use (e.g., passed positionally into a helper or lookup where roles differ). Applicable when the module contains simple role-to-code lookup tables (state owners) and the facade forwards inputs directly into those tables or a capability gate.
knowledge: Reproduce minimal failing calls: exercise the facade with foreground, background (on_color), attrs, and capability flags (no_color/force_color) both by position and by explicit keyword to observe differences and KeyError traces.

Inspect the facade signature and each occurrence where it forwards arguments to helpers or lookup tables; prefer named-argument forwarding (param=param) to preserve semantic binding instead of positional forwarding.
Locate first-use sites of caller values: check which lookup table (e.g., COLORS vs HIGHLIGHTS) is indexed for each parameter and confirm the table identity aligns with the parameter's semantic role.

Verify capability gating flags are passed with correct parameter names to the capability checker (no_color vs force_color) — swapped names invert behavior and can silence or force formatting incorrectly.

Check attribute application ordering and cleanup: confirm attribute codes are applied in the intended SGR stacking order (reverse-order bugs can change effective styling) and ensure RESET (or equivalent cleanup) is appended to the assembled string.

Greps and quick checks: search for positional forwarding patterns (calls that pass variables without names), fmt_str % (HIGHLIGHTS[<var>] vs COLORS[<var>]), and capability gate calls where boolean args appear in the wrong order; add unit tests asserting colored('text', color='cyan') yields expected escape sequences to prevent regressions.

When modifying forwarding sites, prefer explicit keyword passes or a small adapter that maps facade parameter names to internal roles; add targeted tests for combinations (foreground/background/attrs/flags) to catch swaps.

skill.title: Facade/registration wrapper forwards caller arguments in the wrong parameter order to downstream constructor/registration
skill.trigger: A public-facing wrapper or registration API delegates to a downstream registration/constructor and the caller-observable object/resource shows two semantic fields exchanged (e.g., registered endpoint.path == caller.name and registered endpoint.name == caller.path). The failure occurs because the wrapper forwards arguments positionally or with the wrong keyword names to the callee, whose parameter order or names differ from the wrapper's intent.
knowledge: Reproduce a minimal failing call and inspect the created/registered object's attributes (exercise both positional and keyword forms). Differences between positional and keyword invocations often reveal forwarding issues.

Trace the delegation chain (wrapper -> any intermediate add_* helper -> final constructor/registration). Open each callee's signature to confirm parameter names, ordering, and which parameters are positional-only, keyword-only, or accept **kwargs.

Look for positional-only forwarding patterns (calls that pass variables without names) and for cases where wrapper parameters are passed by position into a callee whose parameter order differs. Also watch for misnamed keyword forwarding (e.g., path passed as name=...).

When the callee accepts *args or **kwargs, examine how the wrapper builds its argument list/dict; prefer constructing explicit kwargs mapping wrapper names to callee names (e.g., callee(path=path, name=name)) to avoid accidental reordering.

If fixing, change the wrapper to forward arguments explicitly by name (param=param) or adapt the wrapper→callee mapping with a small adapter that maps semantic roles, and add unit tests asserting the registered object's key metadata (e.g., route.path and route.name) match caller-supplied values.

Greps and quick checks: search the codebase for wrapper functions that call constructors/registration helpers using bare variables (no keywords), calls that pass variables in different orders, and constructor invocations where keyword names differ from wrapper parameter names.

Add targeted tests exercising both positional and keyword API usages and assertions for the registered object's visible fields; include regression tests for the specific semantic pair (e.g., path vs name) to detect future swaps.

If the wrapper also manages registration order (insert vs append), verify that any change to how the object is added (insert(0) vs append) is intentional and covered by tests — but treat that separately from argument-binding swaps.

skill.title: Mapping keys assumed to be strings before filtering/renaming
skill.trigger: A conversion/filtering function raises AttributeError (or TypeError) while iterating a mapping (metadata-like dict) because it calls string methods (e.g., startswith, replace, lower) on keys without verifying they are str. Applicable when code filters or renames keys by prefix or pattern and then passes keys through to downstream serialization or merge logic.
knowledge: Search for functions that iterate .metadata, .meta, or other mapping-like attributes and look for key-level string operations (startswith, endswith, replace, lower, upper, split).
Look for patterns that filter keys using membership in a _VALID_PROPERTIES set or a prefix (e.g., _VALID_PREFIX / 'x-') and then do key.replace or key.startswith without isinstance(key, str) checks.
Prefer explicit guards: check isinstance(key, str) before any str method; skip non-str keys, or coerce with str(key) only when semantically safe (beware changing the key semantics).

When renaming keys (e.g., 'x_' → 'x-'), perform the type check first and only apply replace on confirmed string keys; implement the transformation deterministically in a single loop to avoid double-handling.

Consider tightening the contract: if callers are expected to supply only string keys, document and validate at boundary (constructor/producer) and add defensive tests. If third-party code may add non-str keys, treat metadata as an arbitrary mapping and skip unknown key types.
Add unit tests with non-string metadata keys (objects, ints, bytes) to assert the converter no longer raises and either ignores or coerces keys according to the intended policy.
Check downstream callers (merging functions, serializers) to confirm they accept only string keys; if they do, ensure the converter returns only string-keyed mappings or documents the behavior.
When possible, prefer whitelisting allowed property names over broad pass-through of metadata, reducing the chance of unexpected keys reaching schema output.

skill.title: Per-element serializer composes wrapper delimiters and surrounding whitespace in wrong order or selects wrong link attribute
skill.trigger: A tag-specific serializer (consumer/producer pair: tree walker dispatches child text to a per-tag converter) emits malformed delimiter-delimited output for an element (for example, bracket/parenthesis pairs around link text and URL appear reversed or misplaced, surrounding inline spaces are attached to the wrong side, or autolinks render empty or use the element's title instead of href). Applicable when the converter relies on a shared whitespace-normalization helper that returns prefix/suffix markers (e.g., chomp-like helper) and on element attributes/options to choose between autolink shorthand and bracketed-link serialization.
knowledge: Reproduce minimal examples that show each symptom: regular link output order swap, autolink emitted empty or using title, and space migration around links. Example inputs: text, u, and surrounding text 'foo text bar'.

Open the per-tag converter (convert_a or equivalent) and locate the logic that: unpacks the whitespace helper (prefix, suffix, text), reads element attributes (href, title), decides autolink vs bracketed link, and formats the final string. Confirm the unpacking order matches the helper's documented/implemented return order.

Inspect the shared whitespace helper (chomp/stripper): verify its return order and semantics (which value is prefix, which is suffix, and which is stripped inner text). Look for tuple unpacking assumptions or variable-name mismatches that could swap prefix/suffix when used by converters.

Check the final format/return expression for swapped positions: confirm the format string or f-string places prefix before the wrapper and suffix after it (e.g., return '%s[%s](%s)%s' % (prefix, text, href, title_part, suffix)) rather than swapping prefix and suffix positions.

Verify autolink detection logic: compare text vs href after unescaping/normalization, ensure the code checks href (not title) for the URL to be emitted in angle brackets, and ensure that when autolink is chosen the emitted URL is the href value.

Examine default title handling: if default_title can substitute href into title, ensure the autolink decision excludes cases where title is present (the presence of a title should not enable autolink) and that any fallback to title for display is intentionally ordered.
Search for similar patterns elsewhere (other convert_<tag> methods) to detect copy-paste mistakes (identical swapped prefix/suffix or format strings).

Add unit tests covering: (a) regular links with and without title, (b) autolinks when options.autolinks is True/False, and (c) inline links with surrounding whitespace to lock expected prefix/suffix behavior. Use distinct sentinel characters around text to detect swaps.

If the helper or converter uses default values from element.get(...), check for missing default arguments that lead to None vs '' (e.g., el.get('href', '')). Ensure comparisons and string formatting behave consistently with these defaults.

When fixing, prefer clear local variable names for unpacked helper results (prefix, suffix, inner_text) and colocate the autolink decision and formatting so the relationship between selected attributes (href/title) and output is obvious; run existing conversion tests to confirm no regressions across tags.

skill.title: Runtime callable lacks async invocation entrypoint expected by async call path
skill.trigger: An AttributeError complaining that a runtime callable object (producer) has no attribute like '_async_invoke' appears when an async-enabled consumer (compiler-generated template code or runtime dispatcher) selects an async-specific invocation method rather than the sync path. Applicable when the compiled/dispatching code branches on environment.is_async or similar and dispatches to an object-level async handler that the object's class does not define.
knowledge: Reproduce the failure with a minimal async-enabled template that exercises the callable type (e.g. enable_async=True and a macro or other callable invocation) to confirm the AttributeError and capture the missing attribute name from the traceback.

Search consumer-side code (compiler and generated invocation sites) for branching on async mode and for direct calls to per-object async entrypoints. Grep patterns: 'is_async', '_async_invoke', 'await .*\._async_invoke', or conditional dispatch between _invoke and _async_invoke.

Inspect the runtime callable class definitions (producer) for the expected async entrypoint and its signature. Look for recent diffs or removals that could have deleted the method (scan changelogs, commit history, or nearby diff hunks).

Compare signatures and expectations: verify the consumer expects the same argument list and return handling (e.g. whether the async entrypoint should return a coroutine to await or perform awaiting internally and return the final string).

If the method is missing, consider safe remediation patterns: (a) reintroduce the async entrypoint with the expected signature and behavior (await underlying coroutine, apply autoescape/markup handling); (b) add a fallback/adapter on the producer (hasattr guard) that awaits the underlying function when necessary; (c) alter consumer code generation to call and await the underlying callable result rather than requiring a special per-object method, but prefer keeping a stable runtime API for backward compatibility.

Use stack traces and generated code inspection to locate the exact generated call site (the compiled template code or compiler node for macro calls). That shows whether the consumer expects per-object async methods or a coroutine-returning function.
Check other runtime callable types (filters, tests, macros, blocks) for the same asymmetry — the bug class often affects multiple callable-like objects when async support was changed inconsistently.

Add or update unit tests that exercise both sync and async invocation forms for the affected callable types, including simple returns and coroutines returned/used inside the callable, to prevent regressions.

When ambiguity remains, search for versions or refactor commits that moved async handling into a mixin/helper or renamed the method; look for conditional implementations keyed by feature flags or environment configuration that could cause some runtime objects to lack the new API.

skill.title: Rect→page-space mapping omits or misapplies page /Rotate (rotation-unaware coordinate conversion)
skill.trigger: A page-level producer (constructor/producer) returns x0/y0/top/bottom/doctop values derived from raw parser/layout Rects that are correct for unrotated pages but are inverted, offset, or swapped for pages with non-zero /Rotate (90/180/270). The conversion code computes y-inversion or uses page width/height arithmetic but does not incorporate the page /Rotate/turns transformation (e.g., does not rotate points, does not swap comp = width/height for 90° turns, or uses the incorrect sign/additive offset formula).
knowledge: Locate the Rect→page-space mapping code path used by the failing consumer: follow the consumer (e.g., Page.annots, Page.objects) to the helper that converts raw pdfminer Rect coordinates into page-space fields (x0, y0, x1, y1, top, bottom, doctop).

Compare raw parser Rect values (the raw coordinates from pdfminer) to the library-reported x0/y0/top/bottom for the same annotation across pages rotated 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270°. If raw rects are identical but reported coordinates differ incorrectly, the bug is in the mapping.

Search for small helpers and names like rotate_point, rotate, turns, rotation, comp = self.width/self.height, or expressions using page.width/page.height and modulo 2/4 logic — these often contain the rotation-aware arithmetic or the missing rotation application.

Check whether the mapping uses page.rotation or page.attrs['Rotate'] (or an integer turns count) and whether it swaps width/height for 90/270-degree turns; missing width/height swap is a common source of inverted/offset coordinates.

Inspect y-axis inversion math: confirm whether code uses 'rh - y' (subtraction) versus 'rh + y' (addition) or other sign changes. The correct formula depends on whether rotation was applied and whether comp has been set to width or height for that turn.

Compare this mapping to other producers in the same module (e.g., mapping for chars, edges, or other objects) that already handle rotation correctly; reuse their rotation-aware logic or mirror their approach to ensure consistency.

Verify doctop/top/bottom/doctop consistency: doctop should incorporate initial_doctop and top should be computed consistently with rotation-aware mapping so that higher-level consumers relying on doctop see consistent positions.

Create minimal repro tests that open the same PDF with different page /Rotate values (0/90/180/270) and assert expected relationships (e.g., rotated y0 equals original top after applying the known rotation transform).

If a rotate helper exists, add unit tests for all four turn values; if not, factor out a single rotate_point function used by all object-conversion paths and ensure it is fed the correct comp (width/height) and turn count.
When fixing, prefer applying a single rotation-aware transform matrix or unified helper rather than ad-hoc per-field arithmetic to avoid off-by-sign or width/height swapping errors.

skill.title: Constructed view/object referenced before assignment due to creation/return ordering
skill.trigger: A function/method raises NameError or UnboundLocalError naming a local that should hold a newly constructed view/sub-object (producer) because that variable is referenced or returned on an executed path where its assignment is placed later, is conditional, or is skipped (common in getitem/slice/selectors that instantiate a per-selection view).
knowledge: When an UnboundLocalError/NameError names a variable that sounds like a constructed result (e.g., new_* , result, view, subwindow), grep the function for that name and inspect the control-flow: find where it is assigned (e.g., type(self)(...), constructor calls) and where it is referenced or returned.

Check for misplaced return statements or returns placed before the assignment; ensure the creation/assignment of the result precedes any return or use on all control-flow paths. A common bug is `return X` placed before `X = constructor(...)` because of copy/paste or reordering.

Inspect conditional branches and early exits: the assignment may be inside one branch while consumers run unconditionally. Trace simple execution paths (both common and edge-case inputs) rather than only scanning for names.

Focus on responsibility roles in selection/slicing/getitem implementations: selection inference (e.g., _infer_selection), the construction call that builds the per-selection object (e.g., type(self)(subset,...)), and any alias-prevention steps. Verify that 'subset' or the inputs used to construct the new object are computed before instantiating it, and that the instantiated object is stored into the local name before use.

In code that adapts/forwards to constructor/type(...) calls, prefer assigning the constructed object to the result variable before performing subsequent attribute access or returning it; if multiple constructors/paths exist, ensure each path assigns the same local name.

Add or run small repro tests that exercise column/view selection and edge-case inputs (empty subset, None subset, alternative branches) to confirm the uninitialized path; once fixed, add a unit test covering the previously failing input to guard against regressions.

skill.title: Shared text-write helper applies unintended sequence-reversal to assigned string
skill.trigger: A consumer (underlying element/state owner) contains stored string state that is a character-wise mutated copy (e.g., reversed) of a producer's input value. Multiple high-level property producers delegate to the same element setter or inherited helper (a shared write-path), implicating the shared helper as the likely locus of the mutation introduced at assignment time.
knowledge: When many sibling property setters are byte-for-byte identical and delegate to a common element/helper, inspect the shared helper/inherited writer before assuming each setter is faulty.

Search the codebase for idioms that reverse or reorder sequences in-place or when building new strings: slice reversal ([::-1]), reversed(), list.reverse(), ''.join(reversed(...)), manual index-based loops, or unintended use of reversed iterators when joining.

Locate the shared write helper (e.g., _set_element_text, write_text, set_text) on the element class or a base class/mixin; read its implementation and any override chain (class, base classes, registered element classes).

If the helper is inherited from an external base or registered via parser/registry, inspect the registration points and the class providing the implementation — the defective code may live outside the immediate module.

Confirm the fault is write-time by: setting multiple different properties that share the helper and observing whether all are mutated similarly; reading the getter path (text read helper) to ensure it returns stored state unchanged, which indicates mutation occurred during assignment.

Search for misuse of bytes/bytearray operations or encoding/decoding steps in the write path that could reverse order (e.g., constructing bytes then iterating in reverse), and check accidental application of sequence operations on the input rather than on an auxiliary buffer.

Write a minimal repro that calls the shared helper directly (if accessible) or sets several delegating properties to distinct values to isolate whether mutation is introduced by the helper; add targeted unit tests that assert identity of input and stored text.

If a quick fix is applied (e.g., value[::-1] present), prefer replacing the accidental reversal with the original value and add a unit test covering the property to prevent regression; also audit other shared helpers for similar accidental sequence operators.

skill.title: Surrounding-token classifier misclassifies empty-value positions between mapping/flow/sequence categories
skill.trigger: A consumer (token-level rule or classifier) that inspects a short window of parser-produced tokens (e.g., curr/prev/next/nextnext) to decide the syntactic category of an empty position (block mapping value vs flow mapping value vs block sequence entry) fails to treat terminating tokens (another mapping key, block/mapping end, or equivalent) as evidence of an empty block mapping or sequence entry; as a result, configuration guards that forbid empty values in one category are not consistently applied.
knowledge: Reproduce the token sequence quickly: feed a minimal input that produces consecutive key/terminator tokens (e.g., 'key:' on a line followed by another 'key:' or the end of a block) and capture the parser token stream (token types and marks) so you see the exact curr/prev/next/nextnext sequence the rule receives.

Log the token types and their line/column marks at the rule entry point to confirm what the consumer sees for the failing case versus a passing case. Compare sequences that are flagged vs unflagged to isolate which terminating token values are treated differently.

Inspect the branching that decides mapping/flow/sequence classification. Look for condition order or precedence (e.g., flow-detection checked before block-mapping detection) and cases where the absence of an explicit value (no Scalar/Value token) is only considered when next is a particular token type.

Check whether the classifier treats a following KeyToken or BlockEndToken as a valid signal of an empty block mapping; if not, amend logic so that 'no explicit value and next is a key or block end' is recognized as an empty value in a block mapping.

Pay attention to use of nextnext: when next is a KeyToken or BlockEndToken, the code may be attempting to look further ahead and mis-evaluate the category. Prefer simpler, robust rules: if no value token follows before a terminator that ends the mapping context, classify as an empty mapping value.

Confirm boundary responsibilities: ensure the consumer (rule) is intended to perform this classification rather than relying on upstream parsing normalization. If the parser can provide a higher-level event (e.g., an explicit 'implicit null' token or a per-key value presence flag), prefer that to ad-hoc multi-token heuristics in many rules.

Augment or add unit tests that cover: consecutive keys with missing values, a key followed immediately by block end, keys with explicit null tokens, and mixed flow/block examples. Use tests to assert that the configured forbid flags produce problems in every relevant syntactic form.

When changing logic, be mindful of flow-mapping ambiguity: flow mappings often use different token patterns. Make the detection paths mutually exclusive and explicit (e.g., first detect 'flow mapping' by presence of flow-specific markers, else detect 'block mapping' by absence of flow markers and presence of terminator tokens).

If the rule uses membership tests over token type classes, check for mistaken negation or inverted predicates that might exclude terminator tokens; simplify complex boolean expressions and add comments explaining why each terminator token implies an empty-value condition.

After patching, run the repository's rule tests and also add a small regression test encoded as a token-level assertion that inspects the token stream for the reproduced case to prevent future regressions.

skill.title: Lexer subclass or merge step replaces matched text with empty token values
skill.trigger: A concrete lexer (producer) emits a token stream whose token types appear plausible but every token's value is the empty string (''); the failure is restricted to a single language lexer (and optionally its console wrapper) rather than the shared regex engine. Applicable when the project uses RegexLexer-like match/group machinery and language modules may override get_tokens_unprocessed or perform post-processing/merging of base token streams.
knowledge: Reproduce and isolate the origin: call the base regex engine directly (e.g., RegexLexer.get_tokens_unprocessed(self, text) or an equivalent base implementation) on the same input and compare values to the concrete lexer's output. If the base returns real matched text but the concrete lexer returns '' values, the override or merge step is the likely culprit.

Search the lexer module for yields that supply a constant empty string: grep for "yield .*'', ''" or patterns like "yield index, token, ''" or assignments that set the returned value to '' before yielding. Look for accidental final fall-through yields that replace value with ''.

Inspect any overridden get_tokens_unprocessed implementation: check where it iterates the base generator and how it re-yields triples. Verify it re-uses the original 'value' variable rather than substituting a literal or an empty string; verify control-flow (continues/returns) doesn't cause a default empty yield path.

Check regex rules that use bygroups or explicit group-index extraction: ensure the group index used to construct the token value refers to a populated capture group. Mis-ordered bygroups or wrong group indices can produce empty captures which then propagate as empty token values.

Examine downstream merging or insertion logic (console wrappers, do_insertions, prompt stripping/stitching): these steps may call the language lexer and then re-yield or alter tokens. Verify merging code doesn't replace values (e.g., for prompt lines) with '' for non-prompt tokens and that any 'skip' flags or early continues don't cause lost/empty values.

Look for string transformations that unwittingly change the value variable before membership checks (e.g., value.lower()/upper()) and later yield a different variable; ensure the yielded variable is the original matched text, not a temporary that was cleared or replaced.

Dynamic quick tests: create a minimal sample string and compare list(concrete_lexer.get_tokens(text)) to list(RegexLexer.get_tokens_unprocessed(concrete_lexer, text)). Also instrument the override to print or log the 'value' before each yield to find where it becomes ''.

If the concrete lexer uses mapping sets (keywords, builtins, functions) for reclassification, check that classification logic doesn't accidentally reassign value to an empty literal as part of normalization or error-handling paths. Prefer reclassifying token type only and maintain the original matched 'value'.

skill.title: Multi-step wire serializer emits message components in the wrong sequence (start-line after headers/body)
skill.trigger: A remote consumer or a TCP capture shows a malformed message (for example, an HTTP start-line appears after header bytes and/or body) because a producer (the wire-format serializer/connection-facing component) composes and writes the message in multiple steps and those low-level emits (start-line, header block and terminator, body) occur in the wrong order. Applicable when the serializer uses separate calls or helpers to emit the start-line, individual headers (or an end-of-headers marker), and the body (e.g., sendCommand/sendHeader/endHeaders/transport.write or similar multi-call sequences).
knowledge: Locate the connection/emit entrypoint (e.g., connectionMade, on_connect, send/request helper) where start-line, headers, and body are written. Inspect the exact order of calls that produce writes to the transport (sendCommand/sendHeader/endHeaders/transport.write or their equivalents).

Search the codebase for emission helpers by name (sendCommand, sendHeader, endHeaders, transport.write, _write, write) and inspect call sequences; diffs often reveal moved calls (start-line moved after endHeaders or body writes).

Trace the provenance of values used for each component: the factory/state owner or request object that supplies method/path/headers/body — confirm those fields are populated before the write sequence and that no early returns or control-flow changes reorder emissions.

Instrument or temporarily monkeypatch the low-level write calls to log the exact byte sequences and the order of operations, or reproduce locally and capture a TCP trace (tcpdump/wireshark/netcat) to confirm emission ordering at the wire level.

Be aware of helper semantics: some helpers (e.g., endHeaders) write header terminators immediately; ensure the code does not call endHeaders before emitting the start-line. Understand the library protocol contract (for Twisted: HTTPClient.sendCommand / sendHeader / endHeaders semantics).

Consider callback/timing effects: if emission is split across callbacks or uses deferreds, verify that asynchronous scheduling did not invert intended order (e.g., sending command in a later callback after headers were flushed).

When fixing, prefer composing the start-line, headers, and body in a single, well-documented sequence or assert the correct order with logging/asserts; add a unit/integration test that captures the emitted bytes for a simple request and asserts that the start-line appears before any header bytes.
Search for analogous multi-step serialization code (other protocol handlers or formats) to copy a canonical emission sequence and to avoid copy-paste mistakes that reorder calls.

skill.title: Absent/optional field normalized to empty-string sentinel during parsing/normalization
skill.trigger: Model objects constructed by a format-specific loader show field == '' (empty string) for items where the source format omits the element or marks it as 'NoUnit'/similar. The code path includes a parser/normalizer that maps format tokens (element text, markers in an ignorelist) to the model field; the observable mismatch is that callers and other format-parsers expect None/null for absent metadata but the loader returns an empty string sentinel instead.
knowledge: Trace the producer/consumer pair: find the loader function that extracts the optional element (producer) and the code that constructs the model object (consumer). Confirm the value returned by the extractor is passed directly into the model constructor.

Search for patterns that decide absent/ignored elements: checks like `res is None or res.text in ignorelist` or `if not res or res.text in (...)`. Inspect what those branches return (None vs '' vs res.text.lower()).

Look for ignorelist/token mismatches and casing changes: common mistakes include wrong token strings (e.g., 'No_Unit' vs 'NoUnit'), returning lowercased text without handling None, or unintentionally returning an empty string when res is None.

Confirm the model's contract: inspect the model class/constructor default (e.g., Signal.__init__) and usages to see whether callers check `if field is None:` rather than falsy checks. If callers rely on identity None, returning '' breaks behavior.

Compare parallel loader paths for the same model field (other formats or alternate code paths). If one path uses None for missing metadata while another returns '', the inconsistency pinpoints the normalization fault.
Reproduce quickly with a minimal file/test that omits the element and assert the field is None. Use this to validate fixes and to detect regressions across loader variants.

Repair patterns: preserve None for absent or ignored elements (return None when res is None or res.text in ignorelist). Only normalize/transform non-empty text (e.g., res.text.strip() or res.text.lower()) and return that result. Avoid empty-string sentinels for absent values unless the model explicitly documents and expects them.

If an ignorelist is used, ensure token spelling and casing are correct and consider normalizing res.text before membership checks (but only on non-None values). Add unit tests that assert None for omitted elements and that the ignored tokens are recognized.

When uncertain about consumers, adapt fixes conservatively: prefer returning None to maintain backward compatibility, and add migration notes or API compatibility tests if the project intends to move to empty-string sentinels.

skill.title: Extension-dispatched loader leaves shared result unset or mis-constructed in some format branches
skill.trigger: A public loader/producer dispatches on file extension or declared format and uses a shared local (e.g., content) returned at the end, but calling the loader on certain supported extensions yields None or an empty/no-result sentinel because one or more per-format branches either fall through without assigning the shared result, contain a no-op placeholder, open the file with the wrong mode (text vs binary) or pass the wrong argument type to a parser helper.
knowledge: Locate the dispatch logic: find the extension/format-to-branch mapping and any default/fallthrough path. Confirm whether handlers are expected to assign a shared result variable or to return their parsed value directly.

Search for the shared result variable initialization and final return site. If branches assign into a single local, verify every branch assigns it on all control flow paths (including inside try/except and conditional blocks).

Inspect each per-format branch for explicit no-ops (pass), removed assignments, or early returns that skip assignment. A 'pass' or an empty except that suppresses errors often leaves the shared result unset.

Check file open modes and parser API expectations: e.g., YAML parsers commonly accept text file objects or strings; pickle expects bytes (open file in 'rb' and pass bytes or use pickle.load on the file object). Ensure the code uses the correct mode and supplies the correct type to parser helpers.

Examine helper functions (e.g., pickle_load) and third-party calls (e.g., clevercsv.read_dicts) for their expected inputs/side-effects. Mismatching these (reading bytes but passing a file object, or vice versa) can produce exceptions or no-ops that result in no assignment.

Look for try/except blocks that swallow exceptions and do not set a fallback value; prefer logging/raising or explicitly setting a fallback, and avoid relying on a later shared-return to surface a failure silently as None.

Prefer per-branch explicit returns of the parsed value or use a mapping of extension -> small handler functions that return their result, rather than mutating a shared local—this reduces bugs from missed assignments and improves clarity.

Add targeted unit tests that exercise each supported extension/format and assert non-None parsed content and correct types. Include tests for malformed inputs and missing optional dependencies to ensure errors are surfaced rather than swallowed into a None return.

skill.title: Constructor/factory assigns incoming arguments to the wrong object fields (argument-order or assignment swap)
skill.trigger: A consumer (e.g., formatter, serializer, __str__/format method) produces output that references object fields but shows swapped, incorrect, or malformed values. Applicable when those values are produced by a constructor or factory (producer) whose implementation or its call-sites could have ordered, forwarded, or assigned incoming arguments to the wrong internal attributes or to the wrong parameters of a superclass constructor.
knowledge: Reproduce with the smallest example that raises/creates the problematic object and prints its formatted output; capture both the message and the underlying attribute values (inspect fields after construction).

Open the object's __init__ / factory function: verify the parameter list, each assignment to self.<field>, and any call to super().__init__ — check argument order and whether names/values are forwarded correctly.

Compare the constructor's parameter names and types against how callers create the object: grep for all call sites that construct/raise the object and ensure positional vs keyword usage matches the constructor signature.

Look for common mistakes: swapped variables in assignments (self.param = ctx vs self.param = param), forwarding the wrong variable to super().__init__, or accidental reordering when switching from positional to keyword arguments.

When the object is an exception, pay special attention to calls to the base class constructor (super().__init__): many code paths expect message first, hints second—confirm the correct semantics before forwarding.
If constructor is complex or overloaded, add a targeted unit test that asserts post-construction attributes and the formatted output; use this test to validate fixes and prevent regressions.
Search for similar patterns in sibling classes that override __init__ and call shared formatting code—once found, propagate the same checks to avoid duplicated mistakes.

skill.title: Caller-supplied argument not stored on object attribute consumed later
skill.trigger: A consumer (e.g., a render/save/draw method) fails with AttributeError 'NoneType' has no attribute '...' or similar because it calls a method on an object attribute that is unexpectedly None. Applicable when the attribute is expected to come from a producer (constructor/factory or factory kwargs) or a prior initialization step but may be left unset, stored under a different name (typo), conditionally assigned only on some paths, or overwritten/cleared before the consumer runs.
knowledge: Reproduce with a minimal caller that constructs/creates the object with the problematic argument (use both positional and keyword forms if supported), then immediately inspect the instance attributes to see whether the resource is present and on which attribute name.

Open the producer (constructor/factory) code and verify the parameter list, every assignment to self.<attr>, and any forwarding to super().__init__ or other helpers. Look for missing assignments, typos in attribute names (e.g., embedded vs embeded), or accidental assignment to a temporary/local variable instead of self.<attr>.

Search all call-sites that construct/instantiate the object (grep for the class/factory name). Confirm callers use the intended keyword name or positional ordering; mismatched caller usage can leave the attribute unset if the constructor expects a differently named kwarg.

Audit conditional control flow inside the constructor or initialization helpers: ensure there is no early return, exception path, or branch that leaves the attribute unset. Pay attention to branches that set the attribute only when a related flag is true.
Look for subsequent code that may overwrite or clear the attribute (assignment to None, reinitialization, or reusing the attribute name for another purpose) between construction and consumption.

If the attribute can be created from a path (e.g., embeded_image_path) verify the code actually opens/loads the resource and assigns it to the same attribute the consumer expects; confirm failure modes (file not found) do not silently leave the attribute None.

Add a defensive check in the consumer before calling methods on the attribute: if the attribute is None, raise an informative error or fall back to documented behavior. Use explicit validation in the constructor to raise early on invalid/missing inputs instead of deferring to an AttributeError later.

Add targeted unit tests that construct the object with representative argument forms (kwarg and positional) and assert the instance attribute is set and that the render/save call succeeds. Use these tests to prevent regressions from refactors or renames.

skill.title: Coordinate axis-swap in geometric transform: wrong column or image-dimension used
skill.trigger: A transform (consumer) that maps Nx2 coordinate arrays produces outputs where the unexpected coordinate column changes (e.g., y changes when a horizontal flip was requested) or the implementation uses the wrong image bound (height vs width) in the arithmetic. Structural applicability: the transform is an instance (state owner / constructor) that stores separate dimension attributes (width, height or similar) and an apply_coords-like consumer updates a specific coords[:, index] column using one of those stored bounds or an index constant.
knowledge: Reproduce with a few deterministic points placed on known axes (e.g., points with distinct x and y). Assert which column (coords[:,0] vs coords[:,1]) changes after applying the transform to detect an axis-swap.

Inspect the apply_coords (consumer) implementation for occurrences of coords[:, 0] and coords[:, 1]. Confirm which index is updated and whether the arithmetic references self.width or self.height (or similarly named instance attributes).

Check the constructor (producer / state owner) to see which attributes are stored (width, height, size, image_shape) and whether those names are consistently used by apply_coords and inverse. Mismatched naming or copied logic from the opposite flip (e.g., VFlip -> HFlip) is a common source.

Verify inverse() and any composition: a correct transform should round-trip for representative points. If inverse composes the same mistaken arithmetic, round-trip will fail and highlights the mapping is implemented consistently wrong.

Search the file/module for sibling implementations (VFlipTransform, RotateTransform, etc.) and compare their apply_coords code. Copy-paste errors often flip the index/attribute pair (index 0 ↔ index 1, width ↔ height).

Audit off-by-one adjustments: check whether the arithmetic uses bound, bound - 1, or bound - 0.5 depending on coordinate conventions. Ensure chosen adjustment matches the project's coordinate convention and is applied to the correct axis.
When index arithmetic is used directly, replace magic numeric indices with named constants or local variables (e.g., X_COL=0, Y_COL=1) before making changes to reduce future confusion.

Add a focused unit test asserting both single-axis transforms (apply to points that differ only in x or only in y) and a round-trip test (apply then inverse) for a small set of points to prevent regressions.
If behavior depends on input shape, assert input has shape (N,2) and raise or document clear errors otherwise; ensure code paths for Nx2 vectors do not mix flattened or transposed indexing.

If multiple coordinate conventions exist (pixel centers vs edges, origin top-left vs bottom-left), document the convention and check consistency across transforms and tests; include explicit examples in test assertions.

skill.title: Local value read before assignment across conditional control flow and nested closures
skill.trigger: A function, constructor, or helper closure (producer/constructor) is expected to compute formatting/state values (e.g., formatter, digits, na_rep, fixed_width) but those locals are assigned only on some control-flow paths or are moved after their first use; a consumer (rendering path, nested closure, or later code) unconditionally reads the local and the program raises NameError/UnboundLocalError or produces incorrect output. Applies when per-call or per-instance formatting state is computed in the same function scope or in an initializer and nested closures or unconditional code assume it is already initialized.
knowledge: Confirm the failure and variable: reproduce the NameError/UnboundLocalError and capture the traceback to see which function/closure and which name triggered the error.

Search for the name across the function/class: find all assignments (local and self.*) and all reads. Look for patterns like 'digits =', 'na_rep =', 'formatter =', or reads of self.digits that appear before assignments.

Enumerate control-flow paths: identify branches, early returns, try/except blocks, and conditional assignments. For each path that reaches the read site, ensure the variable was assigned on that path.

Remember Python scoping rules: if a name is assigned anywhere in a function, it is local to that function; earlier references (even textually before the assignment) will raise UnboundLocalError if they occur on a path before the assignment. Nested closures add complexity: if the outer function assigns the name later, closures that reference the name may see it unset at invocation time.

Pay attention to reorders during refactor: moved lines can change the initialization-before-use relationship without changing types. Use the VCS diff to detect assignment lines relocated below consumers.

Check nested helper closures: either assign the required value before defining/invoking the closure, or pass the value explicitly (e.g., as a default argument or parameter) so the closure captures the intended value rather than relying on outer-scope timing.

Distinguish instance attributes vs locals: if other code expects persistent per-instance state, consider storing the value on self (self.digits) and ensuring __init__/constructor sets it deterministically; otherwise prefer local variables computed before use.

Repro unit tests: construct minimal inputs that exercise each branch (e.g., fixed_width True/False, presence/absence of NaNs, complex vs float dtype) to trigger the missing-assignment path and verify the fix.

Fix options: hoist/early-initialize the variable before any conditional/closure that might use it; initialize with a safe default; move assignment above early returns; or pass the value into closures explicitly. Prefer explicit initialization over relying on fall-through control flow.

Broader sweep: search the codebase for similar patterns by looking for formatting/renderer classes and functions that compute per-call state and for occurrences of NameError/UnboundLocalError in recent diffs or tests after refactors.

skill.title: async-timeout repository architecture
knowledge: Public API factories timeout(delay) and timeout_at(deadline) are defined in async_timeout.__init__.py and return a Timeout context-manager object exported by the package (__all__ contains "timeout", "timeout_at", "Timeout").

The repository provides two implementation paths depending on Python version: on Python >= 3.11 a thin wrapper adapts asyncio.Timeout to the package API; on older Pythons a custom Timeout class implements the async context-manager behavior itself.

The custom Timeout implementation manages an explicit state machine (states include INIT, ENTER, TIMEOUT, EXIT) and stores per-instance fields like _task and _timeout_handler to track the monitored task and the scheduled loop handle.

Timeout scheduling and cancellation are performed via the asyncio event loop: the implementation uses loop.call_at / loop.call_soon to schedule the timeout handler, cancels the monitored task on timeout, sets the state to TIMEOUT, and clears the handler reference early.

Responsibility boundaries: the public factory functions hand deadline and (optionally) the event loop into the Timeout object; the Timeout object is responsible for scheduling, state transitions, canceling the task on timeout, and raising asyncio.TimeoutError to signal expiration.

The test suite (tests/test_timeout.py) exercises timeout behaviors, so tests are a reliable place to find expected behavioral contracts for deadline handling, shifting/updating deadlines, and context-manager semantics.

skill.title: Deadline/timing value is transformed, coerced, or converted incorrectly between producer and scheduler
knowledge: Reproduce with the simplest example that uses the public factory (timeout, timeout_at) and a literal small deadline; log whether timeout occurs immediately. Capture loop.time(), passed-in deadline, stored _deadline, and scheduled handler arguments.

Inspect public factories (timeout, timeout_at): confirm whether they accept relative delays or absolute loop times, whether they call get_running_loop() vs new_event_loop(), and whether they convert by adding loop.time() or pass values through unchanged. Look for explicit arithmetic like deadline - 5 or loop.time() + delay.

Open Timeout.__init__, update, shift, and _reschedule: check how _deadline is stored (None vs numeric sentinel), whether sentinels are introduced (0.0, -1.0), and whether update/shift perform correct arithmetic (relative ↔ absolute conversions).

Verify scheduling API usage: call_later expects a relative delay, call_at expects an absolute loop time. Ensure the code does not pass an absolute timestamp to call_later or a relative delay to call_at. Also check callbacks' argument order and whether call_later/call_at are given the intended delay/time value.

Search for accidental sentinel coercion: replacing None with 0.0 or returning -1.0 from deadline property changes control flow checks that rely on None and can cause immediate scheduling or skipped scheduling.

Check event-loop selection and epoch consistency: using a different loop (new_event_loop) or mixing loop.time() values from different loops can produce epoch mismatches. Ensure loop used to compute/interpret deadlines is the same one passed to scheduling calls.

Audit recent diffs for arithmetic offsets, swapped conversions, or changes to how deadlines are stored/returned. Focus on edits that introduce constants, change None handling, or modify scheduling calls.

Add targeted unit tests: small-timeouts using timeout_at and timeout with numeric literals, tests for None/unset deadlines, tests for shift/update behavior. Use tests to assert that no immediate timeout occurs for positive deadlines and that cancelling/rejecting behaves correctly.
skill.trigger: A consumer observes immediate timeouts or ignored deadlines when a deadline/timing value flows from a producer (public factory or caller) into a scheduler/Timeout implementation. Applicable when the code performs arithmetic on the deadline (adds/subtracts offsets), replaces None with numeric sentinels, converts between relative and absolute time bases (loop.time() epochs), selects the wrong event loop, or uses scheduling APIs with mismatched semantics (passing an absolute timestamp to call_later or a relative delay to call_at).

skill.title: Constructor branch omits initializing per-instance runtime state (loop/handler/state)
knowledge: Reproduce with minimal callers: construct the object via each public factory/constructor path (including version-guarded factories) and immediately inspect the private/runtime fields the tests or consumers access (e.g., _loop, _timeout_handler, _state, expired). Do this both before and after __aenter__/enter when relevant to confirm where attributes are expected to exist.

Locate every implementation/branch that can produce the object (factory functions, version checks, subclass choices). Confirm which concrete class is constructed for each environment and follow its __init__ / delegation chain to see where attributes should be set.

Audit constructor control flow (including delegation to super().__init__): ensure that every branch either assigns the same per-instance attributes or documents why those fields are only available after enter(). Pay special attention to branches that call super().__init__ and rely on the base class to provide fields — verify the base actually sets them or add missing assignments in the subclass.

Compare behavior to the previous/older implementation: identify fields that tests or callers have relied on historically (e.g., older custom Timeout set self._loop = loop). Use tests as a specification for required post-construction state when upgrading to delegate-based implementations.

Search for typos, different attribute names, or assignments to local variables instead of self.<attr>. Also check for accidental overwrites (setting to None or reusing names) after initial assignment.

If some state is only meaningful after entering the context, prefer making that explicit in the public contract (docstring/tests) or ensure __init__ still sets placeholder values (e.g., None) so attribute access is well-defined (and can raise a clearer error if misused).

When responsibilities are split between factory and constructor, verify the factory forwards necessary runtime parameters (e.g., loop) and the constructor stores them on the instance consistently in all code paths.

Add targeted unit tests that construct via every factory/branch and assert the expected runtime attributes exist (or that enter() populates them if documented). Use these tests to prevent regressions during refactors or when introducing delegation to stdlib classes.

When fixing, prefer minimal, explicit changes: either assign the missing attributes in the constructor branch (e.g., self._loop = loop; self._timeout_handler = None; initialize internal _state), or change factories/tests consistently if the design intentionally defers initialization until enter(). Avoid subtle defaults (e.g., switching None to 0.0) that change semantics — align with the intended contract.
skill.trigger: A consumer (test or caller) raises AttributeError when accessing private instance fields immediately after construction or entering a context manager because one constructor/factory branch or selected implementation (e.g., a version-guarded subclass or delegated super().__init__ call) does not assign the runtime fields (loop, scheduled handler, state owner) that other branches or previous implementations provide.

skill.title: termcolor repository architecture
knowledge: Package __init__ (src/termcolor/__init__.py) is the public API surface: it re-exports ATTRIBUTES, COLORS, HIGHLIGHTS, RESET, colored, and cprint for top-level imports and defines __all__ accordingly.

Core runtime logic lives in src/termcolor/termcolor.py: it defines the ANSI mapping constants (ATTRIBUTES, COLORS, HIGHLIGHTS) and the RESET sequence and constructs ANSI escape codes used to colorize text.
The module termcolor.termcolor exposes the public functions colored(...) and cprint(...). cprint is a thin convenience wrapper that prints the result of colored().

Color-output decision logic is centralized in a helper (e.g., _can_do_colour) that inspects environment and the output stream (sys.stdout), uses os-level isatty/fileno checks, and explicitly handles UnsupportedOperation from fileno() to decide whether to emit ANSI sequences.
colored and cprint accept override flags (no_color and force_color) to bypass the automatic TTY/environment-based detection.
Type definitions and aliases are provided in src/termcolor/_types.py and are used to document/validate allowed attribute, color, and highlight names for the public API.
A command-line entrypoint exists at src/termcolor/__main__.py which invokes the package's printing/coloring behavior for CLI use.

Tests (tests/test_termcolor.py) exercise the public API (colored, cprint, and constants) rather than internal implementation, so callers should look at the exported functions and constants when reproducing behavior or locating regressions.

Responsibility boundaries: __init__ = API surface; termcolor.py = all logic for deciding color emission and for composing ANSI sequences; _types.py = typing/allowed value definitions; __main__.py = CLI invocation logic.

skill.title: Environment/TTY gating short-circuits terminal formatting
knowledge: Start at the gate: search for a helper/guard that checks environment variables and TTY state and that short-circuits formatting (patterns like `if not can_do_colour: return str(text)` or early returns based on env/tty checks).

Reproduce the environment locally: set/clear NO_COLOR, ANSI_COLORS_DISABLED, FORCE_COLOR and monkeypatch os.isatty/sys.stdout.isatty and sys.stdout.fileno to observe whether the consumer begins emitting escape sequences. Tests often monkeypatch these, so mirror test fixtures.

Check boolean logic and negations carefully: confirm parameter/argument names (no_color vs force_color) are respected and not inverted, and that conditionals use the intended truthiness (look for accidentally-negated conditions or swapped parameter usage).

Inspect precedence and ordering of overrides: user-level flags, function parameters, and env vars may have intended precedence (e.g., explicit function args should override NO_COLOR). Verify implementation honors documented override semantics.

Handle fileno/isatty fallbacks and exceptions: fileno() can raise UnsupportedOperation; ensure code falls back to sys.stdout.isatty() or treats exceptions according to intended semantics (and does not invert the result).

If the gate permits formatting, then inspect the composer: verify mapping tables (color vs highlight) are used in the correct places, RESET/termination codes are appended, wrapping order of color/highlight/attributes matches expectations, and that attribute iteration order is intentional (bugs can make codes appear swapped).

Search for swapped parameter passing between wrapper functions (e.g., cprint calling colored) where arguments or keyword values might be passed in the wrong order or swapped (no_color/force_color inverted when forwarded).

When triaging remotely, prioritize tests that assert colored(...) returns escape sequences — they often indicate the intended gate behavior and show how tests manipulate env/tty helpers to force the gate on.
skill.trigger: A formatting API (consumer) returns plain or unmodified output or omits terminal escape sequences because a producer or gating helper (state owner) that checks environment variables and TTY state (e.g. NO_COLOR / ANSI_COLORS_DISABLED / FORCE_COLOR, TERM value, os.isatty, sys.stdout.isatty, fileno behavior) evaluates to 'disabled' and the implementation short-circuits (early return or skip) before composing terminal sequences. Applicable when the project contains a centralized gate/guard that decides whether the formatter emits effects.

skill.title: Consumer/wrapper swaps arguments or flag values when calling a producer, reversing semantics
knowledge: Locate thin wrappers and adapters: search for calls to the suspected producer (e.g., grep for colored( or other producer name) and inspect nearby wrapper/printing helpers (consumer roles like cprint).

Compare wrapper calls to the producer's declared signature: ensure positional arguments align with parameter order; prefer inspecting keyword usage where present—positional forwarding is a common source of accidental swaps.

Reproduce with and without the wrapper: call the producer directly with identical named arguments and compare repr/output to the wrapper's output to determine whether the inversion occurs at the wrapper boundary.
Check boolean/flag arguments specifically (e.g., no_color vs force_color): confirm the wrapper doesn't swap these values or pass the wrong variable into the wrong named parameter.
When the code uses positional forwarding, review recent diffs or refactors that changed parameter order or added parameters—API signature changes often break positional callers.

If wrappers intentionally reorder or adapt parameters, document and test the mapping; consider replacing positional forwarding with explicit keyword arguments in the wrapper to make the mapping robust and self-documenting.

If the producer composes outputs (e.g., formats or nests strings), verify both producer and wrapper composition orders: a correctly ordered producer can still produce swapped results if the wrapper passes arguments in reversed slots.
Use small focused tests around each boundary: assert that wrapper(text, color=X, on_color=Y) equals producer(text, color=X, on_color=Y) to pin the failure location quickly.
skill.trigger: A caller/consumer (e.g., a wrapper, convenience function, or thin adapter) produces systematically swapped or inverted outputs compared to directly invoking the lower-level producer/constructor because it passes positional arguments in the wrong order or swaps boolean/flag parameters when invoking the producer. Observability: the producer implementation appears to construct correct values for given inputs, but using the public wrapper yields reversed semantics (e.g., foreground/background swapped, flag behavior inverted). Structural applicability: a thin wrapper or re-export immediately forwards arguments to a producer (positional or positional-mixed calls), or the project has recently changed producer parameter ordering or names.

colored and cprint accept override flags (no_color and force_color) to bypass the automatic TTY/environment-based detection.
Type definitions and aliases are provided in src/termcolor/_types.py and are used to document/validate allowed attribute, color, and highlight names for the public API.
A command-line entrypoint exists at src/termcolor/__main__.py which invokes the package's printing/coloring behavior for CLI use.

Tests (tests/test_termcolor.py) exercise the public API (colored, cprint, and constants) rather than internal implementation, so callers should look at the exported functions and constants when reproducing behavior or locating regressions.

Responsibility boundaries: __init__ = API surface; termcolor.py = all logic for deciding color emission and for composing ANSI sequences; _types.py = typing/allowed value definitions; __main__.py = CLI invocation logic.

skill.title: Jinja2 repository architecture
knowledge: The Environment class (src/jinja2/environment.py) is the central orchestration point: it holds configuration, the loader, registered extensions/filters/tests/globals, and is responsible for creating/looking up templates and coordinating compilation and caching.

Template source is processed by a compilation pipeline composed of the lexer (src/jinja2/lexer.py), parser (src/jinja2/parser.py), AST/nodes (src/jinja2/nodes.py and optimizer), and the compiler (src/jinja2/compiler.py) which produces executable code objects consumed by the runtime.

Loaders (src/jinja2/loaders.py) provide template source/metadata to Environment, and bytecode/bytecode-cache support (src/jinja2/bccache.py) is used by Environment to store and retrieve compiled templates to avoid recompilation.

Runtime execution and rendering are performed by the runtime/context modules (src/jinja2/runtime.py and related code); the runtime enforces undefined handling, applies filters/tests, and executes the compiled code objects produced by the compiler.

skill.title: Whitespace-normalization helper removes runs instead of collapsing them to a single separator or uses wrong strip variant
knowledge: Reproduce the symptom with a minimal example: a trimmed templated/localized block containing internal newlines and multiple spaces (e.g., '{%- trans trimmed %}  a\n  b  {% endtrans -%}'). Confirm both render output and extraction/catalog output show concatenated tokens.

Search the codebase for small helpers and regexes related to whitespace normalization (names like trim, chomp, _ws_re, _trim_whitespace, normalize_whitespace) and for calls to regex.sub that operate on message text.

Open the helper implementation and inspect the regex.sub replacement argument — confirm whether it replaces matched runs with '' (empty string) or with ' ' (single space). Replacing with '' causes concatenation; replacing with ' ' collapses runs to a single separator.

Check whether the helper calls string.strip(), lstrip(), or rstrip() before/after substitution. Using lstrip()/rstrip() asymmetrically can remove intended separators at one boundary; strip() preserves the expected single-space normalization semantics when combined with a single-space replacement.

Trace call sites: determine whether the producer that constructs the canonical message lives at parse/AST construction time (parser/constructor) or is performed later by consumers (render/extract). If both runtime rendering and extraction observe the same bad output, prefer producer-side investigation (parser/helper) as the canonical text may be built too early and reused.

Verify that extraction code (message catalog writer) does not apply a second normalization or different helper that could mask/alter producer behavior. If multiple helpers exist, ensure they use consistent replacement strings and strip semantics.

Add unit tests that assert normalization semantics: input strings with leading/trailing whitespace, internal newlines, and multiple spaces should normalize to a single separating space when 'trimmed' is requested. Include tests that cover both rendering and extraction paths.

When fixing, prefer an explicit replacement of runs with a single space (e.g., re.sub(_ws_re, ' ', s.strip())) and use clear local variable names for the helper's steps (raw -> stripped -> normalized). If trimming should only affect internal runs but preserve a single surrounding space policy, document expected behavior near the helper.

If the helper is exported/used across parser and extractor boundaries, ensure it is referenced rather than reimplemented; add a small comment in the helper explaining semantics (why replacement is a single space and why strip() is used).
skill.trigger: A producer (parser/constructor or a small shared whitespace-normalization helper) is responsible for producing canonical, serialized message text for templated/localized blocks. Observable failure: both runtime rendering and message-extraction/serialization produce concatenated tokens (no separating space) where a 'trimmed' or normalization option should yield single separating spaces. Applicable when the repository uses a dedicated whitespace helper (e.g., _trim_whitespace or an _ws_re regex) referenced from parse/AST construction or extraction code paths.

skill.title: pyquery repository architecture
knowledge: The package exports the PyQuery API class from pyquery/pyquery.py (pyquery/__init__.py imports PyQuery).
pyquery/pyquery.py is the core implementation: it handles parsing input (strings/files/URLs), builds element lists, provides selector-based querying and serialization/manipulation methods.
CSS selector translation is delegated to cssselectpatch.JQueryTranslator (pyquery/cssselectpatch.py) which converts CSS selectors to XPath used by the core.
Network and file fetching is centralized in pyquery/openers.py (notably url_opener); PyQuery calls url_opener when given a URL.
Text extraction and formatting utilities used by the core are in pyquery/text.py (e.g. extract_text).

skill.title: Public API returns caller object incorrectly because replacement/insertion path mutates state or returns a different value
knowledge: Search the public API and every helper it calls for all 'return' sites. Ensure every code path that handles the callback/function-argument replacement returns the caller object (self) or otherwise preserves the documented return contract.

If the replacement path delegates to a helper that 'produces' nodes/text, inspect whether the public API returns the helper's return value rather than 'self' (accidental propagation of None). Prefer an explicit final 'return self' at the API boundary.

Audit string/text concatenation sites around insertion points (e.g., previous.tail, parent.text). Confirm whether code uses '+=' vs assignment and verify the intended order (new text appended vs prepended). Compare with equivalent insertion helpers to find intended semantics.

Check cloning/deepcopy and list-slicing logic used to insert cloned nodes. Validate index computations and slice lengths (off-by-one bugs often change ordering or leave/misplace elements). Create small reproducer snippets that exercise i==0 vs i>0 branches to reveal slicing/cloning mistakes.

Trace consumer vs producer roles: label the public method as consumer, helper that evaluates callback as producer. For callback paths, validate both the producer's output shape (list of nodes, strings) and how the consumer uses that output; add defensive normalization if shapes vary.
Look for subtle condition changes (e.g., 'if i > 0' vs 'if i >= 1') that alter whether cloning occurs or which branch executes; test boundary values (i==0, i==1) specifically.

If the method mutates tree text fields (element.text, element.tail), add tests for nodes with and without existing text to cover both None-to-string transitions and empty-string concatenation semantics.

When changing concatenation order, prefer explicit, well-documented operations (e.g., parent.text = parent.text + new_text or new_text + parent.text) and add unit tests asserting expected markup for both insertion-before and insertion-after cases.

Add targeted unit tests that assert both the return value (is the caller returned?) and the resulting document string/markup for function-argument replacement cases. Tests should cover multiple elements and callback return variants (strings, elements, PyQuery fragments).

When refactoring, prefer normalizing producer output to a single expected shape (sequence of nodes and separate text segments) and keep the public API responsible for final return semantics; if changing behavior, make the change at the API boundary and keep helpers pure.
skill.trigger: A public API (consumer) that should return the original caller object for chaining instead returns None or another unexpected type; the API delegates to an internal replacement/producer that evaluates callback/function-arguments and performs text/node insertion. The failure is observed together with incorrect text ordering or node placement (e.g., text prepended rather than appended) indicating concatenation or index-slicing mistakes in the replacement path.

skill.title: sqlfluff repository architecture
knowledge: The public 'simple' API (functions like lint, fix, parse) is implemented in src/sqlfluff/api/simple.py; it composes a FluffConfig and instantiates the core Linter to perform parsing, linting, and fixing (i.e., the simple API delegates work to core components rather than implementing parsing/lint logic itself).

The central linter implementation is the Linter class in src/sqlfluff/core/linter/linter.py; this core linter module orchestrates parsing, rule application, and fixes and returns linted-file/path results used by higher layers.

Configuration is centralized under src/sqlfluff/core/config (e.g., FluffConfig, loaders, ini/toml handlers); CLI and the public API build/resolve configurations via this subsystem and then pass the resulting FluffConfig into the Linter and other core components.

Dialect and grammar selection lives under src/sqlfluff/core/dialects (and related selector helpers); the chosen dialect controls parser behavior. Plugins (under plugins/) provide additional templaters and rules and are a documented extension point.

The CLI entrypoint and user-facing command wiring live under src/sqlfluff/__main__.py and src/sqlfluff/cli/* (commands, formatters, helpers); these CLI components format and display results but delegate core linting/fixing to the core Linter and config subsystems.

skill.title: Producer enumeration loop removed or short-circuited so returned collection remains empty
knowledge: Reproduce with a minimal input that should produce at least one entry, then run/debug to confirm the returned collection is empty while the enumeration path is exercised.

Search the source for the collection's name (e.g., 'variants', 'results', 'entries') and find where it is initialized and where writes (assignment, append, variants[...] = ...) should occur. Look for removed/absent write-sites inside loops.

Inspect loops/generator code that iterate candidate items: check for recently removed blocks that computed an item and then appended/assigned it to the collection. Pay attention to code that computed auxiliary values (score, trace, metadata) immediately before population.

Look for try/except blocks or broad exception swallowing added/removed around the write: a removed try/except that used to guard the compute+write, or a newly added try/except that continues on error, can silently skip population. Also check for added 'continue' or 'return' statements inside the loop.

Search version control diffs/commits around the file for deleted lines that contain the collection write (e.g., 'variants[', '.append(', 'results.append('). Deletions of a few lines inside the loop are a common signal.

Confirm any scoring/trace/validation helper calls used to produce the collection entries still return non-empty results. If helper outputs became empty, trace their inputs to see why (missing inputs or earlier gating).

Consider the consumer's expectations: find sorting/selection code that expects the collection to be populated (e.g., sorted(collection) or selecting top-N). Use those locations to infer the required key/value shape and reconstruct what write-site is missing.

Fix guidance: restore the removed assignment/append or adjust the loop so that successful enumeration paths always perform the write. If exceptions are possible, ensure they are handled without dropping valid items (log/skip invalid ones but still add valid results). Add unit tests that assert non-empty collection for known multi-branch inputs to prevent regression.
skill.trigger: A function (consumer) returns an empty collection/dictionary while upstream enumeration/producer code (a loop or generator inside the same module/class) is expected to populate that collection. The structural sign is a collection initialized locally and later read/returned, but there is no observed assignment/append into it — often caused by a deleted assignment statement inside the producer loop, an early continue/return, or an exception-handling change that skips the write.

skill.title: Hydra repository architecture
knowledge: The core runtime/package is the hydra/ package; hydra/__init__.py is the public surface that re-exports key APIs (e.g., compose, initialize, initialize_config_module, initialize_config_dir, main, utils, TaskFunction, and MissingConfigException).

The CLI and programmatic entrypoint 'main' is provided by hydra/main.py (exported via hydra.__init__), while configuration composition and runtime initialization are implemented in hydra/compose.py and hydra/initialize.py respectively — public helpers call into these modules to perform composition and initialization.
