Extension and launcher integrations live outside the core package under contrib/ and plugins/; for example, contrib/hydra_torchrun_launcher/hydra_plugins/hydra_torchrun_launcher implements a distributed launcher (distributed_launcher.py) that hooks into Hydra's launcher/plugin extension points.

Repository contains auxiliary and non-runtime responsibilities separated from core logic: build and packaging helpers live in build_helpers/ and packaging/setup files, and examples/ and tests/ exercise the public API and plugin interfaces rather than containing core implementation.

skill.title: Guard/branch ordering causes misclassification and wrong user-visible error message
knowledge: Search for code that selects among multiple error messages or handling branches based on scheme/type fields (e.g., source.scheme(), source.path, kind flags). Examine the exact guard order and else/elif arrangement near message construction.

Check for emptiness checks (e.g., path == '' or name == '') being placed after broader branch guards (e.g., scheme == 'pkg' or path-based lookups). Emptiness should often be tested early if it denotes a distinct semantic case.

Trace where the sentinel value is introduced (producer) and where it is consumed by the message-emitter (consumer). Confirm whether the consumer expects that sentinel as a valid path or should treat it specially.
Look for similar message strings nearby; maintainers sometimes accidentally duplicate message construction in multiple branches or forget to move the empty-case into the correct branch.
Add/inspect unit tests that assert the exact message text for edge inputs (empty module name, empty path). Tests that only check for exception type but not message can miss these misclassifications.

When fixing, prefer explicit, narrowly-placed checks for semantic sentinel cases (e.g., if source.path == '': emit module-empty message) before falling back to scheme-specific or filesystem-not-found logic. Keep message construction localized and avoid duplicating logic across branches.

If multiple branches depend on a small set of discriminators (scheme, path emptiness, provider), consider normalizing into a small decision classifier (compute a reason code) then map reason→message so ordering bugs are less likely.
Search commit history or nearby comments to see intended precedence (sometimes a later refactor re-ordered guards inadvertently).
skill.trigger: A consumer (error/diagnostic producer) emits an incorrect user-visible error message for an input sentinel (e.g., empty identifier/path) because conditional guards or scheme-specific branches are ordered or structured so that the sentinel satisfies an unintended branch. Observable symptom: a misleading 'not found' or wrong-domain message is shown even though upstream input should have been recognized as an 'empty' or domain-specific validation error.

skill.title: pdfplumber repository architecture
knowledge: pdfplumber.pdf defines the PDF document model (class PDF). PDF.open is exposed at package top-level (open = PDF.open in __init__.py) and is responsible for opening/repairing streams, parsing with pdfminer, and providing cached document-level properties (pages, objects, annotations, hyperlinks, structure tree).

pdfplumber.page implements the Page model: pages are constructed from pdfminer PDFPage objects, assembled with measured doctop offsets, and provide per-page primitives and extractors (characters, lines, images, annotations) used by higher-level analysis.
pdfplumber.container provides a Container base used by PDF and Page to share caching behavior and common property handling (centralizing lifecycle and cached attribute logic).
pdfplumber.repair contains PDF repair utilities (exported as repair) used when opening broken streams; it invokes external processing (ghostscript-based rebuilding) to produce reparable PDF streams.

skill.title: Literal-token vs primitive decoding branch swapped in transformation helper
knowledge: Search for patterns that iterate mappings (for k, v in obj.items()) and then conditionally call decoding utilities or access `.name`/token fields. These are frequent sites for operand/assignment mixups.

Inspect both the decode expressions and the assigned expression: confirm the variable passed to decode_text (or similar) is the same variable whose decoded result is stored. Look for uses of container[obj_key] or obj[k] instead of the local loop variable v.

Check any prior key-remap logic (e.g., handling when the surrounding object itself is a literal token). Ensure key decoding uses the object representing the key (or its .name) and not a different container reference.

Reproduce by constructing a mixed mapping with both parsed-literal tokens and plain primitives; exercise code paths that build the consumer-visible representation to trigger type errors (AttributeError on .name, missing string methods, or numeric values where strings expected).

Quick remediation pattern: when iterating (k, v), use: if is_literal(v): attr[k] = decode(v) else: attr[k] = v (or the appropriately normalized primitive). Fix swapped branches rather than adding more complex branching unless necessary.

Add defensive checks when decoding token attributes (use getattr(value, 'name', None) or isinstance checks) and add unit tests that include both literal-token objects and raw primitives to prevent regressions.

If the project uses external parser types (e.g., pdfminer PSLiteral), centralize conversion in a small helper (normalize_value(v)) and use it consistently; this reduces duplicated conditional logic and the chance of operand swap mistakes.

When changing the helper, trace all call sites (consumers) so you can verify whether callers expect decoded strings or raw objects; mismatches may require an API-compatible migration or additional adaptation at call sites.
skill.trigger: A consumer reports a type error (e.g., AttributeError) or observes raw parser token objects where decoded strings are expected because a transformation helper iterating mapping entries (k, v) applies decoding to the wrong operand or assigns the wrong source. Applicable when the code contains a branch that detects ‘literal-like’ parser tokens (a producer value, parser boundary, or literal-token type) and then performs decode/assignment expressions — but the decoded expression and the stored value are mismatched (for example, decode_text(v.name) applied in the non-literal branch, or attr[k] = container[k] used instead of attr[k] = v).

skill.title: Pygments repository architecture
knowledge: The public/high-level API lives in pygments.__init__ (functions lex(), format(), highlight()) and delegates work to Lexer and Formatter instances rather than implementing lexing/formatting inline.

Lexer infrastructure is implemented in pygments.lexer: base Lexer classes (and LexerMeta) own tokenization concerns, input normalization (stripnl/stripall/ensurenl/tab expansion) and filter application, and provide analyse_text hooks used by guesser utilities (e.g., guess_lexer).

Formatter infrastructure is implemented in pygments.formatter: the base Formatter resolves styles and encoding options, wraps or chooses appropriate output streams when an outfile is provided or omitted, and format()/format_unencoded return a string/bytes when outfile is None by creating an in-memory buffer (StringIO/BytesIO) depending on formatter.encoding.

Concrete implementations are organized under pygments/lexers/* (language-specific lexer modules) and pygments/formatters/* (output formatters like html, latex, terminal); CLI/console modules (pygments.cmdline, __main__, console) parse options and instantiate the appropriate Lexer and Formatter objects before calling the core API.

skill.title: Producer returns overconfident match scores (boolean/unbounded or boosted) that dominate dispatcher selection
knowledge: Locate analyser/producer implementations (e.g., analyse_text methods). Look for early returns of True/False or other non-float types — booleans may be coerced to numeric 1/0 by the dispatcher and treated as full confidence.
Check initial/baseline score initialization: producers should start from a neutral baseline (commonly 0) rather than a non-neutral value (e.g., 1) that biases selection.

Search for unbounded increments or multiplicative adjustments (e.g., result *= 2) that can blow up scores; prefer bounded additive adjustments and explicit score ranges (e.g., 0.0–1.0) or clamp/normalize at return time.

Inspect special-case handling (shebang, file header, metadata): ensure special-case returns are conservative (e.g., return a modest boost or a documented sentinel handled by the dispatcher) and not unconditional full-confidence values.

Review the dispatcher/guesser contract: how it interprets return values (booleans, integers, floats), how scores are compared/tied, and whether normalization or scaling happens before selection. Add tests asserting expected interpretation (e.g., True != max confidence unless documented).

Reproduce with minimal inputs that triggered the issue (short or punctuation-heavy snippets) and add unit tests to prevent regressions (examples: Brainfuck-like snippets, tiny C fragments, Forth one-liners).

Audit regexes and token matches in analysers for over-permissiveness: broad patterns that match single punctuation sequences or single-character tokens can inappropriately raise confidence for unrelated inputs.

When combining multiple heuristics, prefer composable, bounded contributions (weights that sum to a known range) and document expected output range; consider returning structured scores (e.g., normalized float plus reason) if the dispatcher supports it.

If a producer must return a boolean for legacy reasons, explicitly convert it at the producer-dispatch boundary or document and test its numeric interpretation to avoid accidental full-confidence behavior.
When changing analyser logic, run existing heuristic-based selection tests for nearby languages and add regression tests for tie-breaking scenarios to ensure deterministic, conservative dispatch.
skill.trigger: A dispatcher/guesser selects the wrong handler because a producer/analyser (producer role — e.g., Lexer.analyse_text) returns a boolean True or an excessively large/unnormalized numeric score (or applies aggressive multipliers) for inputs it should only weakly match (common with short or punctuation‑heavy snippets). Applicable when the project uses per-handler numeric/boolean heuristics aggregated by a dispatcher/guesser that lacks strict normalization or when producers may special-case shebangs or apply multiplicative score changes.

skill.title: pydicom repository architecture
knowledge: The package __init__.py re-exports the public API (e.g. dcmread, dcmwrite, Dataset/FileDataset, pixel_array, version info), so top-level imports delegate to implementations in filereader, filewriter, and dataset modules.
filereader.py is the central entry point for reading/parsing DICOM files: it implements dcmread and the data element generator that parses binary input into RawDataElement/DataElement sequences.
dataset.py defines Dataset (a dict subclass) and FileDataset and owns in-memory dataset behavior and private-tag management; higher-level operations on datasets are implemented there.

Pixel decoding is modular: pixel_data_handlers/ and pixels/decoders/ contain pluggable backends (numpy, pillow, gdcm, pylibjpeg, rle, etc.), and pixel-array decoding is dispatched to those handlers rather than being implemented inline in filereader or dataset.

skill.title: Caller forwards positional arguments in wrong order to callee, causing state/flag inversion
knowledge: Locate the callee's function signature (or NamedTuple/tuple field order) and write down the exact positional parameter order and the semantic meaning of each parameter (e.g., length, bytelength, is_undefined_length).

Search (grep) for all call sites that invoke the callee; filter for positional-only or positional-heavy calls. Pay special attention to calls that pass parsed/local variables in the same order the file parser yields them.

At each suspicious call-site, compare the caller's variable meanings to the callee parameter names: confirm that the nth positional argument corresponds semantically to the callee's nth parameter. Look for swapped names (length vs bytelength, sentinel vs boolean) or use of sentinel values in the wrong slot.

If the callee supports keyword arguments, temporarily change the call-site to use explicit keyword arguments to verify whether the bug disappears—this both confirms the root cause and documents a robust fix.

Add minimal unit tests that construct the parsed inputs (or simulate parsed values) and call the callee via the problematic call-site; assert the callee's returned state or object's attribute semantics (e.g., is_undefined_length True/False) to catch regressions.

When a NamedTuple is used as a simple data carrier, check its field order in the definition and all places that build it positionally; prefer constructing NamedTuples via keyword unpacking or by name to avoid fragile order-dependent bugs.

If swapping is found across multiple call-sites, consider centralizing the construction into a single helper with a clear signature or converting positional parameters to keyword-only to make the API safer.
skill.trigger: An observable state or boolean field on an object/returned value has the opposite semantics (e.g., 'undefined' vs 'defined', True vs False) and the code path shows a producer/caller that parses/derives values and then calls another function/factory using positional arguments rather than keywords. Applicable when the callee declares positional parameters (or a NamedTuple/tuple factory) whose order must match the caller's positional invocation.

skill.title: Submodule accesses parent-package symbol at import time (missing package initialization / circular import)
knowledge: Reproduce the failure with the minimal import expression (e.g., 'import package' and 'from package import X') to confirm the NameError arises during import time rather than at runtime later in a constructor.

Open the failing submodule and inspect top-level (module-level) code for references like 'import package', 'package.settings', 'package.usage_tracker', or any package.* attribute reads executed at import time (not inside a function/method).

Check package.__init__.py: if it imports the submodule (e.g., 'from package.submodule import *' or 'from package import submodule'), note that this creates an import-time cycle that can leave the package symbol undefined inside the submodule.
Search VCS diffs or recent commits for removed 'import package' lines or refactors that relocated or deleted the top-level import/initialization call in the submodule.

Distinguish two common patterns: (1) missing top-level 'import package' (simple omission) vs (2) circular import / import-order problem where package.__init__ imports the submodule so package is not fully initialized when the submodule reads package.*.

If the consumer needs package-level settings/state, prefer importing the precise module that provides the configuration (internal module path) rather than referencing the parent package object; or move the import/use inside a function/constructor so it runs after import-time initialization.

As an immediate mitigation, restore the missing import (if it was accidentally removed) or defer package attribute access by moving module-level code into functions/methods or lazily importing within the call site.

When restructuring, avoid package.__init__ importing submodules that themselves read package-level attributes; expose explicit submodule imports from package.__init__ only if those submodules do not depend on package-level mutable initialization.
Add a small import-time unit test (import package) to catch regressions where package import raises NameError or triggers circular-import initialization failures.

When proposing fixes, prefer minimal, explicit changes: reintroduce the missing import line if appropriate, or replace 'import package; package.attr' with a direct import of the provider module or deferred lookup inside runtime code.
skill.trigger: Importing the package (or doing 'from package import X') raises NameError for the package identifier or a related package-level attribute because a submodule performs module-level accesses to package.* (consumer) during its import while the package-level producer (package.__init__ or a top-level import) is absent, removed, or not yet initialized — often coupled with package.__init__ importing that submodule (creating a circular import/import-order dependency).

skill.title: Dynamic-programming consumer invoked or returned-from before DP matrix is produced (premature backtrack / early-return ordering error)
knowledge: Reproduce with a minimal deterministic input and assert the expected alignment or matrix shape; if outputs are wrong but matrix values are missing/zero/undefined, suspect ordering issues rather than neighbor-index arithmetic.

Search for early return statements or calls to the backtracking/consumer function placed before the loop that fills the DP matrix. Pay attention to misplaced calls inserted before initialization (e.g., self.backtrack(...) called prior to building score_matrix).

Look for variable-definition/assignment moves (e.g., len2 assigned earlier) or docstring/comment block edits that accidentally reordered code. Verify that the score/matrix variable exists and has the expected shape and contents at the point where the consumer is invoked.

Instrument the code: add asserts or short runtime checks immediately before backtrack/return points (e.g., assert score_matrix is not None and score_matrix.shape == (len1+1, len2+1)) to catch premature consumption in tests.

Dump/log the DP matrix immediately after population and immediately before backtrack to confirm whether the matrix was built and populated as intended. If the pre-backtrack dump is empty/default, ordering is wrong.

Audit control-flow that handles optional return paths (e.g., return_score_matrix flags, early return for edge cases): ensure each return path only references variables that have been defined in that control flow and do not assume a matrix exists unless it was built on every code path.

Check for accidental reordering introduced by merge conflicts, indentation errors, or block movement — inspect surrounding edits that move variable assignments, returns, or backtrack calls relative to the DP-population loop.

If the consumer is a separate method, verify call sites: ensure no call to the consumer occurs before the caller has fully prepared required inputs. If the consumer is invoked inside get_alignment, ensure the matrix construction completes on all code paths first.

Add focused unit tests that exercise both normal and return_score_matrix / optional branches; assert that matrix-producing code runs before any consumer invocation and that no consumer is invoked when matrix is empty.

If reordering is necessary for refactoring, introduce explicit invariants or helper functions (e.g., build_score_matrix(...) returns the matrix) so call order is enforced and the surface area for ordering mistakes is reduced.
skill.trigger: A function that implements a DP-style algorithm (producer that fills an explicit DP/score/cost matrix) returns incorrect results, raises NameError/UnboundLocalError, or reconstructs a nonsensical path for small deterministic inputs because a consumer (backtracker or return branch) is called or a return executed before the producer finished initializing or filling the matrix/auxiliary data structures. The codebase contains both the producer and consumer responsibilities (matrix fill + backtrack/return) in the same scope such that reordering or misplaced returns can cause premature consumption of uninitialized data.

skill.title: cantools repository architecture
knowledge: The public CLI entrypoint is implemented in src/cantools/__init__.py: it builds an argparse-based top-level parser, dynamically loads subparsers from src/cantools/subparsers, and dispatches by calling a function stored on args (args.func) for the chosen subcommand.

The canonical in-memory CAN database representation is the Database class in src/cantools/database/can/database.py. This Database owns message/signal/node/bus domain objects and provides lookup/registration APIs used by higher-level operations and format loaders.

Format-specific parsing and enrichment is implemented under src/cantools/database/can/formats (modules for dbc, arxml, kcd, sym are present). These format loaders read external files and populate or amend the canonical Database rather than implementing a separate database model.

Diagnostic/UDS functionality (diagnostic database, DIDs, and related tooling) is implemented separately under src/cantools/database/diagnostics, providing a distinct diagnostic database and helpers that interoperate with the core CAN domain model.

skill.title: Local state assigned in the wrong conditional branch (branch reorder/indentation causes None read)
knowledge: Reproduce with a small snippet driving the same control-flow pattern (loop or nested ifs) so you can exercise each branch and observe the local variable (print/debug) before the consumer uses it; check which branches assign, clear, or call cleanup on the local value.

Open the enclosing function and examine the conditional and loop nesting levels: verify that assignments, cleanup calls, and dependent calls are all in the intended branch. Look specifically for swapped else blocks, mis-indentation, or lines moved up/down that change which branch they belong to.

Trace the variable's definition and reassignment across the loop/iteration boundary: ensure the variable is initialized on every path that reaches the consumer and that no path leaves it as None. Pay attention to 'if X: do A; else: do B; use variable' patterns and confirm the variable is set consistently.

Look for paired actions (e.g., compute axes vs. finish_subplot) that must run together; ensure their relative order and branch placement are preserved. A common mistake is moving a cleanup or update call into the same branch as the consumer or into the opposite branch, breaking the intended producer/consumer contract.

Add defensive checks before dereferencing the local value: if None, raise a clear error message or choose a documented fallback. Prefer explicit initialization at the top of the function so the variable has a defined value on all paths, and avoid relying on implicit branch-dependent creation when possible.

Add unit tests that exercise boundary conditions: first-iteration vs subsequent-iteration behavior, missing/empty input sets, and combinations of flags that steer branches. Tests should assert that the local value is set and valid before consumers run to catch regressions from refactors or indentation fixes.

When reviewing diffs, pay extra attention to moved lines and indentation-only changes: these can silently switch a statement between branches. Use git blame / patch context to see whether an assignment or finish/cleanup call was accidentally shifted.

If the function is long or complex, refactor to smaller helpers with explicit contracts (producer returns value or raises). Making producer/consumer boundaries explicit reduces the chance that a local assignment ends up in the wrong branch.
skill.trigger: A consumer in the same function or loop dereferences a local value (e.g., calls .axes or other attribute) and fails with AttributeError/None behavior because earlier assignment or cleanup for that local value was placed in the opposite branch (or mis-indented), or an else/then block was swapped, leaving the local variable None on the path the consumer executes.

skill.title: Astroid repository architecture
knowledge: AstroidManager (in astroid/manager.py) centralizes building and caching of astroid representations: it avoids rebuilding the same module, provides the build entrypoints, and decides between loading from source, stubs, or extensions.
astroid/astroid_manager.py instantiates the global MANAGER singleton (MANAGER = AstroidManager()) and immediately calls register_all_brains(MANAGER) to register inference extensions.

The builder (astroid/builder.py) is the component responsible for constructing astroid trees from source strings/files/objects; AstroidManager delegates actual construction to the builder when needed.
Library- and stdlib-specific inference logic is implemented as separate brain modules under astroid/brain and those brains are registered with the manager to extend inference and type knowledge.

skill.title: Incorrect fallback-branch polarity or call-context construction causes alternative-resolution to return default/uninferable
knowledge: Locate the try/except or guard that attempts the primary lookup and then falls back to an alternative resolution. Confirm the polarity of any isinstance/is-checks or conditionals that decide which branch is the fallback versus the original path.

When an alternative 'methods' or candidate list is produced, check whether bound vs unbound resolution implies selecting first vs last element. Print or trace representative contents (types, bound-state) to confirm which list element is the actual callable to invoke.

Inspect how the call/analysis context is constructed for invoking the resolved method: ensure CallContext/args include the correct callee and that positional arguments match the callee's expectation (missing callee or wrong arg shape can make dispatch raise AttributeError or the call produce Uninferable).

Verify semantics of return/fallback on AttributeInferenceError and related exceptions: ensure the code distinguishes 'no candidate' vs 'candidate present but invocation failed', and returns the appropriate sentinel (e.g., Uninferable) or the node itself in each case according to project conventions.

Trace one concrete repro (typing.List[int], collections.abc.Set[str], or a class defining __class_getitem__) through the code path: log which branch was taken, which candidate method was chosen, and whether infer_call_result is actually invoked on that object. Swapping to the other branch or selecting the other list index should change the behavior in a reproducible way.

Add assertions or unit tests that exercise both primary and fallback branches (including empty candidate lists) and check that the inference result is the expected ClassDef/type rather than the default sentinel. Tests should include builtin generics, typing generics, and a custom class with __class_getitem__.

When modifying fallback logic, prefer explicit handling for 'no methods' (methods empty) and for 'first vs last' selection with a short comment documenting why bound/unbound candidates are at specific indices. This prevents regressions from heuristics that depend on list ordering.

If exception handlers convert one exception to another or to a sentinel, preserve the original exception context when appropriate (raise from) so caller-side diagnostics and traces remain meaningful for debugging.
skill.trigger: A consumer (inference routine, resolver, or node method) attempts an alternative resolution inside an exception handler (e.g., catches AttributeInferenceError or lookup failure) but the conditional/branch used to choose the alternative is inverted or the constructed call context for invoking the alternative is malformed; observable symptom is that the fallback path returns a default/uninferable value instead of the expected resolved object/type.

skill.title: SunPy package top-level initialization and entry points
knowledge: sunpy.__init__.py performs package-level initialization: it calls sunpy.util.config.load_config(), initializes logging via an internal _init_log(config=...), and reads citation metadata (via _get_bibtex()) to populate __citation__ / __bibtex__.

The package root re-exports a small public surface and exposes the test runner: __all__ includes config, self_test, system_info, print_config, log, __version__, __citation__, and __bibtex__; self_test is imported from sunpy.tests.self_test.
The test-runner entrypoint implementation is sunpy/tests/self_test.py (function self_test(...)); callers of the package-level self_test are dispatched to that module.

Utility functions for configuration and environment info (e.g. load_config, print_config, system_info) live under sunpy.util and are relied on by the top-level package initialization rather than being implemented at package root.

skill.title: Caller drops or renames an API argument before forwarding to the downstream consumer
knowledge: Reproduce the failure with a minimal caller invocation that supplies the parameter and confirm what the consumer actually receives (instrument the consumer or add a temporary assert/log to inspect the argument at the boundary).

Search the caller for where the argument should be forwarded: grep for explicit keyword passing or **kwargs in the delegation call (e.g., `consumer(..., resample=resample)` vs `consumer(..., **kwargs)`), and confirm the name is preserved across the call site.

Inspect decorators and compatibility wrappers applied to the caller (deprecation helpers, renamed-argument decorators). Verify their rename mapping and behavior — some decorators intentionally drop, rename, or translate parameters (e.g., deprecated_renamed_argument) and may map a name to None or remove it unless configured correctly.

Audit all control-flow paths in the caller that touch the parameter: look for conditional guards like `if resample:` (truthiness checks) that can change semantics for empty sequences/zeros, assignments that reuse the parameter name (overwriting the original value with None or another sentinel), or early returns that omit forwarding.

Check for accidental defaulting or normalization order-of-operations: e.g., computing a new value using `resample` only after testing it, or multiplying dimensions by `resample` when `resample` may have been reset to None on some paths.

Examine consumer-side normalization/validation: the consumer should validate inputs and either normalize types consistently or raise a clear error. If the consumer silently converts unexpected inputs to None, prefer failing fast or documenting that contract.

Prefer normalizing and ensuring correct types at the producer (caller) before delegation: if callers must convert user-supplied shorthand to a concrete type, do so deterministically and forward the normalized object to the consumer.

Add defensive guards at the boundary: explicit keyword forwarding (`consumer(..., resample=resample)`), runtime assertions (e.g., assert resample is not None or has expected shape), or logging to make contract violations explicit during development.

When decorators are involved, write tests that exercise the decorated behavior, including renamed/removed arguments. Ensure decorator defaults (e.g., new_name=None) do not inadvertently drop parameters for wrapped functions.
Add unit and integration tests for edge cases (None, empty lists, shape/tuple formats) that assert the consumer receives the intended type and values when called through the wrapper/dispatcher.

If a quick compatibility fix is needed, add defensive checks in the consumer (isinstance checks, explicit handling of None) while refactoring the caller/decorator to preserve the long-term contract; document the chosen boundary contract in docstrings.

After making changes, run end-to-end scenarios that exercise both direct consumer calls and calls through the wrapper/dispatcher to ensure the forwarding behavior is consistent and regressions are caught.
skill.trigger: A downstream consumer raises a TypeError/ValueError or performs invalid operations because an API argument (numeric, tuple, or structured value) that was provided to a higher-level caller is observed as None or another unexpected type. The higher-level function is a dispatcher/wrapper/aggregator expected to forward the argument to per-item consumers, and there exist code paths (decorators that rename/remove params, conditional branches, defaulting logic, or reassignments) that can drop, override, or rename the argument before delegation.

skill.title: Click command-line library (core responsibilities)
knowledge: src/click/core.py implements the core command model: Command, Group, Context, argument/option parameter objects, parsing, and invocation lifecycle—public command execution is routed through these classes (e.g. Command.invoke / Context).

src/click/decorators.py provides the @command/@group/@option/@argument convenience decorators that construct and attach core.Command and parameter objects to callables (wrapping callables and building the command/parameter metadata used by core).
src/click/testing.py provides the CliRunner test harness and Result capture objects: it isolates environment and I/O, invokes commands, and captures stdout/stderr/exit code for tests.

src/click/__init__.py is the package public surface: it re-exports core types, decorators, testing utilities, exceptions, and other modules and contains compatibility/deprecation shims so users import the public API from click.

skill.title: Boolean-controlled validation branch has inverted polarity (true/false actions swapped)
knowledge: Locate the conditional(s) that choose between the two validation actions (e.g., clamp vs raise). Search for direct checks of the boolean (if self.clamp, if not self.clamp, if clamp:) near parsing/validation code paths.
Look for accidental negation: explicit 'not' in condition, inverted comparison, or operator precedence that flips intended meaning (e.g., if not (expr) vs if expr).

Check for swapped branch bodies: confirm which branch performs clamping and which raises. A quick way is to add temporary logging/print statements or small assertions to observe branch choice for known inputs.

Verify that the boolean flag is the same attribute read by the consumer as set by the producer/constructor. Search for shadowing or naming mismatches (e.g., constructor stores 'clamp' to a different attribute name, or a property masks the attribute).

Inspect subclass vs base-class relationships: if a shared base routine reads self.flag, ensure subclasses don't override the attribute with inverted semantics or provide a default opposite value via their __init__.

Check call-sites and default argument propagation: the flag might be passed inverted through an intermediary function or helper; examine constructors, factory functions, and any wrapper that builds the validator object.

Look for boolean normalization or decoration that flips truthiness (e.g., using 'not' inadvertently, returning the negated value from a property getter, or using a truthiness test on non-boolean data).

Add or update unit tests that exercise both flag states with representative out-of-range and in-range values (include boundary and off-by-one/open-boundary cases). Tests should assert the exact action (clamped value vs raised exception) for each flag value.

If behavior is centralized in a shared routine, prefer fixing the branch polarity there rather than in every subclass. If subclasses intentionally differ, document and assert that difference in subclass tests.
When patching, include a small regression test that reproduces the inverted behavior and asserts the corrected semantics to prevent reintroducing the inversion in future refactors.
skill.trigger: A consumer (converter/validator, parser boundary, or state-check routine) exhibits the opposite behavior of a boolean flag set by a producer/constructor or state owner: the flag value True leads to action B (e.g., reject) while False leads to action A (e.g., clamp), contrary to the documented/expected semantics. Applicable when the decision is implemented as a direct conditional or branch that reads a boolean attribute/argument (often in a shared routine or base-class) or when subclasses/constructors propagate that flag into a shared handler.

skill.title: moto repository architecture
knowledge: moto.core is the small core framework that owns the mocking lifecycle and public decorators (e.g. mock_aws imported from moto.core.decorator) and provides shared utilities used by services.

Per-service packages live under moto.<service> and follow a stable structure: urls.py binds/exports operations (the entrypoint for mocked API calls), responses.py implements API action handlers that shape AWS-like responses, and models.py owns stateful domain objects/resource representations and their serialization/validation.

Backend storage and dispatch are handled by a backend registry (BackendDict) / BaseBackend machinery in the core: responses call into per-account/per-region backends to create/update BaseModel-derived objects (models.py) so state is partitioned by account/region via that registry.

Extension/adaptation points exist in service subpackages (examples: moto/apigateway/integration_parsers) — pluggable parsers/utilities encapsulate service-specific parsing or helper logic that responses/models consume.

Some services depend on external libraries for domain behavior (example: moto/acm/models.py uses the cryptography library to generate/validate certificates), so heavy domain logic may live in service models rather than core utilities.

skill.title: Handler missing inherited initialization or lifecycle hooks after base-class removal/rename
knowledge: Begin from the exact AttributeError text: it names the missing attribute and the failing expression (e.g., super().__init__, setup_class, dispatch). Grep for that attribute and the handler class name to locate callsites and declarations.
Inspect the handler class definition for its base classes. If it used to inherit a framework base (e.g., BaseResponse) and no longer does, restoring the base or providing an adapter is a likely fix.

If the failing hook is an instance initializer (super().__init__), check the framework base for __init__ existence and expected parameters (including defaults). Mismatched required parameters will surface as different runtime errors — confirm signature compatibility.

If the failing hook is a class-level registration/dispatch method, confirm whether the framework expects a classmethod/staticmethod or a class attribute; look at the dispatcher/router code that invokes it to see how it is called.

Search the core/framework module (e.g., moto/core/responses.py) for recent edits that removed or renamed lifecycle hooks. Use version control history or recent diffs to find refactors that could have removed inheritance or renamed methods.

Consider adapter fixes: reintroduce minimal __init__ on the handler that forwards to the framework provider with the correct arguments, or re-add the small adapter classmethods that preserve the contract if restoring full inheritance is undesirable.

Check for other services or handler classes that use the same base — search repository-wide for the handler/base pattern to ensure fixes preserve the shared framework contract across service packages.
Verify there are no metaclass/ decorator refactors that replaced classes with callables or changed when/where class attributes are defined; such refactors can hide inherited methods.

After making a change, run a minimal repro that exercises the dispatch path (not only unit tests of handler methods) to confirm initialization/registration path is exercised and the AttributeError is resolved.
skill.trigger: A handler raises AttributeError when calling an expected framework hook (e.g., super().__init__(...), or when a dispatcher invokes a class-level hook like setup/dispatch), and the handler class either no longer subclasses the framework base that provided that hook or the hook was renamed/its signature changed.

skill.title: pandas repository architecture
knowledge: pandas.__init__ enforces import-time hard-dependency checks (e.g. numpy, dateutil), contains guards for compiled-extension/build-time issues, selects the package version (meson/get_versions), and re-exports the public API by importing from subpackages (e.g. core.api, io.api, tseries.api, reshape.api).

pandas.core is the primary owner of core data structures and algorithms (DataFrame, Series, Index, dtypes and the bulk of algorithmic implementations) and is the main locus of correctness and behavior for in-memory operations.

pandas.io is the IO/format layer responsible for file-format readers/writers and parsing/serialization logic (CSV, Excel, HDF, JSON, SQL, etc.), i.e. user-visible I/O behavior is implemented under pandas.io and its submodules.

pandas.conftest and the testing utilities (pandas.util._tester, testing fixtures under pandas/) provide pytest fixtures and test configuration helpers used to shape the test environment; test-only behavior and fixtures are separated from normal runtime library code.

skill.title: Validation/error branch references a local value before assignment
knowledge: Search the function for raise/Error constructions, f-strings, or string interpolation that include local names. Grep patterns: 'raise .*{name}', 'f"', '.format(', or direct concatenation with variable names near raise/ValueError sites.

Find all assignments to the referenced name in the function and check their control-flow dominance relative to each use. If any use is reachable without passing through an assignment, the variable can be uninitialized on that path.

Inspect surrounding conditional structure for swapped branch bodies, early returns, missing else, or reordered normalization steps (e.g., input normalization performed after the raise). Reordering a normalization/assignment earlier often fixes the bug.

Check for subtle normalization/validation ordering: e.g., conversions (Index(removals).unique().dropna()), type guards (is_list_like) or import-time assignments that appear after the raise in one branch — these are common culprits.

Consider whether the identifier might be produced by a helper/callee (closure or nested function) or accidentally expected to be set by a different function; prefer the function that contains the raise as the primary candidate unless the callee clearly documents/returns that diagnostic value.

Fix patterns: compute or initialize the diagnostic/local value before any validation/raise, or ensure the raise constructs a message without interpolating the local; add explicit default initialization (e.g., not_included = set()) or move the assignment above branching. Add unit tests exercising the edge cases that previously triggered the NameError (e.g., unknown removals, single-item removals, non-list inputs).

When forming candidates, prioritize functions that syntactically contain the raise referencing the name. If no assignment exists in that function, inspect callers and callees for accidental reliance on caller-local names (rare) or for missing return/context values.

If multiple candidate functions appear, collect concrete evidence: location of the raise, lines where the name is assigned, and control-flow paths from function entry to the raise. Use small repro inputs to trigger each branch and confirm where the exception originates.
skill.trigger: A function raises NameError or UnboundLocalError (or crashes while building an error/raise message) because a validation, guard, or error-raising branch references a local value that is only assigned on some control-flow paths (e.g., assigned later, assigned in the alternate branch, or skipped by an early return). This is applicable when the failing identifier is a local value (diagnostic/context variable) and the use occurs inside the same function's validation/raise logic rather than across a caller/callee boundary.

skill.title: Patsy repository architecture
knowledge: patsy.highlevel is the public high-level API that implements dmatrix, dmatrices, incr_dbuilder and incr_dbuilders and orchestrates evaluation/building: it drives EvalEnvironment, calls the build machinery, and returns either DesignMatrix objects or pandas.DataFrame results depending on return_type.

Parsing/tokenization is owned by patsy.tokens, patsy.infix_parser and patsy.parse_formula; these produce the structured formula representation (ModelDesc/term objects from patsy.desc) that the build/eval pipeline consumes.

Evaluation and matrix construction are implemented in patsy.build together with patsy.eval and patsy.state: these modules evaluate transforms, manage NA handling and incremental builders, and produce the numeric matrices that become DesignMatrix instances.

Design metadata and column information live in patsy.design_info (DesignInfo and DesignMatrix metadata). Splines, mgcv_cubic_splines, and contrasts provide basis/contrast implementations, while compat and user_util contain the repository's pandas/ndarray interop utilities and conversion helpers.

skill.title: Formula-only parser invoked on inputs that may be expressions (wrong conversion API used)
knowledge: Reproduce with minimal inputs: create minimal test strings that represent both a full formula (e.g., "y ~ x") and a plain expression (e.g., "x + 1"). Call the conversion helper directly to see whether the helper always routes to the formula-only API and whether that raises the operator-context error.

Search for conversion helpers or test harnesses that unconditionally call ModelDesc.from_formula / parse_formula: grep for from_formula(...) usages inside loops over test data or helpers that accept arbitrary expression-like strings.

Inspect the expected-format metadata for tests/data: check how test vectors (the mapping of code->expected) are structured—some entries may be expressions rather than formulas. Confirm the helper's branching logic for two formats (formula vs expression).

Check for simple detection/branching opportunities before parsing: a fast heuristic is testing for presence of a formula delimiter (e.g., '~') in the input string and choosing the formula API only when present; otherwise use the expression evaluation API.

If more robust detection is needed, parse with an API that accepts both shapes or normalize inputs first (explicit API that parses both forms). Prefer explicit branching and clear error messages rather than letting lower-level parser raise ambiguous context errors.

When changing caller behavior, add unit tests that include mixed input types to prevent regressions (both full formulas and pure expressions). Ensure the helper's docstring and test data contract document which input shapes it accepts.
Instrument the conversion point to log which branch was taken (formula vs expression) during failing tests to confirm whether the wrong branch was used at the time of failure.

If the codebase centralizes conversion in one helper, prefer that helper export two explicit functions (parse_formula, eval_expression) or accept a 'format' parameter; avoid silent guesswork in deep callers that obscures whether the formula parser or expression evaluator should be used.
skill.trigger: A consumer (caller/test helper) unconditionally delegates string conversion to a formula-only parser (e.g., ModelDesc.from_formula / parse_formula wrapper) while some inputs are plain expressions or mixed formats. Observable failure: parser raises operator/context errors such as "~ can only be used in a formula context" or reports operators outside expected context. Applicable when a single conversion point handles heterogeneous test strings or user inputs without inspecting input shape/format.

skill.title: Red-DiscordBot (redbot) repository orientation
knowledge: Package bootstrap and CLI entry: redbot.__main__ is the CLI entrypoint used to parse command-line options, instantiate the bot, and start the run loop.

Versioning and early runtime policies: redbot.__init__ implements VersionInfo and contains early initialization (version discovery, logging/uvloop/event-loop policy and colorama handling) performed during application startup.

Cog/plugin layout and responsibilities: redbot/cogs is the collection of feature cogs; each cog (e.g. admin, alias) is packaged under redbot/cogs/* and owns its commands, converters, and helper logic for that feature.

Encapsulated audio subsystem: redbot/cogs/audio is a large, self-contained subsystem split into layers — apis/ (API wrappers and persistence adapters), core/ (player, commands, events, tasks, utilities), managed_node/ (Lavalink/managed node support), and integrations (youtube.py, spotify.py) — and therefore is the correct place to look for audio playback, queueing, and external service integration.

skill.title: Numeric limit sentinel accepted causing invalid resource construction and iterator-vs-varargs forwarding
knowledge: Confirm the numeric validation: look for checks like `if not isinstance(limit, int) or limit <= 0:` vs `limit < 0` — decide whether 0 is a legal value for this API. If API semantics require >0, ensure the guard rejects 0 and raises a clear error (TypeError/ValueError) with a helpful message.

Locate where the resource is constructed from the limit (e.g. Semaphore(limit)). Verify the constructor signature and semantics for the target Python/asyncio version — some APIs changed (loop parameter deprecated) and passing incorrect arguments (e.g. loop instead of value) yields confusing TypeError comparisons.

Inspect how tasks are produced: generator expressions or comprehensions (e.g. `(_sem_wrapper(... ) for task in coros_or_futures)`) create iterators. When those are consumed by a variadic API (asyncio.gather), ensure the call unpacks the iterator (`asyncio.gather(*tasks, ...)`) rather than passing the iterator as a single positional argument (`asyncio.gather(tasks, ...)`).

Trace producer/consumer responsibilities: check both the producer that wraps/yields awaitables (bounded_gather_iter-style) for validation and resource use, and the consumer that invokes gather-like APIs (bounded_gather-style) for proper forwarding/unpacking and return_exceptions usage.

Reproduce quickly with a minimal snippet (two simple coroutines, limit=0) to observe the exact exception and stack — this disambiguates whether the failure originates in resource construction (Semaphore) or in argument-shape mismatch at gather.
Search tests and call sites for uses of the API with limit==0 or similar values; update tests to assert a clear validation error if 0 is invalid.

If supporting limit==0 is desired (meaning 'no concurrency' or 'disable') consider explicit handling: either normalize 0 to 1 or special-case behavior rather than passing 0 directly to resource constructors that do not accept it.

When fixing, prefer small, orthogonal changes: (a) correct the boolean comparator in the guard to match intended semantics, (b) construct Semaphore/other resources with the correct argument(s), and (c) call variadic consumers with unpacked tasks. Add unit coverage for limit boundary cases and for iterator vs varargs behavior.
skill.trigger: A utility function that enforces concurrency or resource limits accepts or mishandles a numeric limit sentinel (for example 0) and uses it to construct a resource (Semaphore, pool, etc.), producing a runtime TypeError or ValueError; simultaneously, tasks/awaitables are produced as a generator/iterator and passed to a variadic consumer API (e.g. asyncio.gather) without unpacking. Applicable when code separates a producer (yields/wraps awaitables) from a consumer (calls a variadic gather-like API) or when a numeric 'limit' parameter is used directly in resource construction.

skill.title: Starlette ASGI framework (encode/starlette)
knowledge: starlette.applications (starlette/applications.py) implements the ASGI application entry points and is responsible for composing and applying the middleware stack for an app.
starlette.routing (starlette/routing.py) is the router: it resolves request paths to endpoint callables (including parameter conversion) and dispatches requests to those endpoints.

starlette.requests and starlette.responses (starlette/requests.py, starlette/responses.py) adapt ASGI scope and events into high-level Request and Response objects and manage body streaming, headers, and sending of ASGI messages.

Middleware implementations live under starlette/middleware/* (errors, cors, gzip, sessions, httpsredirect, trustedhost, wsgi, etc.); they implement cross-cutting concerns and are layered by the application when building the ASGI app.

skill.title: Lifecycle handler clears or overwrites per-item instance state used by streaming consumer
knowledge: Search for lifecycle or callback handlers (names like on_*_begin, on_*_end, start/stop, begin_part, end_part) and grep for all assignments to the suspect instance field (e.g., _current_part). Confirm whether handlers assign a new object, set to None, or assign to a local variable by mistake (missing self.).

Trace the call order between lifecycle handlers and consumer callbacks: build a minimal reproducible stream that triggers begin/end callbacks and step through or log each handler to capture the exact sequence and the value of the per-item field before and after each handler.

Look for refactor/regression patterns that replace constructor-like expressions with None or remove object construction (e.g., MultipartPart() -> None) — inspect recent commits or diffs touching the lifecycle handlers or the per-item class.

Check for accidental shadowing: assignments like current_part = MultipartPart() (no self.) or returning/propagating a local variable instead of storing on self.<field> will leave the instance field None for the consumer.

Verify that end/cleanup handlers clear state only after consumers that rely on the state have finished. If clearing must happen, ensure ordering or use ref-counting/flags so consumer methods do not run concurrently with clearing.

Add lightweight assertions or defensive guards in consumer callbacks (e.g., assert self._current_part is not None or raise a clear ValueError) to produce a more informative error and to catch incorrect lifecycle transitions during tests.

Instrument dynamic tests that feed multipart streams in small chunks to exercise interleavings; assert state transitions at each boundary and add unit tests that reproduce the failing sequence (start part -> immediately receive data -> ensure on_part_begin created object).

If the lifecycle handler must sometimes leave state None for a legitimate reason, make the consumer tolerant (check for None and skip or buffer) and document the contract between the handler and consumer clearly in code comments and tests.
skill.trigger: A streaming/iterative consumer (e.g., a method that processes chunks or on_part_data) raises an AttributeError/NoneType error because a per-item instance field (producer-owned state) is unexpectedly None or the wrong type. Applicable when the component uses lifecycle/callback handlers (on_part_begin/on_part_end, start/stop hooks, iterator boundary handlers) that are responsible for creating, initializing, or clearing per-item state and those handlers may assign None, a local variable, or the wrong value instead of a valid per-item object.

skill.title: Tweepy client architecture
knowledge: The legacy API class (tweepy/api.py::API) is responsible for constructing requests for v1 endpoints: it builds URLs/parameters, implements caching and rate-limit bookkeeping, and delegates HTTP execution results to the parsing layer.

The newer API v2 surface is implemented in the Client/BaseClient classes (tweepy/client.py and tweepy/asynchronous/client.py for async). Their .request / AsyncBaseClient.request methods are the central entry points for sending HTTP requests for v2 endpoints.

Authentication credential handling and request signing are implemented in tweepy/auth.py (e.g. OAuth1UserHandler, OAuth2UserHandler, OAuth2BearerHandler, AppAuthHandler); request paths use these handlers to sign or provide credentials before sending.
Response interpretation is owned by the parser layer (tweepy/parsers.py and ModelParser) which converts HTTP responses into Model objects defined in tweepy/models.py (and related model modules).

skill.title: Structured payload field misassignment (parameter values written under wrong keys / swapped)
knowledge: Reproduce with the minimal invocation using distinct sentinel values for each input parameter (e.g., 'TYPE_A', 'MEDIA_999') and capture/print/log the constructed payload right before the network/serialization call to confirm which keys hold which values.

Open the producer function and inspect every explicit assignment into the payload dict: verify the RHS variable for each key matches the intended input name. Pay attention to copy-paste mistakes, similar variable names, or accidental use of the wrong local variable.
Search recent diffs/commits for edits to the producer function or surrounding lines; swapped lines, moved blocks, or accidental variable renames in a small edit often produce these bugs.

If the payload is created by composing helper functions or by forwarding positional arguments, ensure the helper's parameter order matches call-sites. Prefer explicit keyword assignments (payload['type']=attachment_type) over positional forwarding or tuple/unpacking when mapping names to keys.

Add a temporary assert or log immediately before the boundary (e.g., assert payload['type'] == expected_type) to fail fast during local repro and narrow whether the fault is at producer construction vs downstream transformation.
Grepping for other producers of the same payload shape can reveal consistent mistakes or duplicated incorrect mapping; inspect sibling functions and shared helpers for the same misassignment pattern.

Check boundary adapters (serialization helpers, wrapper decorators) for transformations that might reorder or mutate the payload; however, if the logged pre-send payload already contains the swap, the bug is in the producer mapping itself.
When the quick fix is simple (swap the two assignments back), add a focused unit/integration test asserting the exact mapping of input parameters to payload keys to prevent regression.

Consider adding property-based or table-driven tests for payload builders that validate mapping for many distinct inputs and combinations, especially when payload fields are numerous or similarly named.
Document the expected payload contract in the producer's docstring and add explicit mapping comments near complex assignments to reduce future copy/paste or ordering errors.
skill.trigger: A producer function constructs a structured payload (dict/JSON) for an external interface and the resulting payload is syntactically valid but contains fields whose values are swapped or misassigned (e.g., two input parameters appear under each other's keys). Applicable when the code builds a nested mapping immediately before sending it to a consumer/boundary (network call, serializer, or IPC) and the consumer observes incorrect semantics despite receiving a valid payload.

skill.title: sqlglot core architecture
knowledge: Top-level convenience functions (parse, parse_one, transpile, tokenize) in sqlglot/__init__.py delegate to Dialect.get_or_raise to obtain the configured Parser/Generator/Tokenizer for a named dialect, then call the parser/generator to perform parsing or SQL generation.

Dialect classes (sqlglot/dialects/* and sqlglot/dialects/dialect.py) are the central configuration/registration point: they dynamically register available dialect modules, configure which parser_class/generator_class/tokenizer to use, and Dialect.get_or_raise loads/returns the appropriate configured classes for a given dialect name.

The lexical → syntactic boundary is explicit: Tokenizer produces tokens consumed by the Parser (sqlglot/parser.py). The Parser builds Expression AST nodes (defined in sqlglot/expressions.py) using builder helpers and a mapping from function/keyword names to expression constructors.

SQL emission is handled by the Generator (sqlglot/generator.py); generators consume Expression ASTs and produce SQL strings. Dialect modules can customize generation by supplying/overriding generator_class or providing dialect-specific mappings.

skill.title: Stateful cursor/index updated with incorrect arithmetic (off-by-one/wrong-sign) during token consumption
knowledge: Reproduce with a minimal failing input and instrument the parser: assert or log the cursor/index value immediately before and after the suspect helper call to confirm a mis-position (state owner role).

Search the codebase for all write sites of the cursor/index (names like _index, pos, cursor) and for calls to shared advance/retreat helpers; collect each location and the arithmetic used when computing arguments.

Inspect helper semantics: open implementations of advance/retreat APIs and confirm whether they expect absolute positions or deltas; a mismatch (passing an absolute index where a delta is expected or vice-versa) is a common source of wrong arithmetic.

Look for simple arithmetic patterns (+1, -1, +/- N) and swapped signs. Off-by-one errors or wrong sign usage are frequent when handlers compute 'self._index - 1' versus 'self._index + 1' and can be revealed by comparing behavior on boundary tokens.

Check control-flow around early returns and sentinel branches: ensure that arithmetic is computed against the intended index value (e.g., do not use self._index after it has been mutated earlier in the branch), and verify that the value passed reflects the parser state at the intended time.

Compare the failing path with sibling parsing handlers (e.g., other type parsers, CAST vs generic type) to locate consistent arithmetic patterns or a single outlier implementing the wrong sign/offset.

Add a focused regression test that parses the problematic construct and asserts both the produced AST shape and, if reachable, the parser index at key checkpoints; this prevents future arithmetic regressions.

When a numeric update is suspicious but hard to reason about, replace computed arithmetic with an explicit absolute set (set_index) or well-named helper (advance_by, retreat_by) to clarify intent and reduce chance of sign/offset mistakes.
skill.trigger: A parser/consumer or similar state owner produces wrong results or parse failures because its internal cursor/index is advanced or retreated using computed arithmetic (e.g., +/- N) with the wrong sign or offset. This commonly appears in parsing helpers that call advance/retreat APIs with expressions like self._retreat(self._index - 1) or self._advance(self._index + 1) rather than setting an absolute position, and the produced AST or subsequent consumers observe a mis-positioned cursor.

skill.title: DVC repository structure and responsibility boundaries
knowledge: CLI commands live under dvc/commands/* and implement command classes named Cmd* that subclass CmdBase (from dvc/cli/command.py); those classes provide validate_args and run methods used to perform work.

Each CLI command module also provides a parser builder that registers arguments and binds the command class to the parser (e.g., parser.set_defaults(func=CmdAdd)); argument objects may carry completion metadata (e.g., .complete = completion.FILE) used by the CLI completion subsystem in dvc/cli.

The dvc package performs package-level initialization: dvc/__init__.py calls dvc.logger.setup() and re-exports version information (via dvc/version.py), so importing dvc triggers logging and version setup.

Core repository functionality (operations like add/get/checkout and cache management) is implemented in core modules such as dvc/build.py and dvc/cachemgr.py and is exposed programmatically through the dvc/api/* modules which wrap the core logic.

skill.title: CLI option present in source/docs but missing at runtime due to parser wiring, overriding, or name mismatch
knowledge: First reproduce the symptom and observe the CLI help: run the command with --help. If the option does not appear in help the parser used at runtime does not include it.

Search the codebase for the literal flag (e.g., '--allow-missing') and for the expected attribute name (e.g., 'allow_missing'). Grep both the add_argument calls and any uses of the attribute in Cmd.run or downstream calls.

Confirm the parser builder is actually wired into the top-level CLI: verify the module that defines add_parser is imported when the CLI starts, and that the subparser registration (subparsers.add_parser or similar) and parser.set_defaults(func=CmdX) are executed for the matching command name.

Look for other parser builders or duplicate command registrations that may override or replace the intended parser. A different module may register the same subcommand without the option, shadowing the original registration.

Check parent/child parser relationships and use of 'parents=' or shared parent parsers: options added to a parent may be masked or a child parser may be constructed without expected parents. Also check for parse_known_args or custom parsing that alters recognized options.

Verify attribute naming differences: argparse converts option strings with dashes into attribute names with underscores by default (e.g., '--allow-missing' -> args.allow_missing). If the add_argument used a custom 'dest' or the consumer expects a different attribute name, access will fail. Also check for typos in consumer code.

Inspect any set_defaults calls or explicit Namespace construction that might override or remove attributes, and search for parser re-creation at runtime (creating a new parser instance without previously-registered options).

Use git history (blame/log) on the parser builder to see if add_argument was recently removed or changed; a removed registration in a patch is a strong indicator. Check associated tests or docs for recent changes that may have diverged from code.

If the consumer reads self.args.<attr> and the attribute may be missing at runtime, add a defensive default (getattr(self.args, 'attr', default)) or ensure the parser registers the option with a default so the attribute always exists.

When the parser builder and consumer are correct but the behavior still occurs, instrument runtime startup (or add logging) to confirm which module registers the subparser and which parser object is used by the CLI dispatch path.
skill.trigger: A CLI invocation raises an 'unrecognized argument' error or the parsed Namespace lacks an expected attribute, while the repository contains a parser-builder or documentation that registers an option and a command implementation that reads the corresponding args attribute. Applicable when the project uses explicit parser builders/subparsers, parent parsers, set_defaults wiring, or when attribute names may be transformed (e.g., dashes->underscores) or overridden.

skill.title: Paramiko (Python SSH library) - repository orientation
knowledge: paramiko/transport.py owns the SSH transport layer: it defines the Transport thread/class that performs handshake/KEX, negotiates ciphers/MACs, manages encryption state, and drives channel lifecycle; it dispatches to kex_* modules and uses packet.py/message.py for framing and channel.py for channel management.

paramiko/client.py provides the high-level SSHClient API and is the public entry point for initiating connections; SSHClient constructs and interacts with Transport and relies on auth_handler.py and auth_strategy.py to negotiate and perform authentication before channels/sessions are opened.

paramiko/channel.py together with packet.py and message.py implement channel multiplexing and message framing; higher-level subsystems such as the SFTP implementation (paramiko/sftp_client.py, paramiko/sftp_server.py, paramiko/sftp_file.py, paramiko/sftp_handle.py, etc.) run on top of channels/transport rather than implementing their own transport.

Key handling is encapsulated in dedicated modules (paramiko/rsakey.py, paramiko/dsskey.py, paramiko/ecdsakey.py, paramiko/ed25519key.py and paramiko/hostkeys.py); these modules parse, load, and perform public/private key operations and are used by the authentication and host-key verification code paths.

skill.title: Serialization password/encryption parameter omitted or overwritten at delegation/wrapper boundary
knowledge: Reproduce the failure with a minimal invocation that supplies a password and verify the saved file can be read without a password; use both direct and wrapped entrypoints if available.

Search the codebase for public write/save APIs (e.g., write_private_key_file, write_private_key, save, dump) and their helper/delegation sites; grep for the password/encryption param name and for calls to internal helpers (e.g., `_write_private_key_file`, `serialize`, `asbytes`).

Trace the password argument through the call chain: inspect each caller to confirm whether it forwards the argument explicitly (consumer(..., password=password)) or substitutes/omits it. Look for literal None, hard-coded format constants, or different PrivateFormat/encoding values passed at the callsite.

Inspect per-type overrides/implementations (consumer roles): some classes implement convenience wrappers that choose serialization format or intentionally disable encryption for compatibility. Check for `return` of pre-serialized bytes or calls that do not accept/propagate the password parameter.

Check format/constants passed to the serializer (e.g., TraditionalOpenSSL vs PKCS8) — certain format choices or API usages can change whether a password is applied or which encryption routine is used; confirm the combination of format + password actually triggers encryption in the underlying crypto library.

Add lightweight instrumentation or temporary assertions at the shared helper (producer) to log/raise if the received password differs from the caller-supplied one, or to assert that a non-None password is passed when encryption is expected.
If decorators, compatibility shims, or wrapper methods are present, inspect them for explicit argument transformations or defaults that could replace the password on some paths.

When a per-type writer exists, read its implementation for subtle substitutions: e.g., it may choose PKCS8 and pass password=None while the public API expects TraditionalOpenSSL + password. Such format+password mismatches are a common root cause.
Construct unit tests that exercise direct calls and wrapper/override paths with passwords; include negative tests ensuring files written with a password require that password to reload.

Preferred fixes: preserve and forward the original caller-supplied password explicitly at delegation sites, remove hard-coded None unless documented and intentional, or make the decision explicit with clear API/parameter names and unit tests. When format differences matter, document and test them.

As a short-term mitigation, add an assertion or runtime warning when a public API receives a password but the downstream call uses None or an unencrypted format; this prevents silent loss of encryption during development.
skill.trigger: A public save/write API accepts an encryption/password argument but the persisted output is unencrypted (or the downstream serializer sees None/default). The code delegates to a shared/base serialization helper or per-type hook (producer/consumer), and at one or more delegation sites the password or format argument is explicitly not forwarded (replaced with None), overwritten with a fixed literal, or a per-type implementation returns already-serialized unencrypted bytes that bypass the expected encryption path.

skill.title: Pydantic repository architecture
knowledge: BaseModel, its metaclass, and runtime model construction/validation are implemented in pydantic/main.py; dataclass support and integration are provided in pydantic/dataclasses.py.
JSON Schema generation and remapping logic is encapsulated in pydantic/json_schema.py and operates on pydantic-core schema objects (core_schema) as input.
Field descriptors, metadata, default-value handling, and private-attribute behavior are implemented in pydantic/fields.py and are consulted during model construction and validation.

Decorator-based helpers for validation and serialization are implemented in pydantic/functional_validators.py and pydantic/functional_serializers.py, providing compatibility layers for v1-style decorators around pydantic-core functionality.

skill.title: Annotated metadata parsed but not attached to model field due to skipped constructor branch
knowledge: Locate where get_origin(annotation) is compared to Annotated and where get_args(annotation) are inspected. Verify that collected annotation args (FieldInfo or equivalent) are actually assigned to the local field_info/state variable used later by the constructor.

Search for variables and branches named field_info, field_infos, FieldInfo.from_annotation, update_from_config, default_factory, _validate, and code paths that set value/default. Check for 'pass', early returns, or deleted/renamed variables that would result in not applying parsed metadata.

Examine the model/field constructor order: confirm that annotation extraction runs before code that computes default/default_factory, default assignment, and validator population (e.g., ensure _set_default_and_type / _type_analysis / prepare are executed in the right order and not bypassed).

Confirm that when an Annotated Field is present the produced FieldInfo (or core-schema) actually contains keys like description/default; instrument or add temporary logging/assertions to observe the FieldInfo instance just after annotation parsing and again after model-field initialization to detect if/where it is lost.
Check update_from_config and merging logic: ensure config-derived field_info_from_config is merged into the same FieldInfo instance the model will use, not into a discarded temporary.

Add a small runnable reproducer (e.g., Annotated[str, Field(description='x')] and Annotated[str, Field(default='y')]) and unit tests asserting schema contains 'description' and that model.field equals the default when omitted. Use these tests to detect regressions caused by skipped application branches.

When fixing, prefer explicitly creating/assigning a FieldInfo object in the constructor path if none was attached by the annotation parser, or ensure the branch that creates it is not replaced by a no-op (pass) or removed variable initialization.

If multiple code layers exist (producer, model constructor, JSON-schema consumer), collect two discriminating observations: (1) prove the producer writes the metadata key into the parsed object, (2) prove whether the model constructor/consumer reads, renames, or drops it. This helps avoid misattributing the fault to the wrong layer.
skill.trigger: A model or consumer (e.g., JSON Schema generator or runtime validation) shows missing metadata (Annotated Field description/default/etc.) for a field declared with typing.Annotated, and the codebase contains an annotation-aware producer (annotation parser or FieldInfo factory) but the model's constructor/initializer (constructor or state owner like ModelField._get_field_info / _set_default_and_type / prepare) has conditional control flow that can leave the parsed metadata unassigned or bypass applying its defaults.

skill.title: python-markdownify repository overview
knowledge: MarkdownConverter (defined in markdownify/__init__.py) is the core implementation: it parses HTML with BeautifulSoup, walks/traverses the node tree, and implements conversion logic via methods like convert() and per-tag convert_* handlers (looked up via __getattr__).
The public library API is the top-level function markdownify(html, **options) in markdownify/__init__.py — it constructs MarkdownConverter(**options) and calls convert(html).

Command-line responsibilities are separated: markdownify/main.py is the CLI entrypoint responsible for parsing command-line options and invoking the library API (markdownify.markdownify) — tests exercise both converter behavior and CLI argument handling.

skill.title: Element-classification predicate misclassifies elements so trimming applies to inline or unknown elements
knowledge: Reproduce with minimal HTML snippets that show the symptom: examples with spaces around inline tags (e.g., 'foo Hello bar') and small table rows/cells. Confirm trimming misbehavior is correlated with specific tag names or absent element metadata.

Search the codebase for predicates and guards named like should_remove_whitespace_inside, should_remove_whitespace_outside, is_block, is_inline, or similar. Grep for uses of those predicates in process_text/process_tag, inline conversion wrappers, and table-cell converters.

Open the predicate implementation and inspect early None/name handling and any regex-match branches. Common mistakes: returning True for el is None (or el.name is None) when the intention is False; inverting the meaning of heading matches; or returning membership in the wrong tag set (including inline tags instead of block-level ones).

Check whether the predicate's truth value is used upstream (producer) to decide normalization/strip behavior before per-tag converters run, which would cause consumers (like chomp) to see already-trimmed text. Trace both producer and consumer call sites to determine where classification is consulted.

Compare the tag sets used by the predicate with authoritative lists (HTML block vs inline elements) and with tests. If the predicate includes unexpected names (e.g., 'span' or 'td' in the 'remove inside' set) this will explain lost whitespace around inline content or table cells.

Verify related tests (unit tests for conversion of inline tags and tables). Add tests that assert behavior for None/unknown element contexts and for headings so future changes to the predicate are caught.

When fixing, make the predicate explicit and conservative: treat el is None or el.name is None as False (do not remove interior whitespace by default), ensure heading regex branches return the intended boolean, and keep a clear documented list of tags whose interiors may have whitespace removed. Prefer explicit membership checks and short, well-commented logic over complex branching that can accidentally invert roles.

If trimming behavior depends on multiple functions, centralize the element-classification logic or export it so callers use a single authoritative predicate rather than duplicating tag lists in many places.

Document the expected contract: which elements are allowed to lose interior/adjacent whitespace and why (for example block-level tags vs inline tags), and include examples in comments to make future reviewers aware of the boundary cases (None element, headings, table cells).
skill.trigger: A conversion pipeline has a producer or guard predicate (e.g., should_remove_whitespace_inside/should_remove_whitespace_outside) that decides whether surrounding/internal whitespace should be stripped for a node. Observable failure: converted output loses spaces around inline elements or between table cells because the predicate returns True for elements that should preserve whitespace (including cases where element is None or name is None, heading-regex matches are inverted, or the tag membership set is incorrect). Applicable when per-element predicates gate trimming/normalization before/after per-tag converters.

skill.title: apispec repository architecture
knowledge: APISpec (src/apispec/core.py) is the central orchestration object: it holds paths, tags, options and delegates component registration, reference resolution, and OpenAPI-version validation to subordinate modules.

Components (managed from APISpec) implements the components registry for OpenAPI top-level/component subsections (schemas, responses, parameters, headers, examples, securitySchemes).
