It performs lazy registration and resolves $ref references for schemas, parameters, responses, headers, operations, and paths.

The plugin system (src/apispec/plugin.py and plugin hooks called from APISpec) is the stable extension boundary: plugins implement helpers (e.g. schema_helper, response_helper, parameter_helper, header_helper, path_helper, operation_helper) that APISpec invokes to transform/augment objects during registration and path/operation construction.

The marshmallow extension (src/apispec/ext/marshmallow/*) implements conversion of marshmallow Schema and Field objects into OpenAPI components and helpers (field_converter, schema_resolver, openapi helpers) and registers those conversions via the plugin helper interface.

Utility modules (src/apispec/utils.py and src/apispec/yaml_utils.py) provide shared operations used by APISpec and plugins, including $ref construction/lookup, deep-merge/normalize helpers, and YAML rendering for output.

skill.title: Public API returns None because constructed collection is not returned or helper's in-place mutation is propagated
knowledge: Locate callers that immediately assign, iterate, or index the API return value (e.g., operation['parameters'] = resolver.resolve_parameters(...)). These callers establish the expected return contract (a sequence/dict).

Search the API and all helpers it calls for every 'return' site. Confirm the API returns the constructed collection on every control-flow path. Look for early returns (including implicit 'return None') that happen before the collection is initialized.

Inspect helper functions: determine whether they mutate the passed object in-place (append/extend) and return None. If the API uses the helper's return directly, it may accidentally propagate None. Prefer helpers that return the produced value, or have the API ignore helper return and explicitly return the constructed collection.

Check initialization and naming of the result variable: ensure the collection is created before any return that might reference it and that there is no accidental shadowing or reassignment after the return. Look for patterns like 'resolved = []' moved below 'return resolved' or similar ordering mistakes.

Search for uses of '+=' or '+=' with None, and for return expressions that reference variables assigned only in conditional branches (these can yield NameError/UnboundLocalError or implicit None). Grep for 'return', '+=', 'append(', 'extend(' and the result variable name to find suspicious sites.

When the helper is intentionally in-place, normalize at the API boundary: after calling the helper, assign a local result variable (e.g., result = result or result = list(result)) and explicitly 'return result' to guarantee a concrete return value.

Add unit tests that assert both the return type and contents for representative inputs (including empty inputs, inputs that trigger different branches, and inputs where helpers mutate in-place). Tests should capture the contract (e.g., list returned) so regressions are detected.

If fixing code, prefer explicit, minimal changes at the API boundary: initialize the result up-front (result = []) and ensure all branches append/extend into it, then unconditionally 'return result'; or change helper semantics to return the produced object and have the API return that value explicitly.

When refactoring, add defensive checks before returning (e.g., 'if result is None: return []' or 'return list(result)') only when behavior is well-understood — prefer fixing the root cause rather than masking it.
skill.trigger: A public method (consumer) that should return a constructed collection (e.g., list/dict of resolved items) is observed by callers to be None or an unexpected type. Applicable when the method either builds the collection internally or delegates to helpers that mutate inputs in-place and may return None, or when the final return appears before the collection is initialized.

skill.title: Nikola static site generator: core responsibilities
knowledge: The core site object is the Nikola class (defined in nikola/nikola.py); it initializes configuration, path handlers, and maintains collections for posts, pages, timelines, tags, and other build state used to orchestrate scanning and site generation.

Plugin discovery and lifecycle are managed by the repository's plugin subsystem (plugin manager and plugin category modules); plugins are loaded and invoked by Nikola to extend templating, scanners, builders, and other behaviors.

Content parsing and transformation responsibilities are implemented in utility modules such as nikola/metadata_extractors.py and nikola/filters.py; Nikola calls these utilities when scanning content and rendering output.

Persistent build state and metadata are separated into a state/persistor component (the state/persistor modules under nikola) that Nikola uses to record and consult saved build information between runs.

skill.title: Orchestrator computes/assigns local state after calling consumer helpers (producer/consumer ordering bug)
knowledge: Start from the traceback: locate the unbound local name and the stack frame where it is used. Treat that use as a consumer/reader role and find all callers/consumers in the same function.

Search the function for both uses and assignments of the name. If the assignment occurs later, in a different branch, or behind a conditional/early return, the bug is likely an ordering/responsibility mistake in the orchestrator.

Classify roles: label the function as producer/orchestrator if it composes the overall operation and calls helpers; label helper functions or plugins as consumers if they expect the value as an argument or via a shared local/dict. Prefer fixing the orchestrator to compute and pass the value rather than forcing consumers to compute application-specific defaults.

Inspect control flow on all paths (normal, early exits, publish/pending flags, error/log signals). Ensure the assignment precedes every consumer invocation in every control flow path that can reach those consumers.

If a consumer is a generic plugin/helper, check its signature/documentation: does it expect the caller to pass the value (producer responsibility) or to compute/fallback? Use that to decide whether to move the assignment or change the consumer interface.

Look for secondary operations that use the local (e.g., indexing into a dict _depfile[dest]) — these may raise different exceptions if the value is missing. Ensure any dictionary or dependent state is prepared only after the destination is known.

When proposing a fix, prefer the minimal, local change: compute/assign the derived state (e.g., translated_base_path(lang)) before calling helpers and before any code that indexes or writes using that value. Keep logging/signals either after assignment or accept that they can run before but must not cause use of the unassigned name.

Add a small reproducible test exercising the previously failing control-flow (e.g., publish_later vs normal flow) and a regression test guarding that assignment happens before consumers; include comments explaining producer/consumer responsibility for future maintainers.

If the consumer is in another module (plugin), consider adding an assertion or clearer argument requirement in the consumer (e.g., require dest argument not None) so the contract is explicit and future ordering mistakes are easier to catch.
skill.trigger: A function/method (the orchestrator/producer) raises NameError or UnboundLocalError naming a local intended to hold computed state (e.g., destination/path, filename, key) because helper/consumer calls in the same function reference that local on a path where its assignment is placed later, moved below, or skipped. The failing trace or source shows consumers (helpers/plugins) being invoked before the orchestrator computes and stores the needed value.

skill.title: python-docx repository architecture
knowledge: The public API surface is provided by the docx package (notably src/docx/api.py) and exposes the Document() factory and other top-level convenience functions used by callers.

Core in-memory model objects live under src/docx (for example class Document in src/docx/document.py) and implement document behavior (Paragraph, Run, Table, Section, Styles, Settings) while delegating XML details to the oxml layer.
The oxml layer (src/docx/oxml/*) provides element proxy classes (CT_* mappings) that represent WordprocessingML elements; model classes operate on these proxies rather than raw XML strings.

Packaging and part-level I/O responsibilities (reading/writing .docx, relationships, core properties, parts) are implemented in src/docx/opc/* (package.py, part.py, pkgreader.py, pkgwriter.py), separating persistence from the in-memory model.

Block container abstraction (src/docx/blkcntnr.py: BlockItemContainer) centralizes operations for block-level content (body, cell, header/footer) and provides convenience methods to enumerate and add paragraphs and tables used by the model classes.

skill.title: Separator-token misparsing in componentized semantic strings (component index shift)
knowledge: Locate the tokenizer/normalizer that converts the raw string into a canonical component sequence/structure. Print or log the canonicalized output for representative complex inputs (including combinations of separators) to confirm the intended component array/tuple/fields are produced.

Verify property accessors and convenience fields map to the intended component positions of the canonical representation (e.g., main[2] == patch). Watch for off-by-one or removed/renamed intermediate fields that shift indexing when optional segments exist.

Check how separators are handled: ensure prerelease and build delimiters are parsed into separate fields (or explicitly ignored for ordering per spec) rather than truncating or merging adjacent components. Add unit repro cases with combinations like: main.pre-release.build, missing components, and numeric+alphanumeric mixes.

Examine comparison and range-membership logic to confirm it uses the normalized canonical representation (not a stale raw string or partially-parsed fields). If comparisons compose tuples, ensure the tuple structure consistently includes the same component positions and that prerelease/build treatment follows the intended ordering rules.

Run small, focused boundary tests: compare versions at operator boundaries (>, >=, ==) and evaluate range expressions that hinge on equality vs strict inequality (e.g., >1.0 vs >=1.0) to confirm operator semantics align with component parsing.

Search for recent edits that removed or changed intermediate accessors, fields, or normalization steps (for example, deleted a patch property or changed how main/pre-release/build are stored). Such refactors commonly leave accessor indices stale.

If build/prerelease tokens are intended to be ignored for ordering, ensure that logic explicitly strips or separates build metadata before tuple comparison; conversely, if they affect representation, ensure consistent inclusion across accessors and comparisons.

Add unit tests that construct versions containing boundary separators and assert both the canonical component structure and the expected comparison/range outcomes. Lock these tests to prevent future regressions from refactors that change indexing or token boundaries.
skill.trigger: A consumer or accessor (e.g., a property like patch or a comparison method) returns or compares components of a parsed semantic string incorrectly because the tokenizer/normalizer splits or indexes components wrongly when optional separator-delimited segments (such as prerelease or build metadata) are present.

skill.title: Delimiter-separated component assignment swap between producer and consumer
knowledge: Locate all producers that format the compact string and all consumers that parse or split it. Search for both formatting sites (e.g., f"{pfx}:{local}", ':'.join([...]), return of such strings) and parsing/unpacking sites (e.g., tag.split(':') or a, b = tag.split(':')).

For each producer, log or print the exact string it emits on representative inputs. For each consumer, log the parsed component sequence immediately after splitting to confirm the observed order. Minimal repros that independently exercise each side make the mismatch visible.

Confirm that unpacking order matches formatting order: if producer emits prefix:local then consumer must unpack as prefix, local. Watch for reversed tuple assignment, mistaken variable naming, or refactors that swapped field order in constructors or return tuples.

Inspect mapping lookups and key usage (e.g., nsmap[prefix] vs nsmap.get(local)). A swap often manifests as a lookup with the wrong key; check direct indexing and .get() usage and ensure the same semantic token is used as the map key.

Search version-control history and recent refactors that touched either side of the chain (producers or consumers). Renaming or reordering fields, or changing helper return shapes, often leaves callers with stale unpacking assumptions.

Add focused unit tests: round-trip tests that format then parse back the name, and explicit tests asserting that producer output equals the expected 'prefix:local' shape and that consumers map prefix→URI and local→tagroot correctly. Lock these tests to prevent future regressions.

When multiple functions share responsibility (producer/consumer chain), instrument end-to-end and isolated unit-level checks so you can tell whether the incorrect order is produced, consumed, or both; this guides whether to fix the formatter, the parser/constructor, or both.
skill.trigger: A consumer or constructor that splits/unpacks a delimiter-separated name (e.g., 'prefix:local') observes the two components assigned to the wrong semantic slots (prefix ↔ local-name), often in projects where multiple functions produce or consume the same compact representation (producer/consumer chain of formatters and splitters).

skill.title: Conan repository architecture
knowledge: The top-level conan package (conan/__init__.py) exposes core model types and version metadata: ConanFile, Workspace, Version and the __version__/conan_version values used to identify the runtime version.

conan/api/conan_api.py implements the high-level ConanAPI object that initializes environment, configuration, migration, home/cache paths, and constructs the suite of sub-APIs (e.g., CacheAPI, CommandAPI, LocalAPI, LockfileAPI, WorkspaceAPI, ConfigAPI, InstallAPI, GraphAPI, etc.) which implement the repository's domain operations.

The CLI layer (conan/cli/cli.py) is responsible for parsing user arguments, discovering and loading built-in and external command modules, mapping them into ConanSubCommand wrappers, and dispatching execution through a ConanAPI instance while managing help, errors, and exit codes.

Domain behavior is implemented in conan/api/subapi/* (install, export, remotes, lockfile, list, upload, etc.); those sub-APIs orchestrate lower-level implementation modules under conan/internal and some legacy conans.client components (for example, conan/api/subapi/install.py delegates to conan.internal.api.install.generators and conans.client.graph.install_graph).

skill.title: Conversion helper unconditionally casts non-null fields to string
knowledge: Focus search on conversion/serialization helpers that map structured inputs to dicts/JSON: functions named *to_dict, to_json, serialize, dump, asdict, or similar wrappers around a structured object (namedtuple, dataclass, record).

Look for blanket stringification patterns in the helper body: explicit str(value), map(str, ...), f-strings or format() applied to every field, or unconditional calls to repr/__str__ for field values.
Confirm expectations by locating callers and tests: unit tests that assert numeric types or consumers that perform numeric operations reveal whether native types should be preserved.

Distinguish presentation-layer formatting from data representation: if helper is used both for CLI formatting and for machine-readable outputs (JSON, programmatic callers), prefer preserving native types in the representation helper and applying string formatting only at the presentation boundary.

Check None-handling rationale: authors sometimes call str(v) to avoid None -> TypeError in formatting; prefer explicit None checks (e.g., if v is None: keep None) or use conditional formatting only when producing textual output.

Repair patterns: remove the unconditional str() and assign the raw value; apply type-preserving serialization (json.dumps) at the outermost output; or, when needed, selectively format only fields intended for display while leaving data fields unchanged.

When uncertain, reproduce with a minimal snippet (construct the structured input with numeric fields and call the helper) and run relevant unit tests to validate that fixes preserve types and do not break presentation consumers.
skill.trigger: Callers or tests observe that primitives (numbers, booleans) produced by a producer become strings when consumed: type assertions fail or numeric operations break. The code path contains a conversion/serialization helper that iterates fields of a structured input (namedtuple, object, or mapping) and assigns result[field] = str(value) or otherwise formats every non-null value without preserving native types.

skill.title: Unconditional stringification of non-null inputs in conversion/normalization code (helpers or constructors)
knowledge: Search not only for dedicated serialize/convert helpers (to_dict, to_json, serialize, dumps) but also for constructors/initializers and parser-loader loops that iterate tokens or key/value pairs (e.g., Options.loads, __init__, or other normalization loops).

Look for blanket stringification patterns: explicit str(value), map(str, ...), f-strings/format() applied uniformly, .strip() immediately after str(), or comprehensions that coerce every element to string.

Pay attention to assignment sites where values from a parser/loader are stored into model state (state owner, constructor, or setter): these are common places to lose native types even if a separate conversion helper is absent.

Check for band-aid conversions on consumers (e.g., __int__ or __bool__ on stored wrappers) which indicate the codebase adapted to stringified storage rather than preserving types upstream; presence of such methods signals a systemic type-preservation issue.

Distinguish presentation formatting from data representation: if the code path is used both for human-facing output and for programmatic storage, prefer preserving native types in stored/model objects and apply string formatting only at the presentation boundary (CLI printing, logs).

When None-handling is the supposed reason for stringification, prefer explicit None checks (if v is None: keep None) or selective formatting only for presentation outputs instead of blanket str() in storage paths.

Practical search hints: grep for patterns like "= str(" , ".strip()" immediately after a cast, "map(str", and code that splits key/value tokens (split(":",1) or similar) inside constructors/loads; inspect callers of those constructors (parsers/loaders) to see whether they already supply native primitives.

Repair approaches: remove unconditional str()/format calls at storage sites; preserve the raw value assigned to model fields; if parsing textual input, implement targeted converters (int(), bool detection) at the parser boundary instead of coercing everything to string; run and extend unit tests to assert preserved types for numeric/boolean options.

When uncertain, reproduce with a minimal snippet: construct an Options/Model via the parser or constructor with numeric/boolean fields and confirm whether stored values are strings; update tests to assert native types and rerun consumers that expect numeric behavior.
skill.trigger: A parser boundary or constructor/normalizer (producer) consumes parsed tokens or incoming values and stores them on a model/state owner by applying unconditional string conversion or formatting to every non-null input (e.g., v = str(v), v = str(v).strip(), map(str, ...), or f-strings used across all fields). Observables: callers or consumers expect native primitives (ints, bools) but receive strings (type assertions fail, numeric operations break), and the stringification occurs in code that iterates over parsed key/value pairs or initializes model fields (constructor, Options.loads/__init__, or similar).

skill.title: Flake8 CLI architecture
knowledge: CLI entrypoint: src/flake8/main/cli.py defines main(), which constructs an Application() and delegates execution to app.run(argv) and returns app.exit_code().

Application lifecycle: src/flake8/main/application.py implements Application which orchestrates the run: it parses arguments (including plugin discovery), builds the formatter, constructs a StyleGuide/manager and a checker.Manager, runs checks, and drives formatter lifecycle (start/stop/reporting).

Options and plugin discovery: options parsing and aggregation live under src/flake8/options/ (including parse_args) and are responsible for discovering plugins and returning the parsed options and discovered plugin objects to Application during initialization.

Plugin and formatter boundaries: src/flake8/plugins/finder.py locates checker and reporter plugins; reporter.make (and the formatters in src/flake8/formatting/) produce BaseFormatter instances that Application calls to start/stop and emit formatted results.
File checking orchestration: src/flake8/checker.py (Manager) and src/flake8/processor.py own the file-checking pipeline, maintaining statistics and results that the StyleGuide and formatter consume.

skill.title: Configuration field assignment swap between producer and consumer
knowledge: Map producer and consumer roles: find where each option is normalized or parsed (producers: ConfigManager.__init__, Config._normalize, normalization helpers) and where values are assembled into PluginOptions/Namespace or returned tuples (consumers: parse_args, OptionManager.register_plugins, finder.parse_plugin_options).

Instrument both sides with sentinel inputs: choose distinct, easily-observed values for the two fields (e.g., 'SENTINEL_A' and 'SENTINEL_B'), run the producer, and log the exact normalized outputs; separately log the consumer's received arguments or the fields used when constructing the final object to reveal swapped assignment.

Prefer keyword arguments at construction sites: inspect calls that build PluginOptions or return tuples; if positional arguments are used, verify the positional ordering matches the constructor signature. Converting to explicit keyword args often prevents silent swaps.

Check helper-call argument ordering: search for normalization helpers (e.g., normalize_paths, join_paths) and audit every call site for parameter order. Create small unit tests that call the helper with distinct sentinel values to confirm the signature and detect swapped usage.

Search for tuple/dict return shapes and unpack sites: producers that return multiple values (a, b = fn()) or dicts with keys may have had their ordering/keys changed by refactors. Confirm callers unpack or access the same semantic slots the producer now provides.

Look for silent type changes that mask the bug (tuple→list, frozenset→set): these can accompany refactors and make tests pass while semantics are swapped. Compare types at producers and consumers and ensure conversions do not hide mis-assignment.

Add a round-trip unit test: write a focused test that formats a config with distinct values for the two fields, runs the normalization/assembly pipeline, and asserts that the final structured object preserves the original semantics for each field (no cross-assignment).
Inspect recent commits touching producers, consumers, and constructor signatures for reordering or renaming; a one-line refactor that changed argument order is a common root cause.

If fixing, prefer changes that make intent explicit: use keyword args for constructor calls, add parameter names to helper invocations, and add docstrings or type hints on producer return shapes to prevent future mismatch.

When path normalization is involved, also assert path normalization calls with base vs paths sentinel inputs and add unit tests that verify ordering and returned normalized forms (absolute vs relative).
skill.trigger: A consumer/constructor that assembles a structured configuration object or PluginOptions observes two distinct configuration fields (A and B) populated with each other's values (A→B and B→A). This occurs when a producer returns multiple normalized values (tuple, dict keys, or named attributes) or when helper functions are called positionally with swapped arguments (e.g., normalize_paths(base, paths) vs normalize_paths(paths, base)), and the consumer uses positional arguments or the wrong keys when constructing the final representation.

skill.title: alive-progress repository architecture
knowledge: The primary public progress API is the alive_bar context manager implemented in alive_progress.core.progress; core.progress owns the progress lifecycle, rendering loop, and composes timing, animations, and terminal output for a progress instance.

Configuration parsing and runtime configuration are handled in alive_progress/core/configuration.py (the config handler) and its output is consumed by core.progress to determine behaviour and rendering options.

Animation implementations and frame generation live under alive_progress/animations (spinners.py, bars.py, spinner_compiler.py, utils.py); core.progress selects and drives these animation factories to render spinners and bars.

Terminal and I/O abstractions live under alive_progress/utils/terminal (tty.py, non_tty.py, jupyter.py, void.py). Print/output coordination is managed by alive_progress/core/hook_manager.py, which installs hooks to buffer or passthrough printed output so progress rendering and normal prints can coexist.

skill.title: Mixed ternary and logical operators produce wrong boolean guard evaluation
knowledge: When you see a single-line guard that mixes logical operators and a ternary/inline-if, treat it as precedence-ambiguous: reproduce the decision with an explicit truth-matrix of inputs (object with/without isatty, isatty True/False, override flag True/False/None).

Instrument the decision-site to log or assert intermediate subexpressions and the final boolean result (e.g., evaluate and print hasattr(file,'isatty'), file.isatty() when safe, override flag, and the final 'is_tty' or guard expression). This reveals unintended evaluation order caused by the ternary or missing parentheses.

Prefer an explicit, sequential evaluation: evaluate override flags first, then safely query properties (guarding isatty() in try/except), and finally choose the branch. This both clarifies intent and avoids precedence surprises.

If calling the property may raise (AttributeError, OSError), wrap the call in try/except and document fallback semantics; do not rely on short-circuit semantics to avoid calling a missing method unless that is the explicit intent.
Use parentheses when the intent is to preserve a particular operator-binding, but prefer rewriting into multiple statements for clarity and easier testing.

Add unit tests that cover the full matrix: object lacks isatty attribute, object.isatty() == True, object.isatty() == False, and override flag values (True/False/None). Each test should assert which implementation is selected (TTY, non-TTY, jupyter, void) so regressions are caught.

When an override flag exists, make its precedence explicit in code and tests (e.g., 'if force_tty is not None: is_tty = force_tty' before other checks) so readers and future maintainers cannot confuse override semantics with combined-expression behavior.

Search for similar one-line guards elsewhere (compact conditionals mixing ternary/and/or) — they are a recurring source of subtle operator-precedence bugs and benefit from the same rewriting and test-matrix approach.
skill.trigger: A selector/consumer (e.g., terminal implementation chooser, environment detector, or I/O-mode guard) picks the wrong branch because its decision is implemented as a single expression that mixes logical operators (and/or) with a conditional/ternary expression (X if C else Y), often together with an override flag. Applicable when a property read (producer: file.isatty() or environment probe) and an explicit override (producer: force flag) are combined inline, so operator precedence or short-circuiting can change which value is ultimately tested.

skill.title: Bleach HTML sanitizer/linkifier architecture
knowledge: Top-level API functions bleach.clean() and bleach.linkify() are thin public entry points that delegate to Cleaner (bleach.sanitizer.Cleaner) and Linker (bleach.linkifier.Linker) respectively; those classes own the core cleaning and linkification behavior.

Bleach uses a bundled html5lib shim (bleach.html5lib_shim / bleach/_vendor/html5lib) as the parsing/serialization layer. Sanitization and linkification are implemented as html5lib-style filters (subclassing the Filter base) that transform token streams between the treewalker and the serializer.

Linkification behavior is driven by regex construction and callback application inside bleach.linkifier (build_url_re/build_email_re, TLDS, DEFAULT_CALLBACKS). Protocol lists (from html5lib_shim) and callbacks (e.g., bleach.callbacks.nofollow) determine which strings are converted to links and what attributes are applied to generated <a> elements.

skill.title: Tokenizer consumeEntity override misimplements producer contract (return-value and side-effect mismatch)
knowledge: Search the repository for consumeEntity (and similarly-named entity-consumption entry points) and locate any subclass overrides or wrapper implementations in shims; include grep for 'consume_entities' flags or 'consume_entities=' assignments.

Compare the subclass/wrapper implementation to the upstream/vendor version to discover the expected contract: what return values indicate (True/False), which side-effects are performed (mutating currentToken when fromAttribute, appending to tokenQueue, calling stream.unget or stream.get_tag), and whether the method both mutates state and returns a sentinel.

Verify return-value semantics precisely: many HTML tokenizer implementations use the boolean return from consumeEntity to signal 'entity found and consumed'. Ensure an override returns the same boolean for both consuming and non-consuming paths instead of returning None or swapping meanings.

Inspect side-effects when not consuming: if the override must preserve the raw '&', confirm it re-emits the character in the expected place (either by ungetting the character on the stream, appending a TAG_TOKEN_TYPE_CHARACTERS token, or updating currentToken correctly for attribute contexts). Check both data and fromAttribute paths.

Check ordering between tokenQueue and the underlying stream: overrides that append tokens directly to tokenQueue can change token emission order relative to upstream behavior; add unit tests that exercise adjacent token boundaries (text before/after an entity, attribute vs data context) to detect reordering or duplication.

Look for interactions with iterator wrappers (__iter__, tokenize, or ParseError handling) that may intercept or mutate tokens after consumeEntity runs. A wrapper that catches ParseError or that post-processes last_error_token can mask or duplicate emitted characters if the override's side-effects differ.

Reproduce with minimal tests: create a tokenizer instance with preservation disabled (consume_entities=False) and feed strings containing '&' in data and inside attributes; assert the serialized output contains the raw '&' or the expected token sequence. Add tests for both vendor and shim class instances to prevent regressions.

If making a shim override, prefer delegating to super() for the consume path and explicitly implement a single, well-documented non-consuming branch that returns False and performs exactly the minimal side-effect needed to preserve stream/token order (document the contract in a docstring).
When changing behavior, add instrumentation/logging in tests to confirm the boolean return and the sequence of stream/tokenQueue operations (helpful when reasoning about subtle ordering bugs).
skill.trigger: A consumer observes entities (for example, '&' characters) are missing, decoded, or otherwise altered even when a tokenizer instance is configured to preserve raw entities (preservation flag false). Applicable when the codebase contains a tokenizer subclass or shim that either overrides the entity-consumption routine or manipulates tokenQueue/stream/history around entity handling — i.e., when an override exists or a wrapper layer intercepts entity logic and could violate the upstream method's return-value/side-effect contract.

skill.title: feedparser repository architecture
knowledge: feedparser/api.py is the public API entry point: it accepts URLs, filenames, file-like streams, or raw strings, orchestrates opening the resource, coordinates encoding detection/conversion and parser selection, and returns a FeedParserDict with keys like entries, feed, version, headers, and namespaces.

feedparser/encodings.py centralizes encoding and stream handling: it provides stream factory helpers (e.g. get_text_file/get_binary_file/get_file and convert_file_to_utf8) that normalize input into UTF-8 streams used by the parsers.

Parsers live under feedparser/parsers (strict.py, loose.py, json.py) and are chosen by the public API: StrictXMLParser uses the SAX/xml.sax route, LooseXMLParser implements SGML-like/loose parsing behavior, and JSONParser handles JSON feeds. Common parsing behavior and helpers are provided by mixins in feedparser/mixin.py.

HTML processing, sanitization, and namespace handling are factored into dedicated modules: feedparser/html.py and feedparser/sanitizer.py implement HTML heuristics and safe URL/entity handling, while feedparser/namespaces/*.py contain namespace-specific handling (e.g. dc, itunes, mediarss).

skill.title: Timezone offset sign parsed or applied incorrectly (and TZ component locals used before assignment)
knowledge: Locate the TZ-token parsing site: identify where the parser extracts sign, hour, and minute components from the timezone token and where it applies any negation. Verify there is exactly one sign interpretation (do not both negate the parsed components and then invert arithmetic again).

Check timedelta construction and the order/meaning of its arguments. Confirm the values passed are the intended hour/minute magnitudes and signs (explicit keyword arguments reduce error: datetime.timedelta(hours=..., minutes=...)).

Verify the final arithmetic: when converting a local naive datetime to UTC, confirm whether the offset should be added or subtracted. Use small canonical examples: 'UTC+02:00' and 'UTC-02:00' applied to a known local time should produce the expected UTC results.

Test signedness with unit cases: +HH:MM, -HH:MM, TZ strings with/without colon, named zones like 'GMT' or 'Etc/GMT±X'. Detect double-negation by checking a round-trip (apply offset then remove it) or by comparing against Python's timezone-aware conversions for the same numeric offsets.

For UnboundLocalError or similar: ensure tz component locals have safe defaults before conditional parsing (e.g., tz_hours=0; tz_minutes=0) or perform conditional returns/flows so variables are never referenced in branches where they aren't assigned. Prefer explicit initialization over relying on downstream branches.

When tokenizing date parts from a split array, validate index usage and mapping (day/month/year/time/tz). Off-by-index mistakes can co-occur with offset mishandling; add assertions or parsing helpers that map tokens to semantic roles to avoid swapped indices.

When possible, use keyword arguments when constructing timedelta (datetime.timedelta(hours=tz_hours, minutes=tz_minutes)) and avoid relying on positional ordering of many zeros which is error-prone and hides argument meaning.

Add small parser-focused tests that assert conversion of local times with simple offsets to expected UTC tuples. For maintainability, include tests for edge cases (zero offsets, negative offsets, colon/no-colon formats, named zones) to catch regressions.
skill.trigger: A date/time parser (consumer) returns UTC timestamps shifted in the wrong direction or by roughly twice the timezone offset (e.g., parsing '-01:01' yields a UTC time moved the wrong way). The function parses a timezone token into local values (timezone_hours/timezone_minutes or similarly named locals), constructs a datetime.timedelta (or equivalent offset object), and then applies that offset to a naive datetime. Alternatively, a parser raises UnboundLocalError because tz component locals (hours/minutes) are only assigned on some branches but referenced unconditionally.

skill.title: Producer parses request/iterates inputs but never invokes model/backend mutator (missing producer→consumer call)
knowledge: Reproduce the API call and then inspect the model/backend state directly (not just the response); if state is unchanged while the response succeeded, suspect a missing producer→consumer invocation.

Open the response/handler function (producer role) and look for where parsed values should be passed to the model/backend. Check for absent calls (no call to elb.add_tag or equivalent), early returns, or deleted/ commented-out loops that would have invoked the mutator.

Search the repository for expected mutator call-sites (common names like add_tag(s), add_tags, put_tags, tag_resource) to find correct call patterns to mirror; compare the response code to a working sibling or example to see the exact invocation shape and argument names.

Check for wrong method/attribute names or argument keys at the call site (e.g., calling add_tags with a different parameter name or passing TagDescriptions instead of Tags) which makes the producer appear to handle input but not affect the model.

Inspect control-flow guards and duplicate-key checks in the producer: validation or dedupe logic may swallow the path that would call the mutator (e.g., an early raise/return removed the loop that invoked the model).

When code that should call the model is present but not executed, instrument (print/log) the producer to verify whether the call is reached; missing runtime calls indicate omitted invocation or incorrect conditional placement.

If the producer previously called the model, review recent diffs for removed lines or refactors that moved the call outside the executed body (accidental deletion, indentation change, or moved below a return).

Prefer minimal fixes that restore the producer→consumer invocation with correct argument names; add a unit test that exercises the full write-and-read cycle (e.g., create/add tags then describe) to prevent regressions.
skill.trigger: A response-level producer (e.g., API handler or request parser) accepts/parses input (or iterates over parsed items) and completes successfully, but the resource's persistent state (owned by a model/backend role) remains unchanged because the producer does not call the model/backend mutator, calls the wrong method, or passes the wrong argument name.

skill.title: Validator observes original value because normalization/producer result is skipped or not propagated
knowledge: Reproduce with minimal inputs: use a canonical value that must be normalized (e.g., integer ndarray) and confirm the constructor raises the validation error; also try passing an already-normalized value (float) to confirm validator behavior.

Inspect the producer/normalizer code path (e.g., upcast, parsing, conversion helpers). Confirm it executes and that its converted result is assigned to the same local/attribute the validator later inspects (e.g., rebind 'self' or assign to the attribute used by validation).

Check ordering: ensure validation checks occur after the conversion step. Look for early returns or removed branches that could bypass the normalization (deleted code, conditionals that no longer fire).

Watch for view/array aliasing semantics: numpy.view or methods that return views can preserve dtype or produce unexpected aliasing—verify that np.asarray(..., dtype=float).view(cls) actually produces an object whose dtype the validator will inspect.

Verify the validator's input: examine which object/dtype the validator tests (original variable vs. converted variable). If the validator calls a helper (e.g., safe_issubdtype), make sure that helper is invoked on the converted object's dtype, not the pre-conversion dtype.
Search commit diffs for removed/modified lines around the normalization (e.g., removed assignment statements or removed calls to conversion helpers) and for reorderings that moved validation earlier.
If a helper function performs classification (e.g., safe_issubdtype), confirm it receives the right dtype object and that it itself has not regressed (test helper in isolation with known dtypes).

Add small unit tests that assert integer inputs are accepted (i.e., are converted and pass validation) and that the dtype after normalization is floating; this catches regressions where conversion is skipped or discarded.

When fixing, prefer explicit rebind/assignment of the normalized value to the same name the validator uses (e.g., self = np.asarray(..., dtype=float).view(cls)) and keep validation logic simple and ordered: normalize → validate → return. Document that validators must inspect the post-normalization state.

If the normalization/validation interplay is subtle (subclassing, views, side-effect-free conversion), centralize conversion/validation in one small, well-tested function to avoid ordering mistakes and accidental removal.
skill.trigger: A constructor/producer is expected to normalize or convert an input (e.g., int→float) but the public-facing validator (consumer) raises a validation error about the original representation. Structurally, the code contains a normalization/upcast branch or helper that is either removed/skipped, its result is not assigned to the variable later consumed by the validator, or validation runs before the normalization step.

skill.title: python-docx repository architecture
knowledge: The public API surface is provided by the docx package (notably src/docx/api.py) and exposes the Document() factory and other top-level convenience functions used by callers.

Core in-memory model objects live under src/docx (for example class Document in src/docx/document.py) and implement document behavior (Paragraph, Run, Table, Section, Styles, Settings) while delegating XML details to the oxml layer.
The oxml layer (src/docx/oxml/*) provides element proxy classes (CT_* mappings) that represent WordprocessingML elements; model classes operate on these proxies rather than raw XML strings.

Packaging and part-level I/O responsibilities (reading/writing .docx, relationships, core properties, parts) are implemented in src/docx/opc/* (package.py, part.py, pkgreader.py, pkgwriter.py), separating persistence from the in-memory model.

Block container abstraction (src/docx/blkcntnr.py: BlockItemContainer) centralizes operations for block-level content (body, cell, header/footer) and provides convenience methods to enumerate and add paragraphs and tables used by the model classes.

skill.title: Validation/error branch references a local value before assignment
knowledge: Search the function for raise/Error constructions, f-strings, or string interpolation that include local names. Grep patterns: 'raise .*{name}', 'f"', '.format(', or direct concatenation with variable names near raise/ValueError sites.

Find all assignments to the referenced name in the function and check their control-flow dominance relative to each use. If any use is reachable without passing through an assignment, the variable can be uninitialized on that path.

Inspect surrounding conditional structure for swapped branch bodies, early returns, missing else, or reordered normalization steps (e.g., input normalization performed after the raise). Reordering a normalization/assignment earlier often fixes the bug.

Check for subtle normalization/validation ordering: e.g., conversions (Index(removals).unique().dropna()), type guards (is_list_like) or import-time assignments that appear after the raise in one branch — these are common culprits.

Consider whether the identifier might be produced by a helper/callee (closure or nested function) or accidentally expected to be set by a different function; prefer the function that contains the raise as the primary candidate unless the callee clearly documents/returns that diagnostic value.

Fix patterns: compute or initialize the diagnostic/local value before any validation/raise, or ensure the raise constructs a message without interpolating the local; add explicit default initialization (e.g., not_included = set()) or move the assignment above branching. Add unit tests exercising the edge cases that previously triggered the NameError (e.g., unknown removals, single-item removals, non-list inputs).

When forming candidates, prioritize functions that syntactically contain the raise referencing the name. If no assignment exists in that function, inspect callers and callees for accidental reliance on caller-local names (rare) or for missing return/context values.

If multiple candidate functions appear, collect concrete evidence: location of the raise, lines where the name is assigned, and control-flow paths from function entry to the raise. Use small repro inputs to trigger each branch and confirm where the exception originates.
skill.trigger: A function raises NameError or UnboundLocalError (or crashes while building an error/raise message) because a validation, guard, or error-raising branch references a local value that is only assigned on some control-flow paths (e.g., assigned later, assigned in the alternate branch, or skipped by an early return). This is applicable when the failing identifier is a local value (diagnostic/context variable) and the use occurs inside the same function's validation/raise logic rather than across a caller/callee boundary.

skill.title: Validation/error branch references a local value before assignment
knowledge: Locate the exact use that triggers the NameError/UnboundLocalError: find the line building the return value or error/raise message that references the name.

Find all assignments to the referenced name within the same function and determine whether every control-flow path to the use passes through an assignment (control-flow dominance). If any path reaches the use without assignment, the local can be uninitialized.

For property/getter implementations, inspect sibling *_val getters and the corresponding setter in the same class to see the canonical pattern (e.g., child = self.child; if child is None: return None; return child.val). Use these peers as a template for the intended behavior and for naming consistency that might have been copied incorrectly.

Check for common root causes: assignment placed after the guard/return, branches swapped or missing else, accidental removal of the assignment, or use of a different identifier name (typo) introduced during copy/paste between getter/setter implementations.

Fix patterns: initialize or compute the local before any validation/raise/return that references it (move assignment above the guard), or rewrite the guard to avoid interpolating the uninitialized local (return early without using it). When applicable, align the getter with the pattern used by peer getters in the class and ensure setter symmetry.

When forming candidates, prioritize functions that syntactically contain the use/raise that references the name. In class-based code prefer property/getter functions where this pattern is common, and include the corresponding setter in the candidate set when symmetry or naming may have influenced the bug.

Add unit tests that exercise the edge-case paths which previously caused the NameError (e.g., absent child elements, empty values) and tests that assert getter/setter symmetry for the property where relevant.

If no assignment exists in the function, inspect callers/callees only when the identifier reasonably could be produced externally; otherwise prefer fixing the local initialization inside the function that builds the return/raise message.
skill.trigger: A function (often a property/getter) raises NameError or UnboundLocalError (or crashes while building a return/error message) because a local value is referenced inside a validation/guard/return branch but is only assigned on some control-flow paths (for example, assigned after a None-check, only in an else branch, or skipped by an early return). This is especially applicable when the failing use is inside a getter/property implementation and when sibling getters or a corresponding setter exist in the same class.

skill.title: Astroid repository architecture
knowledge: AstroidManager (in astroid/manager.py) centralizes building and caching of astroid representations: it avoids rebuilding the same module, provides the build entrypoints, and decides between loading from source, stubs, or extensions.
astroid/astroid_manager.py instantiates the global MANAGER singleton (MANAGER = AstroidManager()) and immediately calls register_all_brains(MANAGER) to register inference extensions.

The builder (astroid/builder.py) is the component responsible for constructing astroid trees from source strings/files/objects; AstroidManager delegates actual construction to the builder when needed.
Library- and stdlib-specific inference logic is implemented as separate brain modules under astroid/brain and those brains are registered with the manager to extend inference and type knowledge.

skill.title: Name-based registry lookup misses due to inconsistent case-normalization at caller or registry
knowledge: When a name-keyed lookup returns a default or misses for well-known mixed-case identifiers, capture or print the exact string used at the lookup site (instrument the call site or add a temporary log) and compare it to the registry's actual keys.

Search the codebase for nearby .lower(), .casefold(), .upper(), or other normalization calls both at the producer (where qname/name is created) and at the consumer (immediately before the get/lookup). Caller-side normalization is a common, overlooked place to fix mismatches.

Inspect where registry entries are created/registered: determine whether keys are normalized on insertion. If registration normalizes keys, callers must use the same canonicalization; if callers normalize, registration should do likewise — inconsistencies are the root error.

Trace ownership of the name value: identify the producer (constructor, inherited qname method, manager creating names) and the consumer (lookup function/method). Verify whether responsibility for canonicalization is documented or enforced in a single place.

Prefer a single canonicalization policy (registry-normalizes or registration-preserves + documented case-sensitive keys). If changing callers is simpler and lower risk, a targeted change at the lookup site (apply .lower()/.casefold()) can be correct — but prefer to add tests that exercise mixed-case real-world names to prevent regressions.
Add unit tests using representative mixed-case names (e.g. OSError, ImportError, UnicodeDecodeError) to ensure special-case models or mappings resolve and to lock in the chosen normalization policy.

If the registry is shared across modules, search for other lookups/registrations to ensure the chosen normalization is applied consistently; consider adding helper accessors (registry.get_canonical(name)) to consolidate logic.
skill.trigger: A consumer (caller/lookup site) attempts to resolve a model/attribute by indexing a registry with a name string produced elsewhere (producer: qname, type name, or identifier), and either the consumer or the producer applies case normalization (lower()/casefold() or other transformation) while the registry keys are stored with a different casing/normalization policy — leading to missing entries or fallback to defaults.

skill.title: deepdiff — core diff orchestration and supporting subsystems
knowledge: deepdiff.diff.DeepDiff is the primary public entrypoint for computing differences; it orchestrates comparison passes, option parsing, caching/memoization, and assembly of final results.

Hashing and memoization are separate subsystems: deepdiff.deephash.DeepHash implements object hashing and combiners, and deepdiff.lfucache provides LFU and dummy cache implementations that DeepDiff uses to memoize expensive computations.

Result models and containers live in deepdiff.model (e.g. DiffLevel, TreeResult, ResultDict); DeepDiff populates these structures and the serialization/commands layers render them into text/tree or saved forms.

Search and path utilities are provided by dedicated modules: deepdiff.search (DeepSearch, grep) for searching, and deepdiff.path (extract, parse_path) for generating and parsing result paths. The package __init__.py exports the top-level API (DeepDiff, DeepSearch, grep, DeepHash, Delta, extract, parse_path).

skill.title: Iterable values short-circuited to whole-string during command-line rendering
knowledge: Locate the small formatting/renderer functions that convert dict entries into CLI fragments (common names: interpolate, to_str, _; search for patterns like "--{k}" or building a result string while iterating dict.items()).

Search repository for suspicious type-checks and short-circuits: "isinstance(..., Iterable)", "for n, i in enumerate(v)", and one-line branches that append f"{v}" or f"--{k} {v} ". These lines often indicate a container was treated atomically.
Reproduce quickly by calling the renderer with a mapping containing a list/tuple value and inspecting the returned cmd string to see whether the list appears as a repr or as expanded tokens.

Check ordering of type checks: ensure strings (str, bytes) are handled before Iterable, or use Sequence with explicit exclusion of str/bytes. Prefer explicit element-iteration for Sequence-like containers instead of relying on broad Iterable checks.

If a one-line short-circuit (e.g. result += f"--{k} {v} ") exists in an Iterable branch, remove it and replace with element-wise logic that escapes items and/or repeats the flag per element, matching the intended CLI format.

Verify escaping, spacing, and flag-repetition semantics (e.g., "--k a --k b" vs "--k a b") and add a unit test that passes heterogeneous list items (ints, strings) to ensure correct flattening and escaping.

Also inspect nearby small helpers and call sites (Context.resolve_str, DataResolver.resolve) to confirm the renderer's contract: whether callers expect a flattened token string or a single scalar; correct the renderer rather than callers when the renderer violates that contract.
skill.trigger: A producer/renderer function that builds command-line strings from a mapping returns a cmd string containing Python-style container representations (e.g. "[1, 2, 'foo']") for dict values that are lists/tuples. Applicable when the renderer contains an isinstance(..., Iterable) or similar branch (or a single-line short-circuit) that runs before explicit scalar/string handling or before element-wise iteration, causing containers to be treated as atomic and stringified rather than flattened into CLI tokens.

skill.title: Renderer/stringifier treats strings as iterables and applies sequence operations (reversed/join/slice) producing per-character artifacts
knowledge: Locate small stringify/renderer helpers and call sites (common names: stringify, to_str, stringify_element, render, format_element, _). These helpers are frequent single points of failure when iterables and scalars are handled together.

Search the repo for sequence-oriented operations applied to generic variables: reversed(, [::-1], ''.join(, for c in value, list(value) ) and patterns like isinstance(value, Iterable) or isinstance(value, Sequence) without excluding str/bytes. Code that reverses or joins an input is suspicious when that input can be a str.
Reproduce with a trivial input: call the helper with a simple string (e.g. 'key') and inspect output. If characters are reversed, look for slicing or reversed/join immediately before the return.

Verify type-dispatch order: ensure explicit scalar/string handling comes before Iterable branches. Prefer guards like isinstance(value, (str, bytes)) or use Sequence with an explicit exclusion of str/bytes, rather than broad Iterable checks.

If the code must treat iterables specially, implement element-wise formatting rather than applying sequence operations to the raw value. When flattening is intended, iterate elements and escape/join appropriately; when the value should remain atomic, return its string form directly.

Search for helpers imported into model/representation modules (e.g., stringify_element used by model classes). Check both the helper implementation and places that post-process its result (e.g., result[::-1] or other slicing in caller methods).

Add unit tests that include heterogeneous inputs: plain strings, lists of strings, and nested containers. Tests should assert that strings remain atomic and that list flattening behaves as intended (and that no character-level reversing occurs).

When fixing, prefer changing the helper rather than callers when the helper's contract is to return an element's textual representation. If callers expect a different contract, make the contract explicit and add/adjust tests and documentation.
skill.trigger: A producer/renderer/serializer or small stringify helper returns a string whose characters are reordered or shows per-character artifacts (e.g. 'key' -> 'yek', characters joined with separators), and the implementation applies sequence-oriented operations (reversed(), [::-1], ''.join(...), element-wise iteration) or contains broad isinstance(..., Iterable) / single-line short-circuit branches that do not special-case str/bytes. Applicable when small formatting helpers (producer, constructor, or parser boundary) are responsible for element normalization or flattening and are reused by model/representation code.

skill.title: oauthlib repository architecture
knowledge: oauthlib.common is the shared utilities module used across protocols: it implements URL encoding/decoding, CaseInsensitiveDict, nonce/timestamp/token generation, and the Request abstraction that protocol code consumes.
Package-level controls live in oauthlib.__init__: a module-level debug flag (set_debug/get_debug) and a package logger/NullHandler are provided for global debug and logging behavior.

The codebase is organized by protocol and RFC namespaces (oauthlib/oauth1/rfc5849, oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749, oauthlib/oauth2/rfc8628, oauthlib/openid/connect/core); each subpackage contains protocol-specific endpoints, grant_types, clients, tokens, parameters, and validators.

Endpoints are the primary control boundary: endpoint modules validate inputs, invoke RequestValidator callbacks (interfaces defined in the repository's request_validator.py modules and meant to be implemented by consumers), orchestrate grant type/token creation, and construct protocol responses.

skill.title: Unimplemented algorithm-specific verification or token-request secret-retrieval branch (no-op/pass)
knowledge: Locate dispatcher/switch/if-elif chains that branch on signature_method or is_token_request. Grep for signature constants (e.g., SIGNATURE_RSA_SHA256) and for is_token_request, resource_owner_key, get_request_token_secret, get_access_token_secret.
Inspect the branch bodies for 'pass', 'return' with a default value, 'raise NotImplementedError', or comments like TODO; these are red flags that an intended behavior was never implemented.

Check whether the branch should call a verifier helper (verify_rsa_sha256/verify_rsa_sha1/verify_rsa_sha512) and whether that helper is invoked with a retrieved rsa_key; if rsa_key is missing because get_rsa_key was not called, the verification will be skipped or fail.

For token-exchange flows, verify the endpoint calls the appropriate request_validator method (get_request_token_secret) when is_token_request is true; missing that call can leave resource_owner_secret unset and cause signature validation to fail only on token requests.
Search for early-return patterns before the dispatch (e.g., setting valid_signature = False and returning) that prevent later algorithm-specific logic from running.

Confirm the producer/consumer roles: the dispatcher (producer of verification decision) must call algorithm-specific verifiers and the endpoint (consumer) must obtain secrets from request_validator. Trace call sites to ensure the rsa_key and resource_owner_secret values are obtained and passed through to the verifier.
Run or extend unit tests to reproduce failures for the specific algorithm and for token-exchange requests; add targeted tests that exercise the previously-empty branch to prevent regressions.

If repairing, implement the missing call(s): retrieve rsa_key via request_validator.get_rsa_key and call the appropriate verify_rsa_sha256 helper; for token requests call get_request_token_secret when is_token_request is true. Prefer minimal, well-documented changes and add unit tests covering these branches.
skill.trigger: A consumer reports failed validation (e.g., endpoint.validate_request returns False or signature validation yields False) only for requests that use a particular algorithm or only for token-exchange requests with a resource_owner_key. Applicable when the code contains an explicit branch or dispatcher for that algorithm or an is_token_request branch in an endpoint, but that branch body is a no-op (pass), an early return, or omits the call to the validator callback that would produce an rsa_key or request_token_secret.

skill.title: Representation/serialization producer returns empty argument list
knowledge: Reproduce the mismatch by exercising producer and consumer in isolation: call the producer helper directly and capture its raw return value before the consumer formats it. Materialize iterables to lists for inspection (e.g., list(attrs_names), list(attrs)).

Check attribute-name selection logic: if the producer chooses between __slots__ and __dict__, materialize that selection (e.g., names = list(self.__slots__) if self.__slots__ else list(self.__dict__.keys())) and assert the instance actually holds those attributes.

Detect generator/exhaustion issues: ensure the producer does not return a generator that's iterated elsewhere first. Convert generator expressions to lists inside the producer if the consumer may iterate multiple times or debugging needs a stable snapshot.

Inspect final filtering predicates: e.g., filters that drop None or falsy values can remove all entries if attributes are None/False/0. Confirm the intended semantics (should None be omitted?) and ensure tests cover falsy-but-present values.

Verify getattr calls and descriptor behavior: getattr(self, name) may raise AttributeError or return unexpected values if name is wrong, if attributes are defined as properties, or if __getattr__/__getattribute__ intercepts lookups. Log or assert the (name, value) pairs obtained from getattr to spot missing attributes.

Check types and values of attrs_names: ensure names are strings and not an empty iterable (e.g., __slots__ can be an empty tuple or None). If __slots__ is present but empty, fallback to __dict__ must run; confirm the conditional is correct and not bypassed by a truthiness bug.

Distinguish producer vs consumer faults: call consumer with a small synthetic list of args to confirm it formats them correctly. If consumer produces expected output given a non-empty list, fault is in producer selection/filtering/return type.

Search for accidental stubs or regressions (e.g., producer replaced with `return []` or early return) and for recent edits that changed a comprehension into a conditional that yields no names. Use blame/history to spot such regressions.

Add targeted unit tests that: (1) call the producer directly and assert it returns expected name/value pairs; (2) construct objects with attributes set via __init__ and verify both __dict__ and __slots__ selection paths; (3) exercise falsy attribute values to ensure filters behave as intended.

Fix patterns: return concrete lists instead of bare generators when a stable snapshot is needed; ensure fallback branches produce list-like iterables; avoid identity/`is` checks that compare values to `self` unless intentional; make filter predicates explicit (e.g., filter out only when value is sentinel or deliberately absent).
skill.trigger: A consumer (repr/pretty-printer/serializer) produces an empty representation (no name/value pairs) even though instance attributes appear present at runtime, and the codebase contains a separate producer helper responsible for enumerating attribute names or yielding name/value pairs (e.g., __repr_args__ or similar). Applicable when the producer's attribute-selection branch, returned iterable type, or final filtering step can cause the producer to yield no entries while the consumer simply formats whatever iterable it receives.

skill.title: Parso repository architecture
knowledge: Grammar loading and generation is implemented under parso/grammar.py and parso/pgen2/*; these modules construct Grammar objects from grammar files and drive the pgen2 generator/grammar_parser pipeline.
The parser core is parso/parser.py: Parser objects consume a Grammar and a token stream to produce the generic Node/Leaf AST model.

Python-specific tokenization and parsing are implemented in parso/python/* (e.g. tokenize.py, token.py, parser.py) and Python-specific node logic lives in parso/python/tree.py; this directory implements language frontend behavior layered on the parser core.

The package exposes top-level convenience APIs (parso.parse, parso.load_grammar) from parso/__init__.py; utilities for encoding, line splitting, file I/O, and caching are provided by parso/utils.py, parso/file_io.py, and parso/cache.py and mediate reading source and caching/parsing behavior.

skill.title: Reordered or duplicated statements (refactor/merge) cause local read-before-assignment
knowledge: Scan the failing function top-to-bottom looking for initialization statements (object/array creation, list initializations, index calculations) that appear after a use of the same name; flag any producer placed below its first consumer.

Look for duplicated or very similar blocks, moved docstrings/comments, or interleaved reassignments that indicate a refactor/merge/copy-paste reshaped the original flow (e.g., the function contains the same handful of statements in two different orders).

Check for accidental reinitialization: a variable (e.g., res_values, taker, obj) created earlier may be reassigned/reset later, causing earlier computed values to disappear or leaving later uses uninitialized.

Compare the current function body to nearby historical versions (git blame/patch, prior commit) or sibling implementations to recover the intended linear sequence of producer->consumer steps; refactors often scramble that sequence.

When a NameError/UnboundLocalError occurs, identify the exact failing use line and then find the nearest preceding assignment to that name; if none exists before that use, search for blocks that were moved below or for renames that left a misspelled assignment in a different location.

For long functions, consider extracting or mentally grouping logical stages (validate inputs -> prepare data/obj -> iterate/compute -> finalize/resolve output). Ensure each stage's producers run before any consumer in subsequent stages.

When forming candidates, prioritize long procedural functions and recent changes touching them (constructors, apply/_apply_* helpers, and any function that creates intermediate containers used later). Also include functions that call or are called by them when the initialization might be delegated to a different responsibility (constructor vs helper).

Fix patterns: restore the correct ordering (move initialization above consumption), remove unintended duplicate blocks, avoid reinitializing containers before their final use, and add unit tests covering the sequential flow so future refactors are caught by regression tests.
skill.trigger: A function (often a long, procedural method) raises UnboundLocalError or NameError during normal API execution because a producer/initialization statement (producer: constructor/local initializer) was moved, duplicated, or reinitialized after a consumer read of the same local. This pattern commonly appears after a refactor, merge, or copy/paste that splits or reorders blocks (e.g., reinitializing a list after it was consumed, creating an object after it was used, moving the docstring or block boundaries so assignments occur later).

skill.title: cantools repository architecture
knowledge: The public CLI entrypoint is implemented in src/cantools/__init__.py: it builds an argparse-based top-level parser, dynamically loads subparsers from src/cantools/subparsers, and dispatches by calling a function stored on args (args.func) for the chosen subcommand.

The canonical in-memory CAN database representation is the Database class in src/cantools/database/can/database.py. This Database owns message/signal/node/bus domain objects and provides lookup/registration APIs used by higher-level operations and format loaders.

Format-specific parsing and enrichment is implemented under src/cantools/database/can/formats (modules for dbc, arxml, kcd, sym are present). These format loaders read external files and populate or amend the canonical Database rather than implementing a separate database model.

Diagnostic/UDS functionality (diagnostic database, DIDs, and related tooling) is implemented separately under src/cantools/database/diagnostics, providing a distinct diagnostic database and helpers that interoperate with the core CAN domain model.

The CLI dynamic subparser loader uses an _ErrorSubparser placeholder when a subparser module fails to import, allowing the top-level argparse structure to remain usable while surfacing the import error at invocation time.

skill.title: Consumer accessor mutates stored identifier (case-normalizing on read)
knowledge: Compare the internal storage attribute set in the constructor (e.g., self._name) with the value returned by the public accessor/property (e.g., def name(self): return ...). If they differ, the accessor is mutating the stored value on read.

Search the class for property definitions, __str__, __repr__, or other read-side helpers that reference the attribute; grep for .upper(), .lower(), .casefold(), .title(), format() and similar transformations near these methods.
Instrument or log both the stored attribute and the accessor return in a small repro (print(self._name, self.name) inside tests or temporary debugging code) to confirm where transformation occurs.

If the accessor is used as a registry key or for lookups, prefer normalizing once at storage/registration time or expose both raw and canonicalized forms explicitly (e.g., .raw_name and .canonical_name) so callers can choose the intended semantics.

Decide and document the canonicalization policy: either preserve original source casing everywhere and avoid transforming on read, or consistently normalize at storage and ensure all accessors and tests expect the canonical form.

Add unit tests that assert both the stored/raw attribute (if accessible) and the public accessor return the expected forms for mixed-case real-world identifiers to prevent regressions from accidental presentation-side transformations.

When making a change, update all places that rely on the accessor’s current behavior (lookups, serialization, tests) and consider adding helper accessors (get_raw_name(), get_canonical_name()) to make intent explicit and avoid hidden transformations.
skill.trigger: A consumer (property/getter, __str__/__repr__, or other read-side accessor) returns a transformed version (e.g., .upper(), .lower(), .casefold(), or formatted variant) of an internally stored identifier or metadata while the constructor/storage code preserves the original form — observable when the stored attribute value differs from the accessor’s returned value or tests expecting source-case names fail because the accessor presents a normalized case.

skill.title: Tweepy client architecture
knowledge: The legacy API class (tweepy/api.py::API) is responsible for constructing requests for v1 endpoints: it builds URLs/parameters, implements caching and rate-limit bookkeeping, and delegates HTTP execution results to the parsing layer.

The newer API v2 surface is implemented in the Client/BaseClient classes (tweepy/client.py and tweepy/asynchronous/client.py for async). Their .request / AsyncBaseClient.request methods are the central entry points for sending HTTP requests for v2 endpoints.

Authentication credential handling and request signing are implemented in tweepy/auth.py (e.g. OAuth1UserHandler, OAuth2UserHandler, OAuth2BearerHandler, AppAuthHandler); request paths use these handlers to sign or provide credentials before sending.
Response interpretation is owned by the parser layer (tweepy/parsers.py and ModelParser) which converts HTTP responses into Model objects defined in tweepy/models.py (and related model modules).

BaseClient._process_params is responsible for translating Python method parameters into HTTP request parameters — e.g. converting lists into CSV strings and formatting datetime objects to ISO timestamp strings before sending requests.
