skill.title: Caller forwards an incorrect endpoint path or HTTP verb literal to the downstream requester
knowledge: Reproduce the failure with a minimal caller invocation and instrument the shared request layer to log the endpoint string, final URL path, and HTTP method received; confirm the literal the caller forwarded vs what the requester used to build the URL.

Search the caller for hard-coded endpoint strings or simple mappings (grep for strings like 'saved_searches' or '/1.1/' usages) and inspect recent commits for changed literals—string replacements are a common cause.

Compare sibling methods (e.g., create_saved_search, get_saved_search, get_saved_searches) for consistent endpoint naming and mapping patterns; a copy-paste or edit in one function often introduces the wrong literal.
If endpoint names are composed with formatting, verify the format pattern and arguments to ensure the path fragment is assembled correctly (e.g., 'show/{id}' vs 'list').
Instrument or add a temporary assertion in the caller before delegation (e.g., assert endpoint in KNOWN_ENDPOINTS) to surface incorrect constants during development and testing.
Check for thin wrappers or decorators that might replace or map endpoint names (search for endpoint-selection helpers) and validate their mapping tables.
When the requester accepts both an endpoint name and params, ensure the caller is passing the correct role (endpoint vs id) and not mixing argument positions or names.
Add unit tests that assert the caller delegates the expected endpoint and method (mock the requester and verify call args) and integration tests that exercise the end-to-end request construction.
Consider centralizing endpoint constants or small helper functions to build endpoint names to reduce risk of typos and make single-point fixes easier.

As a short-term mitigation, the requester can validate known endpoint names and raise a clearer error if an unknown/unsupported endpoint is passed; long-term, fix the incorrect literal at the producer.
skill.trigger: A downstream HTTP requester returns an error (404/400/unexpected resource) or the wrong resource is fetched because a higher-level caller constructs and forwards an incorrect endpoint string or HTTP method literal. The caller is responsible for choosing or assembling the endpoint/method at the call site (literal, mapping, or simple formatting) rather than letting the requester derive it, so a mistaken constant, refactor, or typo changes the effective request path/method.

skill.title: Static class/module literal points to wrong resource/path
knowledge: Start by locating the attribute name in the repository (grep for the attribute identifier) and open the declaring module to confirm whether the value is a class- or module-level literal.

If the attribute is a class literal, check for an __init__ (or classmethod/classmethod-based factory) that might override the attribute at construction time; if none exists, treat the literal as the authoritative value.

Inspect registration/mapping code (e.g., plugin registries or _mapping modules) to see whether registration changes which module is reported/used by consumers or whether it might monkey-patch or wrap the class; do not assume registration changes attribute literals unless code assigns to the attribute.

Confirm the consumer's expectation by finding call sites that read the attribute and observing how they derive the resource path (e.g., concatenation with module name, passing to importlib.resources, direct open()). Reproduce at runtime by instantiating the producer and printing the attribute to ensure the observed incorrect value matches the report.

Compare the attribute literal against repository layout (package/module directories and packaged resources). Common mistakes include hardcoding the wrong subdirectory name or using an alias (module name vs package subdir) instead of the module where the resource actually resides.

Check for inheritance/subclassing: a base class may define the attribute with a placeholder and a subclass in another module should override it; ensure the consumer instantiates the intended subclass.

When fixing, prefer computed/package-aware lookups over hard-coded literals if the resource location should follow the module (e.g., compute path from __module__ or use importlib.resources/package_data). If a literal is correct, update the class/module literal and add a unit test that asserts resource existence for that attribute to prevent regressions.

If the attribute is intentionally configurable, consider moving it into constructor args or configuration and document the contract so registration/consumers do not rely on fragile module-relative literals.
skill.trigger: A consumer (caller) reads a class-level or module-level resource/path attribute (producer: class or module) and uses it to locate a file/resource, but the observed value is an incorrect literal. The attribute is defined as a static (class- or module-level) assignment and there is no constructor/initializer or registration code observed that would reliably override it at import or instantiation time.

skill.title: Producer computes serialized record offsets/lengths using wrong transfer-syntax flags or hard-coded byte constants
knowledge: Treat the failing symptom as an incorrect producer value: instrument the producer that computes offsets/lengths to log fp.tell() at key points (before/after writing headers/values) and the exact bytes written. Compare the logged tell() values and the computed stored-offsets — offsets must match absolute byte positions as consumed by the writer.

Check encoding/transfer-syntax flags used while measuring sizes (e.g., is_little_endian, is_implicit_VR). Size and header length for a Data Element depend on VR and transfer syntax; toggling these flags changes header byte counts and therefore any fp.tell() + constant arithmetic.

Avoid trusting small hard-coded constants. Instead of fp.tell() + C, compute the stored offset from the actual bytes written (write element to a temporary buffer and use its length) or compute header size from the chosen encoding mode. If a constant is used, document its derivation (which VR/transfer-syntax it assumes) and assert the encoding flags that make it valid.

Verify special-case tag handling (e.g., Offset Of The Next Directory Record (0004,1400) and Offset Of Referenced Lower Level Directory Entity (0004,1420)). Understand whether the stored offset is defined relative to the start of the enclosing record or start-of-file and whether the VR encoding for UL uses 4 bytes and a fixed header overhead.

If code adjusts or normalizes encoding flags for the purpose of measurement (e.g., setting is_little_endian = False to compute a canonical length), ensure the same convention is used consistently when computing offsets and when writing/serializing the final output, or convert the measured value into the writer's convention explicitly.

Inspect loop/control-flow around element emission. Changes like continue -> break can alter which elements are included in size calculations (e.g., skipping trailing group elements vs stopping at a sentinel group), leading to systematic offset shifts.

When tests fail with lookup KeyErrors using numeric offsets, add focused unit tests that construct minimal records and assert the computed offsets equal the positions where the writer actually serializes the corresponding record. Create tests for multiple transfer syntaxes/VR modes (explicit little, explicit big, implicit) if the code toggles those flags during measurement.

If possible, centralize offset computation into a single helper that returns absolute stored offsets derived from actual encoded bytes or consistent header-size calculations for the active transfer syntax. Instrument and assert invariants (e.g., stored_offset == position_of_element_value_start).

When assessing patches, pay attention to subtle final adjustments (e.g., subtracting a small constant from total length). These often mask attempts to reconcile inconsistent conventions and should be replaced by explicit conversions between conventions with comments and tests.

When encountering mysterious +6/+8 or -N adjustments, reconstruct the expected header length for each VR/transfer-syntax combination and verify the arithmetic. For DICOM UL offsets, confirm whether the offset is computed as fp.tell() + header_len where header_len matches the encoding flags in effect when the element is written.
skill.trigger: A writer/consumer (e.g., a DICOMDIR writer) fails to find or correctly place records (KeyError lookups, corrupted layout, or incorrect file offsets) because a producer function computes stored offsets/lengths by inspecting an in-memory write buffer but uses incorrect transfer-syntax encoding flags (endianness/explicit vs implicit VR) or applies small fixed arithmetic (±N) to fp.tell()/length values to derive stored offsets rather than deriving them from actual encoded bytes.

skill.title: Producer returns scalar or differently-shaped value while consumer expects a multi-element iterable/tuple
knowledge: Reproduce the failure with a minimal mock producer that returns the scalar/sentinel (e.g., a MockOutput.checkout returning True or None) to confirm the consumer's unsafe unpacking triggers TypeError.

Enumerate all producer implementations and return sites: grep for the producer method name (e.g., checkout/_checkout) and inspect every return. Compare actual returns against docstrings, type hints, and annotations (Optional[bool] vs tuple[...] signatures).

Audit the consumer sites that unpack/iterate the return: look for patterns like `a, b = result` or `for x in result` and identify callers that assume tuple/iterable shapes rather than checking types or values.
Decide normalization direction: prefer normalizing at the producer (make implementations consistently return the documented shape) when feasible to keep a single clear contract.

If producers are numerous or backward-compatibility sensitive, add defensive normalization at consumers: detect scalars (isinstance(result, (bool, type(None), str))) and coerce to the expected shape (e.g., treat a truthy bool as ("modified", [str(obj)]) or map None/False to (None, [])).

When coercing at the consumer, handle edge cases explicitly (strings are iterable—guard against treating a filename string as a list of chars), and document the compatibility behavior with deprecation notes if you plan to change producer contracts.
Add or update unit tests that assert the normalized behavior for both old and new producer shapes; include tests for both producer-side normalization and consumer-side guards to prevent regressions.

Update docstrings and type hints to state the canonical contract unambiguously (exact tuple shape, element semantics). Consider introducing a small data struct (namedtuple/dataclass) instead of bare tuples for clearer semantics.
If changing producer API surface is breaking, provide a compatibility shim or transitional layer and emit warnings so callers/producers can migrate.
Add runtime assertions or explicit checks in development/debug builds to fail fast with informative messages when the contract is violated, making future regressions easier to diagnose.
skill.trigger: A consumer (caller, aggregator, or dispatcher) immediately unpacks or iterates a callee/producer's return value assuming a multi-element iterable (e.g., (flag, details) or (added, modified)), but one or more producer implementations sometimes return a single scalar/sentinel (e.g., bool or None) or a differently-shaped value. The mismatch causes TypeError (e.g., "'bool' object is not iterable"), unpacking errors, or incorrect control flow when callers treat the value as the expected tuple/sentinel.

skill.title: MONAI package initialization and module-loading architecture
knowledge: monai.__init__ is the central package initializer: it sets the package version (via monai._version.get_versions()), enforces minimum Python requirements, installs custom warnings/logging filters, performs TF32 and environment detection, and coordinates loading of subpackages.

Submodule discovery and import is delegated to monai.utils.module.load_submodules (or similar module loader): this utility enumerates and imports subpackages and applies exclude patterns so optional or platform-specific components are not loaded by default.

Compiled/optional extensions (e.g., monai._C, .so artifacts, and certain optional packages like nnunet, handlers, bundle, fl) are treated as optional: monai.__init__ explicitly excludes or guards against their absence so initialization tolerates missing native extensions.

Utility helpers for environment checks (e.g., monai.utils.tf32, monai.utils.misc / MONAIEnvVars) are invoked during init and encapsulate platform/EnvVar detection logic separate from package-loading responsibilities.

skill.title: Composite loss branches on channel count and selects wrong CE/BCE computation path
knowledge: Reproduce quickly: call the loss object's subcomponents directly (e.g., instance.ce(input, target) and instance.bce(input, target)) using a minimal single-channel tensor pair to see which helper returns zero or raises/consumes the input silently.

Search the class for shape/flag guards that decide CE vs BCE (patterns like input.shape[1] == 1, input.shape[1] != 1, if n_classes == 1, or conditional use of include_background). Those branches are prime suspects for misrouting.

Inspect initialization of the loss objects: locate where CrossEntropyLoss and BCEWithLogitsLoss (or equivalents) are constructed and check the semantics of their `weight`, `pos_weight`, and `reduction` parameters; mismatched initialization can make one path effectively inert.

Examine helper implementations for target/shape handling: CrossEntropyLoss expects class indices (Long) and typically removes the channel dim, while BCEWithLogitsLoss expects floating targets with the same shape as logits. Confirm any dtype/shape conversion (e.g., target.to(dtype=input.dtype), argmax/one-hot conversions) is present and correct in each helper.

Check for early-return, sentinel, or zero-return behavior inside either helper: a helper might catch exceptions or return 0 when inputs are mis-shaped — find try/except or explicit zero returns and ensure they either raise or warn instead of silently changing loss semantics.

Look at the forward composition line(s) that compute sub-terms and combine them (e.g., ce_loss = self.ce(...) if ... else self.bce(...)). Verify the condition is correct for intended semantics and consider unifying logic (single helper that handles both binary and multiclass) to avoid divergent behavior.

Confirm documentation and parameter naming match runtime behavior. If the API allows single-channel use, ensure the code path produces meaningful CE contributions or documents/raises when CE is inapplicable.

Add unit tests that call both the overall forward and the individual subhelpers with single-channel and multiclass inputs, asserting that per-term contributions are nonzero when lambda_ce>0 and that behavior is consistent across shapes.

When fixing, prefer a single, well-documented CE helper that normalizes inputs/targets for both binary and multiclass, or make the branch explicit with a clear warning/error when a user configuration is unsupported. Avoid silent switching that causes a visible sub-term to be dropped without warning.
skill.trigger: A composite loss (producer: forward) exposes a per-term subloss (consumer: ce or bce helper) that evaluates to exactly zero (or otherwise becomes a no-op) for single-channel inputs. The class contains both multiclass CE and binary BCE helpers or loss objects and forward contains a shape/flag-based branch (e.g., input.shape[1] checks or include_background flags) that routes single-channel inputs to the alternate helper or bypasses the multiclass CE path.

skill.title: Aggregated metrics computed with reversed operands or swapped key assignments
knowledge: Compare raw producer counters to the consumer's inputs: instrument or print the raw integer counters (files, violations, clean, unclean) immediately before the consumer computes derived values to confirm the source counters are correct.

Validate sum/merge usage and argument order: when using helper functions (e.g., sum_dicts or similar), confirm the order of operands and that the helper returns the expected merged result (some helpers are non-commutative if used for accumulating).

Inspect each arithmetic expression for operand order and zero-division guards: ensure divisions use numerator=desired_count and denominator=files (or correct semantic mapping), and that any fallback (when denominator==0) returns a sensible default (usually 0), not 1 or inverted values.

Check derived-key assignments and mapping: verify that computed values are stored under the correct output keys (e.g., 'clean files' := clean, 'unclean files' := unclean). Watch for accidental swaps like assigning clean to unclean and vice versa.

Verify boolean/conditional logic that determines status/exit codes: ensure the condition (e.g., violations > 0) maps to the intended status and exit code in the correct truth branch, not inverted branches.

Search for tuple/unpack or positional-value swaps: when merging or unpacking tuples/dicts, check that variable order matches the intended semantic order (e.g., sum_dicts(a,b) vs sum_dicts(b,a); unpacking (partial, fname) vs (fname, partial)).

Reproduce with minimal inputs and unit tests: craft small test cases (zero files, one clean file, one unclean file, multiple violations) that exercise boundary conditions and assert expected averages, rates, labels, and exit/status behavior.

Prefer explicit, named operations in consumers: use keyword arguments, explicit variable names, and small helper functions with clear contracts for computing rates/averages to reduce accidental operand or key swaps; add targeted tests for these helpers.
skill.trigger: A consumer/aggregator computes derived metrics (averages, rates, ratios) and assembles labeled outputs from per-item integer counters, and the observed outputs contain systematically inverted numeric results (e.g., avg = total_items/total_errors instead of total_errors/total_items), incorrect zero-division fallbacks, or swapped labels/values for two related counters (e.g., clean↔unclean, status/exit-code reversed). Structural applicability: the code performs arithmetic on counters or merges per-item stats into an overall dict (sum/merge helpers, explicit division, dict key assignments) rather than simply forwarding values.

skill.title: Red-DiscordBot (redbot) repository orientation
knowledge: Package bootstrap and CLI entry: redbot.__main__ is the CLI entrypoint used to parse command-line options, instantiate the bot, and start the run loop.

Versioning and early runtime policies: redbot.__init__ implements VersionInfo and contains early initialization (version discovery, logging/uvloop/event-loop policy and colorama handling) performed during application startup.

skill.title: AttributeError when runtime object comes from a different package/version or a shadowed module
knowledge: Confirm the runtime object's identity before diving into source: inspect type(obj), obj.__class__.__module__, obj.__class__.__qualname__ and repr(obj) to verify which module/class was actually instantiated.

Locate the loaded module file and loader: check obj.__class__.__module__ in sys.modules and use sys.modules[module].__file__ or inspect.getsourcefile to find the filepath; compare that path to the repository path you inspected.

Check import resolution and sys.path order: print sys.path and find_spec/importlib.util.find_spec for the module name to see if an installed distribution or a different path is shadowing the repo version (look for site-packages, eggs, .pth files, and packaged .egg-info directories).

Compare package metadata and versions: run pip show <package>, pip list, or examine installed distribution metadata (egg-info or dist-info) to verify whether an installed release is being imported instead of local source.

Detect proxies, wrappers, or monkeypatching: verify that the object is an actual instance of the expected class (isinstance checks), inspect for attributes like __wrapped__ or __class__ reassignment, and search project for runtime monkeypatches or conditional redefinition code paths.

Confirm the attribute's declaration shape: ensure the attribute is an instance method on the class (not a module-level function, @staticmethod, or conditional definition), and that name-mangling or different signature/visibility isn't the cause.

When necessary, reproduce import in an isolated interpreter: from the project root run a small script that prints importlib.util.find_spec, module.__file__, and the class definition to confirm what file Python imports in the current environment.

If a mismatch is found, fix by aligning the environment: adjust PYTHONPATH or sys.path, uninstall the conflicting package, install the correct editable/local package (pip install -e .) or change packaging/installation so the expected source is imported, or remove the shadowing file that overwrites the module name.
skill.trigger: A caller (consumer) raises AttributeError 'object has no attribute <name>' while a repository source file (producer) visibly defines that attribute on the expected type; the failure is reproducible at runtime and the repository copy does not match the object actually loaded (e.g., different installed distribution, duplicate package on sys.path, import shadowing, or monkeypatch/proxy wrapping).

skill.title: Consumer reads per-thread stack at wrong index (oldest vs most recent) and mishandles empty-stack sentinel
knowledge: Locate the thread-local object or state owner (e.g., threading.local() instance) and identify its stack/list attribute name (common patterns: .stack, .contexts, .frames). Grep for creation sites and all readers/writers (push, pop, direct assignments, insert(0), setdefault, reassignments).

Inspect consumer-side index expressions: prefer last-element access (_stack[-1]) for LIFO semantics. If code uses index 0, a fixed index, or enumerates then picks first element, treat it as a likely logic error when the stack is intended LIFO.

Check empty-stack handling and sentinel semantics: the consumer should catch AttributeError/IndexError (stack absent or empty) and then either raise (when not silent) or return None (when silent). Watch for inverted conditions (raising when silent=True or returning a new default instance instead of None).

Examine producer functions (push/pop): ensure push uses append (or equivalent) and pop uses pop() without an index so they produce LIFO order. Also search for any code that mutates the stack by inserting at 0, replacing the stack object, or reassigning _local.stack to another collection, which can invert perceived order.

Search the repository for direct assignments to the stack attribute or uses of list.insert, list.reverse, or other operations that change element order. A global search for '.stack[' , '.stack =', "insert(" and 'setdefault(" helps find surprises.

Verify typing/overload or compatibility shims that may create default values or different control-flow in some builds (e.g., returning Context() vs None). Ensure overloads/forwarding code do not return constructed defaults when the intended behavior is to indicate absence.

Construct minimal tests exercising both branches: call the consumer when no context is active with silent=False (expect RuntimeError) and with silent=True (expect None). Also test within active contexts to ensure the consumer returns the most-recently pushed context.

When proposing a fix: change index access to -1 for LIFO, or centralize last-element lookup into a small helper to reduce repeated mistakes; normalize empty-stack handling to catch AttributeError/IndexError and implement if not silent: raise; else: return None. Avoid constructing new default context objects in absence cases unless the API contract specifies it.

If multiple threads are involved, double-check thread-local initialization patterns: prefer _local.__dict__.setdefault('stack', []) and avoid mutating a shared list across threads. Add tests for concurrent or multi-threaded scenarios if relevant.
skill.trigger: A consumer function (public API or library helper) that should return the most-recently-pushed per-thread context instead: (a) returns the oldest entry or a freshly constructed default when no active entry exists, or (b) a boolean 'silent'/sentinel parameter that should suppress an error instead causes a RuntimeError. Applicable when code reads a thread-local/owner-managed stack/list (e.g., _local.stack[index]) and performs index-based access or exception-based empty-stack handling rather than a clear LIFO lookup and sentinel-aware error/None return.

skill.title: Jinja2 repository architecture
knowledge: The Environment class (src/jinja2/environment.py) is the central orchestration point: it holds configuration, the loader, registered extensions/filters/tests/globals, and is responsible for creating/looking up templates and coordinating compilation and caching.

Template source is processed by a compilation pipeline composed of the lexer (src/jinja2/lexer.py), parser (src/jinja2/parser.py), AST/nodes (src/jinja2/nodes.py and optimizer), and the compiler (src/jinja2/compiler.py) which produces executable code objects consumed by the runtime.

Loaders (src/jinja2/loaders.py) provide template source/metadata to Environment, and bytecode/bytecode-cache support (src/jinja2/bccache.py) is used by Environment to store and retrieve compiled templates to avoid recompilation.

Runtime execution and rendering are performed by the runtime/context modules (src/jinja2/runtime.py and related code); the runtime enforces undefined handling, applies filters/tests, and executes the compiled code objects produced by the compiler.

skill.title: Compile/emit consumer rejects incorrect AST root/shape
knowledge: Locate the failure string or exception site in the compile/emit consumer. Open the consumer to confirm it performs an explicit shape/type guard (isinstance, type check, or error raise) on the AST root.

Check the guard for common refactor mistakes: inverted condition (negated/isinstance swapped), wrong exception text left behind, or recent changes that reorder constructor args or change return/stream semantics so the consumer receives the wrong object.

Trace the direct caller chain from the consumer back to the producer(s): parser.parse, environment.from_string/get_template, loader, and any caching or bytecode cache layer. Identify which component constructs or forwards the AST root value.

Instrument or reproduce: add temporary logging/print of type(node) and repr(node) just before the consumer's guard to observe the runtime type/shape being passed in. A minimal repro that prints type() clarifies whether it's an Expr, list, sentinel, or already a Template.

Inspect parser return paths: verify top-level parse functions always return the correct root node type (not an expression node, list, or sentinel) on all control-flow paths, including error paths and simple expression-only inputs.

Search for call sites that might forward the wrong value (e.g., functions that parse an expression then incorrectly pass that result to the compiler rather than wrapping it in a Template node), or for use of parser helpers (parse_expr, parse_list) whose outputs are not Template roots.

Check caches and serialization boundaries (bytecode caches, pickling, or persistent caches): ensure cached values hold the expected Template-shaped AST or compiled code and that cache retrieval does not return a placeholder/sentinel used elsewhere.

When the consumer check is legitimate, add clear assertions/documentation and harden the producer/caller to guarantee the contract (convert or wrap expression nodes into a Template-root where appropriate); when the consumer check is wrong (inverted or overly strict), fix the condition and add unit tests covering basic templates and expression-only inputs.

Add small regression tests that exercise: basic template parsing/rendering, expression-only templates, cached retrieval paths, and any public API surfaces (Environment.from_string, get_template) to prevent future parser/consumer contract regressions.
skill.trigger: A compile/generate function throws a type/validation error complaining the input is not the expected root node (e.g., "Can't compile non template nodes"), and the codebase separates an AST-producing component (parser/loader) from a compile/emit consumer that uses type-based guards or isinstance checks to enforce a specific root node shape.

skill.title: pdfplumber repository architecture
knowledge: pdfplumber.pdf defines the PDF document model (class PDF). PDF.open is exposed at package top-level (open = PDF.open in __init__.py) and is responsible for opening/repairing streams, parsing with pdfminer, and providing cached document-level properties (pages, objects, annotations, hyperlinks, structure tree).

skill.title: Inconsistent normalization of heterogeneous 'children' representations (single-object dict vs list/ref)
knowledge: Locate the helper that builds or normalizes the element's children (e.g., _make_element, _resolve_children). Inspect every control-flow path that assigns the children value and record what concrete types it can produce (int, list, PDFObjRef, dict, etc.).

Trace uses of the low-level resolver (resolve1 or equivalent) at both the helper and consumer boundaries. Ensure resolve1 is applied consistently: either normalize children to a list of refs and let consumers call resolve1, or normalize to a list of resolved dicts so consumers need not re-resolve.

Be suspicious of special-case branches that wrap the original raw object (e.g., children = [obj['K']]) instead of wrapping the resolved value. Those branches commonly cause representation mismatches and should be replaced with wrapping the normalized/resolved value.

At the consumer boundary (the traversal that iterates children), add defensive normalization and clear contract checks: accept ints/refs by resolving, accept dicts as already-resolved objects, and always coerce to a list/iterable before iterating. Add explicit assertions or docstrings that state the expected shape and element type.

Add unit tests and a small corpus fixture that exercises all variants: no children, single-child represented as dict, single-child represented as ref/int, and multi-child lists. Tests should assert that the traversal does not raise and that the normalized shapes are as documented.

When fixing, prefer a single authoritative normalization strategy (document it): either (A) children is always a list of resolvable references (consumers call resolve1 per child), or (B) children is always a list of resolved dicts (helper calls resolve1 for entries). Update helper/consumer accordingly and update comments/docs to prevent regressions.
skill.trigger: A consumer/traversal raises KeyError or TypeError while iterating or resolving an element's 'children' because the normalization helper for that element's children field returns heterogeneous shapes (int, list, reference object, or a raw dict) and at least one control-flow path leaves a single-child object as a raw dict or differently-wrapped value; the consumer expects a consistent iterable of resolvable references or consistently-resolved dicts.

skill.title: fvcore repository architecture
knowledge: The package version is defined in fvcore/__init__.py via the __version__ variable (used by setup.py).
fvcore/common/file_io.py exposes a global PathManager that wraps iopath functionality and registers URL/path handlers (e.g. HTTPURLHandler, OneDrivePathHandler) for repository-wide file I/O.

skill.title: Consumer/wrapper swaps arguments or flag values when calling a producer, reversing semantics
knowledge: Locate thin wrappers and adapters: search for calls to the suspected producer (e.g., grep for colored( or other producer name) and inspect nearby wrapper/printing helpers (consumer roles like cprint).

Compare wrapper calls to the producer's declared signature: ensure positional arguments align with parameter order; prefer inspecting keyword usage where present—positional forwarding is a common source of accidental swaps.

Reproduce with and without the wrapper: call the producer directly with identical named arguments and compare repr/output to the wrapper's output to determine whether the inversion occurs at the wrapper boundary.
Check boolean/flag arguments specifically (e.g., no_color vs force_color): confirm the wrapper doesn't swap these values or pass the wrong variable into the wrong named parameter.
When the code uses positional forwarding, review recent diffs or refactors that changed parameter order or added parameters—API signature changes often break positional callers.

If wrappers intentionally reorder or adapt parameters, document and test the mapping; consider replacing positional forwarding with explicit keyword arguments in the wrapper to make the mapping robust and self-documenting.

If the producer composes outputs (e.g., formats or nests strings), verify both producer and wrapper composition orders: a correctly ordered producer can still produce swapped results if the wrapper passes arguments in reversed slots.
Use small focused tests around each boundary: assert that wrapper(text, color=X, on_color=Y) equals producer(text, color=X, on_color=Y) to pin the failure location quickly.
skill.trigger: A caller/consumer (e.g., a wrapper, convenience function, or thin adapter) produces systematically swapped or inverted outputs compared to directly invoking the lower-level producer/constructor because it passes positional arguments in the wrong order or swaps boolean/flag parameters when invoking the producer. Observability: the producer implementation appears to construct correct values for given inputs, but using the public wrapper yields reversed semantics (e.g., foreground/background swapped, flag behavior inverted). Structural applicability: a thin wrapper or re-export immediately forwards arguments to a producer (positional or positional-mixed calls), or the project has recently changed producer parameter ordering or names.

skill.title: Caller forwards wrong argument index or swaps flag/argument values when invoking a lower-level producer/factory
knowledge: Locate both sides of the boundary: find the registration/consumer site that calls the factory and the factory/producer implementation that interprets the forwarded parameter (grep for registrations that pass integers/indices or boolean flags).

Trace parameter flow for numeric index/flag parameters: follow where a numeric index (e.g., affine_arg_index) originates and verify that the factory uses the same convention (0-based vs 1-based, meaning of the index vs expecting a tensor/None).

Compare the caller's invocation against the producer's declared signature and semantics. Prefer inspecting calls that use positional forwarding, numeric indices, or bare booleans—these are high-risk spots for silent misinterpretation.

Reproduce with focused tests that toggle the suspect flag/index: assert that behavior (e.g., FLOP totals, formatting, on/off features) changes when the flag or attribute is toggled; write a small test that calls the producer directly and via the wrapper/registry to pinpoint which side misinterprets the value.

Check for factories that ignore the passed parameter or replace it with a hard-coded access pattern (e.g., using inputs[1] instead of inputs[affine_arg_index]) — both mistaken interpretation and ignored parameters produce similar symptoms.

If a factory expects an attribute (weight/bias) rather than an index, prefer checking presence/shape (get_shape(inputs[i])) at the producer rather than relying solely on a caller-supplied index. Consider defensive assertions in the factory to validate incoming indices or flags.
When possible, replace positional or numeric-index-based contracts with explicit keyword arguments or small descriptor objects to make intent explicit and reduce fragility across modules.

When refactoring or registering handlers, add unit tests that exercise boundary cases (e.g., affine=True/False, missing optional inputs) and tests that call both the low-level producer and the public wrapper/registry entry to ensure parity.
skill.trigger: A consumer/registry that constructs or registers a handler/factory passes a positional argument, numeric index, or flag that the lower-level producer/factory interprets as enabling or disabling behavior (e.g., detecting an 'affine' transform). Observable: a computed result (metric, FLOP count, formatted output, etc.) is insensitive to toggling an obvious input flag or yields inverted semantics. Structural applicability: a thin wrapper, registry, or adapter immediately forwards positional args or numeric indices to a producer/factory (including numeric 'index' parameters), or the project uses factories that expect positional/indexed parameters rather than explicit named attributes.

skill.title: Conan repository architecture
knowledge: The top-level conan package (conan/__init__.py) exposes core model types and version metadata: ConanFile, Workspace, Version and the __version__/conan_version values used to identify the runtime version.

conan/api/conan_api.py implements the high-level ConanAPI object that initializes environment, configuration, migration, home/cache paths, and constructs the suite of sub-APIs (e.g., CacheAPI, CommandAPI, LocalAPI, LockfileAPI, WorkspaceAPI, ConfigAPI, InstallAPI, GraphAPI, etc.) which implement the repository's domain operations.

The CLI layer (conan/cli/cli.py) is responsible for parsing user arguments, discovering and loading built-in and external command modules, mapping them into ConanSubCommand wrappers, and dispatching execution through a ConanAPI instance while managing help, errors, and exit codes.

Domain behavior is implemented in conan/api/subapi/* (install, export, remotes, lockfile, list, upload, etc.); those sub-APIs orchestrate lower-level implementation modules under conan/internal and some legacy conans.client components (for example, conan/api/subapi/install.py delegates to conan.internal.api.install.generators and conans.client.graph.install_graph).

skill.title: Configuration- or platform-gated emission removed from producer so expected metadata/property is omitted
knowledge: Compare the failing generator/template with a sibling or earlier commit that still emits the metadata to see what local variables or property getters controlled the emission (e.g., 'is_win', 'auto_link', feature flags).

Search the template/renderer source for property-getter calls and local booleans used immediately before the emission block (patterns: get_property(...), settings.get_safe(...), local 'is_<platform>' checks). Verify those values are still computed and passed into the template context.

Inspect template strings/blocks for conditional sections that append or set the property; look for removed/edited branches such as {% if set_interface_link_directories %} ... {% endif %} or equivalent. Diffs that delete only that conditional block are a strong signal.

Check for removal of variable initialization (assignment of the guarding flag) or removal of the flag from the template render context (the context dict no longer contains the key used by the template).

Search version control diffs/hunk deletions around the template and its producer for deleted lines that compute flags or the conditional emission (deleted lines often include the flag name or the emitted property name).

Reproduce with a minimal package that exercises the guarded path (e.g., a package with empty link-libs to trigger auto-link behavior) and inspect the generated file; use that to correlate which branch should have emitted the metadata.

If emission was intentionally gated, confirm the gate's default or configuration source (settings, options, global config). Consider restoring the guard and defaulting it to the previous behavior or making the gate explicit and documented.

Add unit/integration tests asserting presence of generated metadata for the expected configuration/platform combinations to prevent regressions (for template producers, test both context keys and rendered output).
skill.trigger: A producer (generator/template/renderer) produces generated output (files/target blocks) that omits an expected metadata/property (e.g., INTERFACE_LINK_DIRECTORIES) while a sibling implementation includes it. The structural sign is that emission was previously behind a computed local flag or platform check (constructor/local value or property getter) and the generated output now lacks the conditional block or its guarding variables.

The test-runner entrypoint implementation is sunpy/tests/self_test.py (function self_test(...)); callers of the package-level self_test are dispatched to that module.

skill.title: Resource-resolution guard ordering invokes remote fetch before checking local/bundled resource
knowledge: Locate the resolver function/property and the exact sequence: (1) construction of local/bundled path or resource handle, (2) any os.path.exists/open calls, (3) calls into download/cache helpers. Confirm that local existence checks or direct open attempts occur before any network/download invocation.

Search the codebase for direct download or cache-fetch calls (e.g., download_file, requests.get, cache.get_or_fetch) near resource resolution sites. If a download call appears before a local-check, the guard ordering is suspect.

Inspect try/except and fallback blocks: ensure the primary (fast/local) path is tried first and only on local-failure (FileNotFoundError, os.path.exists False) is the remote path invoked. Beware try that wraps the remote call and then 'falls back' to local — that inverts the intended precedence.

Check for side-effects that force the remote path earlier than expected: property getters evaluated at import-time, memoization decorators that call the fetcher on first access, or cache initializers that trigger network access while computing keys. Prefer lazy evaluation and explicit local checks before invoking such wrappers.

Prefer explicit local-open attempts (open/local_file) or importlib.resources/pkgutil.get_data for bundled resources rather than os.path.exists+download anti-patterns; using an attempt-to-open pattern (try: open local; except FileNotFoundError: download) avoids race/TOCTOU concerns and documents intent.

If the code uses a cache helper with cache=True semantics, inspect whether the helper itself triggers a download on cache-miss. If so, ensure callers check local packaged locations before calling the cache helper or provide a cache API variant that only reads local caches.

Add unit tests that simulate offline/no-network conditions (monkeypatch network layer to raise) and assert that the resolver returns the packaged/local resource. Also test the remote-path behavior when local resource is absent so the fallback remains covered.

When fixing, move the local-existence guard or open attempt to precede any remote/caching call, or restructure as: try open local → return; else try download → cache → return. Add a short comment explaining precedence (local authoritative), and add logging that records which branch was used for easier future diagnostics.

If multiple resource locations exist (package data, user cache, remote), normalize resolution ordering into a small, documented decision sequence (e.g., packaged → user-cache → remote) to avoid accidental reordering in later refactors.

When changing code that affects packaged-data lookup, prefer using importlib.resources or the project’s established packaged-data API rather than manual path manipulation, to avoid platform/path pitfalls that made local checks fail silently.
skill.trigger: A resource-resolver or producer (function/property that returns a file/resource) attempts a remote fetch, download, or cached-fetch API call before verifying the presence of a local or bundled resource (state owner: package data directory, local cache, or embedded resource). Observable symptoms include network errors (URLError, timeout), unnecessary remote traffic, or exceptions when offline despite a local file existing; the structural applicability is resolver code that composes a local path or bundled-data lookup and also calls a network/caching helper or download API.

skill.title: Paramiko (Python SSH library) - repository orientation
knowledge: paramiko/transport.py owns the SSH transport layer: it defines the Transport thread/class that performs handshake/KEX, negotiates ciphers/MACs, manages encryption state, and drives channel lifecycle; it dispatches to kex_* modules and uses packet.py/message.py for framing and channel.py for channel management.

paramiko/client.py provides the high-level SSHClient API and is the public entry point for initiating connections; SSHClient constructs and interacts with Transport and relies on auth_handler.py and auth_strategy.py to negotiate and perform authentication before channels/sessions are opened.

paramiko/channel.py together with packet.py and message.py implement channel multiplexing and message framing; higher-level subsystems such as the SFTP implementation (paramiko/sftp_client.py, paramiko/sftp_server.py, paramiko/sftp_file.py, paramiko/sftp_handle.py, etc.) run on top of channels/transport rather than implementing their own transport.

Key handling is encapsulated in dedicated modules (paramiko/rsakey.py, paramiko/dsskey.py, paramiko/ecdsakey.py, paramiko/ed25519key.py and paramiko/hostkeys.py); these modules parse, load, and perform public/private key operations and are used by the authentication and host-key verification code paths.

skill.title: Probe/dispatch then class-specific deserializer mismatch (wrong class or mutated bytes)
knowledge: Reproduce minimally: create a small fixture of the original raw file/blob and run both the probe-only detection path and the class-specific parser path; compute and compare simple invariants (length, SHA-1/MD5 hash, byte-prefix) of the bytes seen by each step.

Check dispatch logic in the probe/producer: confirm how key/class is chosen (string literals, isinstance checks, cryptography.load_* helpers). Ensure the chosen class matches the expected key type for the blob and that no fallthrough or mistaken literal (e.g., 'RSA' vs 'DSA') is used.

Verify how bytes are passed to the class parser: is the file reopened and read again, is a file object repositioned, or are bytes passed directly? If reopening, confirm the reopened read returns identical bytes; if reusing a file_obj, check for file-pointer at EOF or partial reads.

Detect accidental mutations in consumer code: search for explicit byte/sequence operations (slicing, reversing like [::-1], encoding/decoding applied twice, in-place transforms) and for mistaken assignments that swap operands when calling decode/parse helpers.

Validate PEM/ASN.1 handling expectations: ensure the consumer expects the same raw format the probe used (PEM vs OpenSSH vs DER). Check that base64 decoding, header/footer stripping, and decryption steps are applied exactly once and in the correct order.

Instrument and log at the probe and consumer boundary: record which key_class was selected, the exact bytes (or their length and hash), and which parsing branch was taken. These diagnostics quickly reveal mismatched class selection or byte mutation.

If the producer and consumer are both available, prefer a single canonical read: read the raw bytes once, compute a detection result, then pass an immutable copy of the raw bytes to the class-specific parser to avoid file-pointer and reopen inconsistencies.

Add unit tests that include golden blobs for each supported format: test detection-only, consumer-only, and end-to-end loading paths. Include assertions that the raw-bytes seen by both steps are identical and that the selected class matches the known-good type.
When changing behavior, include clear error messages on dispatch failures (e.g., 'detected type X but dispatched to Y') to make future regressions in selection or parsing visible in logs/tests.
skill.trigger: A loader first probes a raw blob to determine a target class and then re-opens or re-parses the same raw bytes with the chosen class-specific parser. Observable failure: callers attempting to load keys/objects of type X raise classification or parsing/decoding exceptions, or the decoded payload differs from the original bytes (e.g., corrupted, reversed, truncated, or interpreted with the wrong format branch). Applicable when code separates type-detection/dispatch from a subsequent class-specific parse on the same input blob.

skill.title: Radon CLI and metric responsibilities
knowledge: The package exposes a main CLI entrypoint (radon.__init__.main and radon.__main__) that delegates to the command dispatcher defined in radon.cli (which uses mando.Program for subcommand dispatch).

radon/cli implements the public CLI commands (cc, raw, mi, hal, etc.). Those command handlers build a Config/FileConfig and instantiate Harvester classes (defined in radon/cli/harvest.py, e.g., CCHarvester, RawHarvester, MIHarvester, HCHarvester) which are responsible for collecting metrics from paths and producing various output forms (to_terminal, as_json, as_xml, as_md, as_codeclimate_issues).

Configuration loading is centralized in the CLI config component (radon/cli.FileConfig and related Config helpers): it attempts to read pyproject.toml via tomllib/tomli when present and falls back to radon.cfg / setup.cfg (INI-style) and user config; CLI commands rely on these to produce typed config values.

Numeric metric calculation is implemented in the radon modules (radon.complexity, radon.metrics, radon.raw, radon.visitors). CLI harvesters call into these metric modules to compute values, then formatting and output utilities (radon/cli/log_result, radon/cli/tools, radon/cli/colors) handle presentation and error logging.

skill.title: Exporter/serializer method returns a placeholder/default value instead of signalling unsupported functionality
knowledge: Search for exporter/serializer method names in the codebase (common patterns: as_xml, as_md, as_json, to_xxx, format_xxx) and inspect their bodies for explicit literal returns (strings, empty containers) or 'pass'/'return' that could mask unsupported behavior.
Grep for suspicious literal tokens like 'Placeholder', '', '<xml>', or other sentinel strings that might have been introduced as temporary scaffolding.

Look for recent edits via git blame/diff on the suspect methods to detect changes replacing 'raise NotImplementedError' (or other exceptions) with 'return <literal>' or early returns; accidental edits often stand out in history.

Confirm the contract by reading docstrings/tests/call sites: find callers that expect an exception (try/except) or code paths that rely on failure signaling; write a small reproducer that calls the exporter and asserts the expected exception is raised.

When multiple exporter methods fail (e.g., as_xml and as_md), search for shared helper functions or shared rendering pipelines. If absent, treat each exporter as an independent producer; if present, inspect the shared helper for placeholder/default returns.

Inspect nearby formatting helpers for subtle logic regressions that cause malformed outputs: reversed iteration or reversed results.items() will change ordering; swapped variable order when composing names (e.g., raw_name/raw_classname) will swap columns; using indexing vs .get can raise KeyError or return unexpected values—prefer .get with explicit defaults where appropriate.

Check mappings and lookups (e.g., type_letter_map[block['type']]) and prefer .get(key, default) to avoid KeyError and to make defaults explicit; verify default semantics (e.g., 'U' or 'N/A') match callers' expectations.

Run or extend unit tests to cover negative/unsupported paths: assert that unsupported-export calls raise the documented exception; add snapshot tests for serialization to catch column ordering/field swaps.

If repairing, restore the documented/expected behavior (reintroduce raise NotImplementedError with the original message) or explicitly update the API/documentation and callers to accept the new sentinel behavior (prefer the former for backward compatibility). For serializer composition bugs, correct loop order (remove unintended reversed()) and fix variable placement when building composed names/columns.

Add a short comment or docstring near exporter methods documenting the expected behavior for unsupported formats and the response type (exception vs sentinel value) to prevent future accidental replacements.
skill.trigger: A consumer calling an exporter/serializer method (producer role) observes a literal placeholder or default value returned (e.g., '<xml>Placeholder</xml>', empty string, empty list/dict) where the API contract, documentation, or callers expect an exception (NotImplementedError or similar) to indicate an unsupported format. Applicable when the project defines exporter/serializer methods (as_xml/as_md/as_json or similar) or formatting helpers and the method body contains an explicit literal return, early return, default value, or a no-op that would mask an unsupported-path exception.

skill.title: Graphene repository architecture
knowledge: graphene.types.schema.Schema (defined in graphene/types/schema.py) is the primary entry point that composes a graphql-core GraphQLSchema and exposes execution/inspection entrypoints (sync and async execute/subscribe and introspection).

graphene.types.schema.TypeMap (in graphene/types/schema.py) is the central registry/factory that builds and caches graphql-core GraphQLType objects from Graphene type classes and performs type lookup used during schema construction.

Graphene type classes under graphene/types (e.g., ObjectType, Interface, Union, Enum, InputObjectType and scalar helpers) carry metadata (via _meta) and field/argument definitions that TypeMap reads to construct GraphQL types and wire resolvers.

Relay-related responsibilities live under graphene/relay (e.g., graphene/relay/node.py, graphene/relay/connection.py); relay node, connection, and global id behavior are implemented there and integrated into the schema/type system via the TypeMap/Schema construction.

skill.title: Container-type stringification uses incorrect delimiter tokens
knowledge: Reproduce the symptom with a minimal example that constructs the container type and prints or introspects it (e.g., List(String) and print(str(list_type))). Confirm the exact characters observed and the expected canonical notation.

Grepping/search: locate per-type formatting functions (__str__, __repr__, to_string, render) on container-type classes and any shared representation helpers or base-class renderers (e.g., Structure.__str__, format_helpers, representation utilities).

Inspect the container class (producer/constructor) implementation: if it defines its own __str__/__repr__, check the body for literal delimiter tokens or format strings (look for '[' ']' '(' ')' in f-strings, format calls, or string concatenation). A single-character mistake here explains the symptom.

If the container class delegates to a shared renderer, open that helper and examine how it composes prefix/suffix delimiters and how it obtains the element representation (ensuring the helper uses the right pair for lists vs tuples or other container kinds).

Trace how the element representation is retrieved (call to of_type.__str__ or similar) and whether that call is wrapped by delimiters in the same function; ensure delimiter insertion is not accidentally using tuple/parenthesis syntax or language-specific tuple notation.
Search for copy-paste or refactor mistakes: delimiter tokens are often constants; check surrounding types (e.g., Tuple, NonNull, Option) to see if a wrong delimiter was reused by mistake.

Check tests and schema-introspection output: add or update unit tests that assert canonical string forms for container types (use distinct sentinel element names to avoid accidental matches) to prevent regressions.

When applying a fix, prefer using named constants or small helper functions for delimiter pairs (e.g., LIST_DELIMITERS = ('[', ']')) and colocate the delimiter selection with the container type so future renames/refactors don't interchange delimiter pairs.

If multiple containers share a renderer, consider making delimiter selection an explicit parameter (container_kind) rather than implicit assumptions, and add tests for each container-kind to lock expected behavior.
After patching, run a quick repository-wide search for the old delimiter tokens in representation code to detect other instances of the same slip (use both single- and double-quoted forms).
skill.trigger: A consumer (for example, a __str__/__repr__ method, renderer, or schema-introspection formatter) emits container-type values with wrong surrounding delimiter characters (e.g., prints '(T)' when the canonical notation is '[T]'). Applicable when the project exposes container/value classes (constructors or type objects) that either implement per-type formatting methods or rely on a shared representation helper that composes delimiters around element renderings.
